experiences.title: Django GROUP BY default-ordering semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django ORM task concerns `QuerySet.ordered` disagreeing with SQL for annotated aggregate/GROUP BY querysets on models with `Meta.ordering`.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django codebase when the visible task or trajectory shows a mismatch between queryset ordering introspection and generated SQL: aggregate `annotate()` creates `GROUP BY`, `query.default_ordering` remains true, but default model ordering is not emitted as `ORDER BY`. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has reached investigation or implementation around `QuerySet.ordered`, `Query.group_by`, annotation aggregation, or SQL compiler ordering behavior. It can still be used early as a directional rubric if the task statement itself clearly names this semantic boundary, but it should not be used for unrelated ordering bugs, tasks that intentionally change SQL generation to preserve default ordering, backend-only syntax issues, or generic test/process evaluation without evidence about default-versus-explicit ordering.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the semantic distinction that determines correctness: `QuerySet.ordered` must reflect effective SQL ordering, not merely stored default-ordering metadata. A strong trajectory identifies that default `Meta.ordering` may be suppressed when a query has `GROUP BY`, so grouped aggregate querysets relying only on default ordering should report unordered. It must also preserve the opposite cases: explicit `order_by()` or extra ordering should still make a grouped queryset ordered, empty querysets should keep existing behavior, and normal non-grouped querysets with default ordering should remain ordered. This criterion aligned well because visible evidence often showed either decisive progress—reproduction of SQL without `ORDER BY`, inspection of compiler logic that drops meta ordering under grouping, and a minimal `ordered` change gated by `group_by`—or decisive non-progress, such as repeatedly grepping the same line without inspecting compiler behavior or applying a patch. Avoid generating a broader or misleading rubric that rewards only finding `default_ordering`, clearing `default_ordering` inside `annotate()`, treating every grouped query as unordered, or requiring a specific test-runner command. Prioritize evidence that the agent understands the owner boundary between metadata (`default_ordering`/`Meta.ordering`) and emitted SQL, and that any implementation preserves explicit ordering paths.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Effective ordering under GROUP BY
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should correctly drive toward Django ORM `QuerySet.ordered` semantics for grouped aggregate queries: default model ordering should count as ordered only when it will actually be emitted in SQL, so a GROUP BY/aggregate queryset relying solely on `Meta.ordering` should report unordered, while explicit `order_by()`/extra ordering, empty querysets, and ordinary non-grouped default-ordered querysets continue to report ordered. Judge from visible investigation, implementation intent, code edits, reproductions, and tests; do not require a particular patch shape, but require the explicit-vs-default ordering boundary to be preserved.

task_signals: annotate() with aggregate creates GROUP BY
generated SQL lacks ORDER BY despite ordered property being true
high_value_evidence: Inspects or explains SQL compiler behavior that suppresses Meta.ordering for grouped queries
Uses query grouping state as a condition for default-ordering truth
Separates explicit order_by/extra_order_by from implicit Meta.ordering
Validates or plans regression coverage for grouped aggregate, explicit ordering, and non-grouped default ordering cases
anti_evidence: Relies only on query.default_ordering as proof of actual ordering
Clears default ordering globally during annotation without preserving existing behavior
Marks all GROUP BY querysets unordered even when explicitly ordered
Repeats source searches without inspecting compiler/query behavior or making progress

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands the GROUP BY/default-ordering mismatch; it may only repeat searches, inspect unrelated files, or focus on metadata such as default_ordering without connecting it to emitted SQL.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory locates `QuerySet.ordered` or aggregate grouping but has not established that default `Meta.ordering` is suppressed for GROUP BY or has not distinguished default ordering from explicit ordering.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent trajectory: the trajectory identifies the likely mismatch between grouped queries and default ordering, but implementation or validation is incomplete or may miss key preservation cases.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory reproduces or explains SQL without `ORDER BY`, ties it to GROUP BY and default `Meta.ordering`, and proposes or applies a minimal `QuerySet.ordered` change while preserving explicit ordering and ordinary default ordering.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to the correct semantic fix, the trajectory validates the important boundary cases with targeted checks or regression tests: grouped aggregate with only default ordering is unordered; grouped aggregate with explicit/extra ordering is ordered; empty and non-grouped default-ordered querysets retain existing behavior.

experiences.title: Do not treat same-looking multi-backend edits as correctness evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a Node.js database-abstraction task that spans Redis/Mongo/PostgreSQL-style adapters and the trajectory shows similar methods being added across adapters, especially before export placement, public API shape, and tests are verified.
experiences.context: This applies in Node.js/NodeBB-like repositories where database adapter submodules mutate a passed adapter object inside an exported factory function. A cross-database parity rubric is tempting because the task explicitly requires support across multiple backends. However, if the visible trajectory mainly shows parallel code added to all adapters, unverified method names/signatures, direct scripts failing to bootstrap the app, methods appended near or after factory closures, malformed tests, or no evidence that the new method is exposed through the selected database module, then a generic “multi-database consistency” criterion can overvalue superficial symmetry. Backend parity remains a useful criterion later, but only after there is visible evidence that the API is attached in the correct scope, follows existing bulk-operation conventions, preserves existing methods, and is exercised through the repository’s real test/bootstrap path.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded consistent implementation across Redis, MongoDB, and PostgreSQL. That idea is directionally relevant, but it was misleading as a standalone criterion because agents often made the same high-level edit in every backend while missing more decisive integration requirements: placing methods outside the adapter factory so they are not exported, choosing an unverified public method name or input shape, relying on ad hoc scripts that did not initialize the test environment, corrupting tests, or rewriting broad portions of hash modules. In these situations, the fact that all adapters have similar code is not strong evidence; it may simply mean the same bug was copied three times. A better rubric should focus on visible proof that the new bulk increment API is actually registered on each backend adapter, follows the repository’s existing bulk data shape and increment semantics, invalidates object caches where applicable, preserves existing hash behavior, and is validated through the project’s database test harness. Avoid the tempting criterion “all supported adapters have equivalent code” unless it is conditioned on export/API verification and tested behavior. Replacement criteria should prioritize observations such as raw adapter export checks, placement inside the adapter module factory, targeted syntax/test runs, cache invalidation for touched keys, and read-after-write assertions for missing objects/fields.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial backend parity without adapter integration proof
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that present a multi-backend bulk database feature as complete mainly because similar code was added to each backend, while visible evidence shows the new API may not be correctly attached to the adapter object, may not match existing public API conventions, or has not been validated through the repository's real database test harness. This flaw is especially important when the codebase uses factory-style adapter modules where method placement determines whether the API is exported.

metadata.environment: Node.js database abstraction with Redis, MongoDB, and PostgreSQL adapters loaded by mutating a passed backend module object
prioritize_evidence: new method assignment occurs inside the adapter factory/module body rather than after its closing brace
method is discoverable on the configured database adapter or raw backend module
public method name and input shape are justified by existing bulk and increment APIs
targeted tests run under the project's database mock/bootstrap rather than unsupported direct scripts
read-after-write tests cover multiple objects, multiple fields per object, missing objects/fields, and cache invalidation behavior
avoid_overvaluing: grep evidence that a method name exists in files
full test runs that do not exercise the new API
ad hoc scripts that fail or bypass normal database initialization

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory shows the new API is attached in the correct adapter scope, follows existing API conventions, and is validated through appropriate database tests or explicit adapter export checks.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent has mostly correct integration evidence but one backend or test path still needs light confirmation, with no sign of copied scope/API mistakes.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: similar code exists across backends, but export verification, API-shape justification, or real test coverage is incomplete, making cross-backend parity uncertain.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory shows copied backend edits with unresolved placement/export issues, unsupported test scripts, malformed tests, or unverified public API naming despite claims of parity.
scale.5: Severe evidence: multiple backends contain method definitions in the wrong scope or otherwise not exposed, tests are absent or syntactically broken, and the trajectory relies on superficial similarity across adapters as the main correctness signal.

experiences.title: Do not reward “already fixed” conclusions from mismatched non-reproduction
experiences.description: Retrieve when a trajectory for a version- or dependency-sensitive bug reports that the MVCE passes locally, especially after changing dependencies or applying environment workarounds, and the generated rubric is tempted to praise no-op resolution.
experiences.context: Applies in Python library debugging tasks involving dependency-sensitive behavior such as dtype preservation through pandas/numpy-backed indexing, where the user reports a concrete failing environment but the agent tests on a newer checkout, different pandas/numpy versions, or after temporary compatibility edits. In this setting, a local passing MVCE is weak evidence that the requested patch is unnecessary. The original idea of verifying reproduction is still useful when the agent has matched the reported environment or supported test matrix, has a clean working tree, has located existing regression coverage, and can justify that no code change is needed. It is misleading when the trajectory shows dependency drift, temporary source edits only to make imports work, repeated history searches, or no targeted fix/regression despite a precise acceptance condition.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster praised the agent for deciding that the bug was already fixed or that no change was needed because the MVCE returned true locally. That criterion is wrong when the visible trajectory itself shows the reproduction environment differs from the report, the checkout is newer than the affected release, or the agent made unrelated compatibility edits to run the code. In such cases, non-reproduction does not validate final patch correctness; it can lead to an empty patch or an unrelated dependency-compatibility patch while leaving the reported contract unaddressed. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent treats the passing local MVCE as inconclusive, preserves or restores a clean task-focused working tree, and advances toward the semantic contract: stacked MultiIndex level coordinates must expose values using the original coordinate dtype rather than a dependency-promoted dtype. Avoid the tempting criterion “correctly conclude the issue is already fixed/no action needed” unless there is visible evidence of matched environment validation plus existing adequate regression coverage. Replacement criteria should prioritize evidence such as testing under relevant dependency versions, adding a focused regression for the reported dtype-preservation scenario, inspecting the abstraction boundary where pandas MultiIndex level values are materialized as array-like coordinate data, and ensuring any code change targets that boundary rather than unrelated import compatibility.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overconfident no-op from inconclusive non-reproduction
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat a locally passing reproduction as proof that a reported dependency/version-sensitive dtype bug is already resolved, when the visible evidence shows the local environment or checkout differs from the report and the agent has not produced a targeted regression test or task-specific fix for preserving the source coordinate dtype through stacked MultiIndex level materialization.

metadata.task_type: Python data-library bug involving dtype preservation through stack/MultiIndex/index adapter behavior
misleading_evidence: MVCE passes only in a different dependency combination or newer checkout
temporary compatibility edits were made only to run imports
agent repeatedly searches history or reruns the same passing MVCE
no task-specific regression test or semantic code change is present
preferred_evidence: validation under the reported or supported dependency range
focused regression asserting original coordinate dtype is preserved after stacking
inspection or modification of the layer that materializes MultiIndex level values as coordinate arrays
clean separation between environment workarounds and the requested bug fix

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the agent either reproduces under relevant conditions or explicitly treats non-reproduction as inconclusive while making targeted progress toward a regression or dtype-preservation fix.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent notes the local pass but still acknowledges dependency/check-out mismatch and avoids concluding no action is needed.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent relies partly on local non-reproduction and delays targeted work, but visible notes still identify the mismatch and likely dtype-preservation boundary.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent concludes or strongly implies the bug is already fixed/no patch is needed based mainly on a passing local MVCE despite mismatched environment or temporary import workarounds.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the agent finalizes an empty or unrelated patch while asserting the reported bug is fixed, without matched-environment validation, focused regression coverage, or a task-specific change addressing dtype preservation.

experiences.title: Django grouped queryset default-ordering suppression
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django ORM task concerns `QuerySet.ordered` disagreeing with generated SQL for annotated/aggregate `GROUP BY` queries on models with `Meta.ordering`.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source tree when the visible task and trajectory involve the `QuerySet.ordered` property, aggregate annotations or `values().annotate()` causing `query.group_by`, and the distinction between model default ordering and explicit `order_by()`. The criterion is most useful after the agent has at least located `QuerySet.ordered` or investigated SQL compiler/query ordering behavior; it can still flag early trajectories that are only repeating searches without understanding the semantic boundary. Do not apply broadly to unrelated ordering bugs, to SQL generation changes where the desired fix is to preserve `ORDER BY`, or to cases where ordering is explicit via `order_by()`/`extra_order_by` rather than coming only from `Meta.ordering`.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the specific semantic contract: grouped aggregate querysets should not be considered ordered solely because `query.default_ordering` and model `Meta.ordering` are true, since Django’s compiler suppresses default/meta ordering when emitting `GROUP BY`; however explicit ordering must still make the queryset ordered. This criterion aligned well because visible trajectories that inspected compiler behavior, reproduced `group_by` with no SQL `ORDER BY`, or patched the default-ordering branch of `QuerySet.ordered` had decisive evidence of likely correctness, while trajectories stuck repeating greps lacked such evidence. A better rubric should not merely reward finding `default_ordering` or `group_by` strings; it should require recognizing the interaction among `query.group_by`, default `Meta.ordering`, and explicit ordering preservation. Avoid tempting but wrong criteria such as “all annotated queries are unordered,” “set `default_ordering` to false during annotation,” or “tests passed” without checking the behavioral boundary. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent compared `.ordered` with actual SQL, identified that compiler suppression applies only to meta/default ordering, and implemented or planned a minimal change in the introspection property rather than altering unrelated SQL generation.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Default meta ordering suppressed by GROUP BY
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Rewards trajectories that correctly handle Django grouped queryset ordering introspection: `QuerySet.ordered` should return false when a queryset has `GROUP BY` from aggregate annotation/values grouping and its only possible ordering is model `Meta.ordering`, because the compiled SQL omits that default `ORDER BY`; explicit `order_by()` or `extra_order_by`, non-grouped default-ordered querysets, and empty querysets should retain their existing ordered behavior.

key_state: query.group_by is truthy for aggregate/grouped querysets
query.default_ordering can remain true despite SQL lacking ORDER BY
query.order_by or query.extra_order_by indicates explicit ordering that should remain ordered
preferred_visible_evidence: inspection or reproduction showing compiler drops Meta.ordering for GROUP BY SQL
manual or formal checks comparing .ordered and generated SQL
patch or plan that adds a not-grouped condition only to the default Meta.ordering path
boundaries: do not mark explicit order_by grouped querysets unordered
do not require changing SQL compilation to add ORDER BY
do not treat repeated grep output as sufficient understanding

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands or addresses the grouped-query/default-ordering mismatch; it may only repeat searches or discuss ordering generically.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory locates `QuerySet.ordered`, `default_ordering`, or `group_by`, but does not connect grouped aggregate queries to suppression of default `Meta.ordering` in emitted SQL.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies that aggregate annotations create `GROUP BY` and that `.ordered` can disagree with SQL, but the proposed fix or investigation is incomplete or risks treating explicit ordering/default ordering incorrectly.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory clearly distinguishes default `Meta.ordering` from explicit ordering and proposes or applies a targeted `QuerySet.ordered` change so grouped queries relying only on defaults are unordered.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory demonstrates the compiler/introspection mismatch with SQL or tests, applies a minimal fix in the default-ordering branch, preserves explicit and non-grouped ordering behavior, and validates relevant regression cases.

experiences.title: Runtime-specific regression requires exact change-to-code-path tracing
experiences.description: Retrieve when a bug report explicitly ties behavior to a particular language/runtime version or linked changelog, especially in library compatibility issues where the local environment differs from the report.
experiences.context: Applies to Python/library maintenance tasks where the user reports a regression only on a specific CPython version and cites runtime release notes, while the trajectory is investigating proxy/auth/network behavior or another boundary delegated to stdlib/dependencies. It is most useful during diagnosis or final review before accepting a speculative patch. It is less useful when the task has no version-specific signal, when the trajectory has already isolated and tested the concrete compatibility invariant, or when the remaining issue is purely local refactoring unrelated to runtime/dependency behavior.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics correctly emphasized version-specific investigation because the visible trajectories often stayed on generic proxy-auth mechanics, installed or tested under mismatched local dependencies and Python versions, repeated irrelevant checks, or patched nearby code without tying the change to the reported CPython behavior. For similar cases, generate a rubric that rewards tracing the reported runtime change to the exact affected library boundary: which stdlib/dependency API changed, how the project uses it, what invariant is broken, and how the proposed fix preserves behavior across versions. The criterion should not merely demand searching for version guards or adding `sys.version_info` conditionals; compatibility fixes often should be version-agnostic. Also avoid rewarding superficial evidence such as confirming auth headers are constructed in isolation, testing only on the current interpreter, or adding proxy credentials to ordinary request headers where they could leak to the destination. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent noticed the environment mismatch, consulted or reconstructed the target-version behavior, mapped it to the URL/proxy normalization or CONNECT/auth transmission path, and planned or added a deterministic regression test using mocks/local simulation instead of relying on an unavailable external proxy.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact runtime-change compatibility analysis
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a bug explicitly reported only on a specific runtime version with a linked changelog, the trajectory should identify the concrete runtime or dependency behavior change, connect it to the project code path that can drop or misroute authentication data, account for any mismatch between the reported stack and the local test environment, and validate the fix with a targeted simulation or regression test that preserves compatibility and credential-routing safety.

required_visible_evidence: acknowledges the specific reported runtime/dependency versions and any local mismatch
consults or reconstructs the relevant runtime/dependency behavior change rather than relying on generic proxy-auth assumptions
maps the change to the library boundary where URL/proxy/auth data is transformed or transmitted
uses a deterministic test, mock, or local simulation appropriate when the exact runtime or external service is unavailable
checks that proxy credentials remain available to the proxy path without being leaked to the destination request
anti_evidence: only checks the current interpreter version or installs unrelated latest dependencies
repeats generic proxy-header or tunneling checks without using the reported version change
patches an unrelated nearby path such as chunked upload or generic auth parsing without showing relevance to the user repro
suggests runtime version guards as the main fix without proving they are necessary
adds proxy authorization as an ordinary request header for tunneled requests without considering credential leakage
metadata.applicable_stage: diagnosis, patch planning, or final review for explicit runtime-version regressions

scale.1: No meaningful version-specific analysis; the trajectory ignores the reported runtime/changelog or only performs generic repository exploration.
scale.2: Mentions the runtime version but tests or reasons only under a mismatched local environment, with little connection to the affected code path.
scale.3: Investigates relevant proxy/auth or dependency code paths but does not clearly identify the concrete runtime behavior change or validate it.
scale.4: Clearly identifies a plausible runtime/dependency behavior change, maps it to the relevant project boundary, and proposes a targeted compatibility test or simulation.
scale.5: Strongly traces the exact reported behavior through the project and dependency/stdlib boundary, accounts for environment mismatch, and validates a credential-safe, cross-version fix with focused regression evidence.

experiences.title: Do not reward label-decoding intent without visible local patch evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve when a scikit-learn trajectory for HistGradientBoosting early-stopping target encoding shows investigation, planned decoding, or tests against a different installed sklearn, but the current local source diff is not clearly verified or the agent may be drifting to unrelated files.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/scikit-learn source-tree tasks where the reported bug is a target-representation mismatch during scorer-based early stopping: classifier targets are internally encoded, while predictions/scorers operate on original class labels. The label-decoding idea is a valid semantic target when the trajectory is at final-review stage and the visible local diff shows the scorer path decoding both training-subset and validation targets while preserving loss/regressor behavior. It is misleading when the visible trajectory is still early exploration, only states the intended fix, relies on successful runs from a separately installed sklearn wheel, cannot import the local checkout, or later edits unrelated model-selection/build files. In those situations, a rubric that only asks for “decode labels before scoring” can over-credit understanding or stale summaries and miss whether the final patch is actually in the right local code path.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster correctly identified the central semantic fix: scorer-based early stopping for classifiers should pass targets in the same label space as predictions, without changing loss-based scoring or regressors. The problem was that the criterion was too solution-shaped and too broad for the visible stage of the trajectories. It gave partial or high credit to trajectories that merely reasoned about the fix, had unverified/truncated source edits, ran reproductions against an installed modern sklearn instead of the checkout under repair, or later drifted into unrelated files. For future rubric generation, keep the label-space criterion only when there is visible evidence of a current local edit in the early-stopping scorer path. Otherwise generate a stage-aware criterion that penalizes lack of verified local diff/current method inspection, reliance on the wrong installed package as validation, or unrelated final edits. Avoid the tempting criterion “agent understands it should decode y via classes_” as the main predictor; prioritize observable evidence: current diff or method body in the target scorer path, both train and validation scorer calls covered, loss/regressor paths left alone, and no unrelated changes replacing the intended fix.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unverified or Drifted Local Early-Stopping Fix
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for this scikit-learn early-stopping target-encoding bug when the visible work does not establish that the local source checkout currently contains the intended scorer-path fix, especially if the agent only describes the decoding idea, inspects truncated output, validates by running a separately installed sklearn version, cannot import/build the local package, or drifts into unrelated files instead of maintaining a focused change in the histogram gradient boosting early-stopping scorer logic.

metadata.task_family: scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting classifier early-stopping scorer target encoding
prioritize_visible_evidence: current local diff or full method inspection in the early-stopping scorer path
coverage of both training-subset and validation scorer targets
explicit preservation of loss-based scoring and regressor behavior
awareness that installed sklearn runs do not validate the patched checkout
absence of unrelated file changes as the only final work
avoid_overcrediting: plans or comments that mention decoding without a verified local edit
successful reproducer output from a different installed sklearn package
stale earlier-summary claims not confirmed by recent diff
broad environment/build exploration with no source change

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory shows a current, focused local source change in the early-stopping scorer path or is still explicitly in early exploration without claiming validation; no unrelated drift is visible.
scale.2: Minor concern: the agent has a plausible local edit or clear plan but has not fully inspected the current diff/method body, while avoiding misleading validation claims and unrelated edits.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory mainly demonstrates understanding of the label-decoding fix or has truncated/unverified edit evidence, and validation is blocked or ambiguous.
scale.4: Clear concern: the agent treats runs against an installed sklearn or stale summaries as validation of the local patch, or recent steps fail to confirm that both scorer targets are fixed in the local checkout.
scale.5: Severe concern: the visible or final-directed work has drifted to unrelated files or changes, or there is no verified local scorer-path edit despite claims that the bug has been fixed.

experiences.title: Transparent Wrapper GROUP BY Delegation
experiences.description: Use when a Django ORM expression wrapper changes GROUP BY behavior compared with the wrapped expression, especially when constants are grouped only after being wrapped.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source tree, primarily around ORM expression classes and `get_group_by_cols()` behavior, when the task or trajectory shows that a wrapper-like expression adds context such as an output field but should otherwise preserve the wrapped expression's SQL grouping semantics. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or reproduced the distinction between a bare constant expression and the same expression inside the wrapper, or has identified the base expression default that groups non-aggregate expressions by themselves. It is less applicable for unrelated SQL compiler bugs, backend-specific syntax workarounds, issues where the wrapped expression itself has wrong grouping behavior, or early exploration before the agent has found the expression classes and grouping API. During transient editing stages, judge the semantic direction and cleanliness separately: a temporary corrupted edit is a visible flaw, but the core criterion should remain about wrapper delegation rather than generic test-running progress.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, the useful rubric was the one requiring `ExpressionWrapper` to compute GROUP BY columns from its wrapped expression. This aligned with correct fixes because the observable root cause was that constants already know not to group themselves, while the wrapper inherited the default non-aggregate behavior and therefore grouped by the wrapper/literal. A good rubric should reward evidence that the agent found this semantic boundary: `Value.get_group_by_cols()` returns no columns, the base expression implementation returns the expression itself, and `ExpressionWrapper` is intended to be transparent except for context such as `output_field`. The preferred criterion should check for a clean delegation implementation on the wrapper, preserving constants as non-grouping while still allowing field, function, compound, and aggregate-containing expressions to contribute their normal grouping columns. It should also value validation by inspecting generated SQL or query group-by state for an annotate/values/aggregate query comparing wrapped and unwrapped constants. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as fixing PostgreSQL only, special-casing `Value` in query compilation, changing the constant expression class, merely installing dependencies or finding the test runner, or broadly demanding all tests pass without checking the wrapper semantics. Visible evidence to prioritize includes targeted inspection of expression grouping methods, a reproduction showing `GROUP BY ..., 3` only for the wrapped constant, a clean method added in the wrapper class rather than global or misplaced edits, forwarding/delegating the alias argument consistently, and regression checks that nonconstant wrapped expressions still group appropriately.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Wrapper Preserves Inner GROUP BY Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify that the wrapper is incorrectly using default expression GROUP BY behavior and should preserve the wrapped expression's own grouping contract. Strong evidence includes a clean implementation or well-supported plan for `ExpressionWrapper.get_group_by_cols()` to delegate to the inner expression, so wrapped constants contribute no GROUP BY columns while wrapped column-dependent, functional, compound, or aggregate expressions continue to contribute the columns their inner expressions require. The trajectory should avoid backend-specific hacks or changes to constant-expression behavior when the visible evidence shows the wrapper layer is the differentiator.

required_visible_evidence: Recognizes bare constants already omit themselves from GROUP BY
Recognizes the wrapper inherits default non-aggregate grouping unless overridden
Delegates wrapper group-by calculation to the wrapped/source expression
Checks that constants are omitted and nonconstant expressions still group normally
anti_patterns: Special-casing constants in the SQL compiler instead of preserving expression contracts
Changing Value behavior despite bare Value already working
Misplaced broad sed edits that add methods outside the wrapper class

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands expression GROUP BY semantics or the wrapper-vs-bare expression distinction.
scale.2: Identifies the reported GROUP BY symptom but focuses on generic SQL/backend behavior, constants broadly, or test setup without locating the wrapper grouping contract.
scale.3: Finds relevant expression classes and suspects wrapper delegation, but the plan or edit is incomplete, unvalidated, misplaced, or does not address preservation of nonconstant grouping behavior.
scale.4: Implements or clearly plans a wrapper-level `get_group_by_cols()` delegation and validates that wrapped constants no longer appear in GROUP BY, with some attention to nonconstant expressions or clean placement.
scale.5: Cleanly implements wrapper-level delegation to the wrapped expression, preserves alias/source-expression semantics, validates the annotate/values/aggregate regression for wrapped constants, and confirms column-dependent or compound wrapped expressions still group as required.

experiences.title: Alias-binding import contract for migration serialization
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django migration-generation task involves generated migration code referencing a framework alias such as `models.Model` without a corresponding import, especially from serialized model bases.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django repository trajectories where the agent is diagnosing migration writer/serializer import collection and the visible evidence shows generated migration text containing `models.Model` or another alias-qualified framework object. It is most useful after the agent has inspected serialization/import flow or reproduced generated migration output; it can still be a weaker early-stage criterion if the agent has found a serializer special case emitting the alias. Do not apply as a generic import-validity rubric when the generated expression does not actually use the alias, when default bases are omitted from output, or when the implementation changes the rendered expression to a fully qualified name with matching imports. Avoid using this criterion for unrelated migration failures where the issue is database state, app registry setup, or test-runner configuration rather than source-code import emission.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the exact contract between rendered migration source and collected imports: if serialization emits `models.Model`, the generated migration must bind the name `models`, preferably via `from django.db import models`, and the writer may then consolidate it with the migrations import. This aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was not merely that migrations should be valid Python; it was that the agent found a class/type serializer special case rendering `models.Model` while returning no import, reproduced a migration header lacking `models`, and then verified output containing a valid Django `models` import while preserving the original bases expression and app-local imports. A better rubric should prioritize that evidence: identification of the serializer import contract, use of an import that actually binds the alias used in generated code, and validation on the mixed-base/custom-field scenario where no other field serialization necessarily forces a `models` import. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as adding special handling only in the migration writer for `bases`, requiring `bases` to be expanded for formatting, accepting `import models` or `import django.db.models` even though they do not bind the `models` name used by `models.Model`, or judging primarily on whether the agent managed to run the full upstream test suite in a difficult environment. Regression tests or manual `makemigrations`/writer-output validation are valuable, but the core judgeable criterion is whether the trajectory makes every emitted alias resolvable without changing unrelated serialization semantics.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Serialized alias has matching import
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should ensure that whenever migration serialization emits a source expression using the `models` alias, such as `models.Model` in a non-default model bases tuple alongside an app-local mixin or custom class, the generated migration imports Django's models namespace in a way that binds that alias. Strong evidence includes locating the serializer/import contract that produced the alias without imports, rejecting imports that do not bind the emitted name, preserving existing serialization of custom fields and app-local bases, and validating generated migration output or an equivalent writer serialization result.

metadata.required_binding: from django.db import models or equivalent alias-binding import
metadata.representative_trigger: non-default serialized model bases containing both an app-local class and the framework base model
invalid_proxies_to_penalize: import django.db.models while still emitting models.Model
ad hoc writer insertion that ignores serializer import contracts

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory connects the emitted `models.Model` expression to a required import binding for `models`; it focuses on unrelated setup, broad migration validity, or formatting-only changes.
scale.2: Recognizes a missing import problem but proposes or accepts an import that may not bind the emitted alias, or does not distinguish alias resolution from generic Django import presence.
scale.3: Identifies that generated migration code using `models.Model` needs a corresponding Django models import, but provides limited evidence about the serializer/import source or validation of the mixed-bases scenario.
scale.4: Clearly traces the missing import to migration serialization/import collection, uses an alias-binding import such as `from django.db import models`, and validates generated output for a scenario where `models.Model` appears in bases.
scale.5: Fully establishes the serializer contract: the emitted `models.Model` string contributes a matching Django models import, invalid alternatives are rejected, existing app-local/custom-field serialization is preserved, import consolidation remains compatible, and the fixed output is validated as valid migration Python in the representative mixed-base case.

experiences.title: PostgreSQL dbshell psql argument-order invariant
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django-style database shell task concerns PostgreSQL `psql` ignoring extra `dbshell` parameters because they are placed after the database name.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django repository where the task explicitly states that PostgreSQL `psql` requires command-line options or user-provided dbshell parameters before the positional database name. The trajectory should have reached the PostgreSQL dbshell/client argument construction code, or at least identified that backend-specific command construction is the likely repair site. This guidance is strongest once the agent has inspected or edited the argument list builder and there is visible evidence about where `parameters` and the database name are appended. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before PostgreSQL-specific code is found, and should not be generalized to other database backends whose CLIs may intentionally order database names and parameters differently.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic command-line contract: for PostgreSQL, generated `psql` arguments must keep the executable and connection flags first, then append user-supplied dbshell parameters, and leave the database name as the final positional argument when present. This was discriminative because the task is not about generic dbshell execution, subprocess handling, or installing/running tests; it is about one ordering invariant that determines whether `psql -c ... dbname` works instead of treating `-c` as an ignored extra argument. A better rubric should judge visible evidence that the agent located the PostgreSQL-specific command builder, recognized the existing `dbname`-before-`parameters` bug, changed only the ordering so parameters precede the database name, and preserved existing user/host/port/password/SSL/environment behavior. Manual or unit-test evidence should be valued when it directly prints or asserts the constructed argument list with parameters before the database name. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as requiring successful full test-suite execution in an environment with missing dependencies, rewarding only test updates, changing shared dbshell/base client behavior, or applying PostgreSQL ordering rules to MySQL/SQLite/Oracle clients.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserve PostgreSQL psql argument ordering contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the trajectory is converging on the PostgreSQL `psql` argument-order fix: user-provided dbshell parameters/options must be inserted before the optional database name, with the database name remaining the final positional argument, while existing connection flags and environment handling remain unchanged.

required_visible_evidence: Identifies PostgreSQL-specific dbshell/client command construction as the relevant implementation area
Recognizes that placing the database name before additional parameters causes `psql` to ignore later options
Shows or describes an edit that appends user parameters before appending the database name
Preserves existing executable, user, host, port, password, SSL, and environment option behavior
Optionally validates with an argument-list assertion or printout demonstrating parameters before database name
non_requirements: Full test-suite success is not required when dependency or settings setup blocks execution
Other database backends need not be changed
Regression tests are helpful but should not substitute for the implementation ordering fix

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has found the PostgreSQL command builder or understood the `psql` ordering requirement.
scale.2: The agent mentions PostgreSQL or dbshell parameters, but the visible plan or edits do not clearly ensure parameters appear before the database name.
scale.3: The agent has identified the correct ordering issue and likely target area, but the visible evidence is incomplete, unverified, or risks disturbing unrelated connection behavior.
scale.4: The agent visibly changes or plans the correct localized ordering so parameters precede the database name, with reasonable preservation of existing connection options.
scale.5: The agent makes the localized PostgreSQL ordering fix, preserves surrounding connection/environment semantics, and provides direct validation or test expectations showing generated `psql` args with parameters before the final database name.

experiences.title: Do not require auto-name restoration when the reverse path is intentionally a no-op
experiences.description: Use this when evaluating Django migration `RenameIndex` fixes for unnamed indexes identified by `old_fields`, especially when the visible test/source says reversing is a no-op and then re-applies the forward operation.
experiences.context: In Django migration operation tasks involving `RenameIndex(..., old_fields=...)`, the tempting interpretation is that backward migration must physically restore the old auto-generated index name. That interpretation is misleading when the visible regression test or existing source comments show `database_backwards()` for unnamed indexes is expected to issue no queries and leave the new named index present, then verify that re-applying `database_forwards()` does not crash. A reversibility/restoration rubric can still be appropriate for explicitly named indexes, for migration operations whose tests require the old database object name after rollback, or when the task/test explicitly asserts the new name disappears on backward. It should not be used merely because the operation participates in a forward/backward/forward cycle.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics often demanded that `database_backwards()` compute and restore an auto-generated index name. That criterion led toward patches that changed the intended no-op reverse behavior, guessed backend naming details, or rewrote tests to expect the new index name to disappear. In this scenario, the better evidence is whether the trajectory recognizes that after a no-op reverse the physical index may already have the target `new_name`, so the forward path must avoid renaming an index to the same name. A replacement rubric should focus on an idempotence guard in the forward rename logic: after resolving the current index by fields/columns, if the discovered/current index name already equals the requested new name, the operation should return without invoking the schema editor rename. Avoid generating a criterion that says backward must be a true inverse or must restore an auto-generated name unless visible tests or source behavior require that. Prioritize visible evidence such as: preserving the no-op reverse assertion, adding or considering a re-apply-forward regression check, inspecting the column-based index lookup in the forward path, and preventing self-renames or duplicate target-name renames.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Misapplied backward restoration requirement
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a Django `RenameIndex` unnamed-index task where visible evidence shows the backward operation is intentionally a no-op and the regression is a forward re-apply after that no-op, penalize trajectories that treat auto-generated-name restoration in the backward path as the required fix. This includes implementing or validating a backward rename to a computed auto-generated name, changing tests to expect the new named index to disappear after backward, or judging success primarily by backward/forward inverse symmetry instead of by preventing a forward self-rename when the current index already has the target name.

metadata.operation_pattern: RenameIndex with unnamed index specified by fields
metadata.misleading_visible_cue: task wording mentions backward/forward cycle or auto-generated name
metadata.decisive_visible_cue: source/test indicates reverse is a no-op and still asserts the new index name exists before re-applying forward
metadata.preferred_fix_evidence: forward path detects current index name equals target name and skips schema-editor rename
metadata.avoid_fix_evidence: backward path computes auto-generated name and renames the index back solely to make the operation symmetric

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory preserves the no-op reverse behavior or focuses on forward idempotence/self-rename avoidance.
scale.2: Minor risk: the trajectory discusses restoring an auto-generated name as a possibility but has not made it the main criterion or patch direction.
scale.3: Moderate flaw: the trajectory frames the issue as general bidirectional reversibility while also acknowledging the no-op reverse behavior or forward re-apply collision.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory’s main solution or rubric requires `database_backwards()` for unnamed indexes to restore a computed auto-generated name despite visible no-op expectations.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory implements or endorses a backward auto-name restoration patch, changes tests/expectations away from the no-op reverse behavior, and does not address the forward self-rename/idempotence condition.

experiences.title: Expose Existing Internal Command Options Through the Shared CLI Path
experiences.description: Use this when a Django-style management command task asks to make an existing internal/stealth option available from the command line, especially when execution logic already consumes the option.
experiences.context: Apply in a Python/Django-like management command framework after the trajectory has identified or edited the shared command parser, the existing execution-time option key, and the programmatic command invocation path. The criterion is most useful once there is visible evidence of parser wiring, execution semantics, or compatibility checks. It is premature during repository discovery before the agent has found the parser/execution flow. It may not apply to a brand-new option with no existing execution hook, to a command-specific flag that belongs only in one command, or to a task that intentionally changes broader behavior such as migration checks rather than only automatic system checks.
experiences.experience: For these cases, the useful rubrics focused on whether `--skip-checks` is wired into the common management-command CLI as the existing `skip_checks` option and whether that value flows into the already-present system-check bypass. That was more discriminative than merely checking that help output contains the flag. A better rubric should reward evidence that the agent uses the shared parser rather than per-command hacks, uses a boolean CLI action that produces the same option key consumed by execution, preserves default CLI behavior when the flag is absent, skips only automatic system checks when present, and does not regress programmatic invocation behavior such as omitted versus explicit `skip_checks` values. It should also value validation on a command that actually runs automatic checks, preferably by mocking/registering a check failure; testing only the `check` command, commands that opt out of automatic checks, or `--help` output is a weak proxy. Avoid an overly rigid criterion that requires keeping an option in a stealth-options list unchanged, because once it is parser-defined, compatibility depends on the programmatic invocation path and defaults, not the exact list membership. Also avoid making exact help ordering or patch shape the main criterion unless the trajectory has explicit evidence that the project enforces common-option help ordering. Prioritize visible evidence of semantic wiring, backward compatibility, adjacent parser syntax remaining intact, and meaningful behavioral validation.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Shared CLI Wiring Preserves Existing Skip-Check Semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the new `--skip-checks` command-line flag is added through the shared management-command parser, maps to the existing `skip_checks` option consumed by command execution, defaults to normal system-check execution when absent, skips only automatic system checks when present, and preserves existing programmatic invocation semantics for omitted and explicit `skip_checks` values.

required_visible_evidence: The option is added in the shared/common parser path rather than duplicated in individual commands.
The CLI action stores a boolean value under the same option key already used by the execution path.
The existing execution guard for automatic system checks is reused rather than replaced with a separate code path.
Programmatic command invocation remains compatible for omitted `skip_checks` and explicit true/false values.
Adjacent common options and parser syntax are not corrupted by the edit.
strong_validation_evidence: Parser/help or parse-result evidence shows the flag is accepted and defaults correctly.
Behavioral validation uses a command that normally performs automatic system checks and shows checks are bypassed only when the flag is supplied.
Validation does not rely solely on `--help`, on a command that implements checks manually, or on commands that opt out of automatic system checks.
boundary_conditions: Do not require a specific internal list membership if parser-defined options already participate in programmatic validation.
Treat help ordering or conditional display for commands that do not run checks as secondary unless project conventions or tests make it explicit.
Do not credit changes that skip migration checks or other unrelated validations unless the task explicitly requests that behavior.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the CLI flag is connected to the existing management-command option or execution path; changes may be absent, per-command only, or syntactically broken.
scale.2: Weak evidence of parser exposure, such as a tentative flag insertion or help-output check, but unclear mapping to the existing option key, no behavioral validation, or visible risk of breaking adjacent parser/programmatic behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent state: the flag is plausibly added to the shared parser and maps to `skip_checks`, but validation is limited or compatibility with programmatic invocation and automatic-check semantics remains only partially examined.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the shared parser wiring, default false CLI behavior, execution-time skip behavior, and programmatic compatibility have been considered or tested, with no visible parser corruption or unrelated behavior changes.
scale.5: Complete evidence: the shared CLI flag is cleanly wired to the existing execution option, automatic system checks run by default and are skipped only when requested, programmatic invocation semantics are preserved, unrelated checks are unaffected, and focused tests or equivalent behavioral validation cover both parser acceptance and real check bypass.

experiences.title: Default ordering is suppressed for grouped ORM queries
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a Django ORM trajectory about an ordering/introspection bug where aggregate annotations create GROUP BY and model Meta.ordering no longer appears in the emitted ORDER BY.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django repository when the task concerns QuerySet ordering semantics, especially an `.ordered`-style property that should reflect whether SQL will actually contain ORDER BY. The relevant visible situation is: the agent has identified aggregate `annotate()` or `values().annotate()` as creating grouped queries; model default ordering remains recorded in query metadata; final SQL for grouped queries omits default Meta ordering; explicit `order_by()` may still be preserved. This criterion is most useful once the trajectory has enough evidence from ORM query/compiler inspection, reproduction output, or a proposed patch to distinguish default ordering from explicit ordering. It is less useful for unrelated SQL ordering bugs, non-grouped querysets, backend-specific ordering behavior without Django ORM grouping semantics, or very early exploration where the agent has not yet connected annotation, grouping, and default ordering.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the semantic boundary that determines correctness: GROUP BY suppresses default model ordering, but not necessarily explicit ordering. This made the criterion discriminative because visible trajectories either showed the agent discovering that `default_ordering`/Meta ordering can remain true while grouped SQL lacks ORDER BY, or showed the agent stuck repeating greps without reaching that compiler/property mismatch. A better rubric should reward evidence that the agent will make the public ordering property mirror emitted SQL: first honor explicit ordering, then treat default Meta ordering as effective only when the query is not grouped. It should also reward validating both sides of the boundary: normal default-ordered querysets remain ordered, grouped aggregate querysets with only default ordering become unordered, and grouped querysets with explicit `order_by()` remain ordered. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion such as generic 'understands Django query compilation' or 'checks default_ordering'; that proxy misses the bug because the metadata flag can persist even when SQL ordering is removed. Also avoid a blanket 'GROUP BY queries are unordered' criterion, because explicit ordering can still produce ORDER BY. Prioritize visible evidence such as inspecting the ordering property, tracing aggregate annotations to grouped query state, finding compiler behavior that drops default Meta ordering for grouping, reproducing SQL/`.ordered` mismatch, and proposing a targeted property-level condition rather than mutating unrelated query state.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Grouped query default-ordering boundary
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the agent understands and preserves the key Django ORM boundary: explicit ordering makes a queryset ordered, but default model ordering should not make a grouped aggregate queryset report ordered when the SQL compiler omits ORDER BY. Strong evidence includes tracing aggregate annotation to grouped query state, recognizing that default ordering metadata may remain true despite no emitted ORDER BY, and shaping or validating a fix so the ordering introspection property reflects actual SQL ordering without breaking normal default ordering or explicit `order_by()` behavior.

metadata.issue_type: public queryset ordering introspection diverges from generated SQL
prioritized_evidence: aggregate annotation or values-annotation creates grouped query state
model default ordering remains in metadata but grouped SQL omits ORDER BY
explicit order_by or extra ordering remains a separate ordered case
proposed fix or tests distinguish default ordering from explicit ordering
avoid_as_primary_evidence: generic compiler exploration without the grouping/default-ordering boundary
assuming every GROUP BY query is unordered

scale.1: No evidence that the agent connects grouped aggregate queries with suppression of default model ordering; trajectory may only repeat searches or discuss ordering metadata generically.
scale.2: Weak evidence of the issue area, such as locating annotation or ordering code, but no clear recognition that default ordering metadata can remain true while grouped SQL has no ORDER BY.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent trajectory: the agent identifies relevant ordering and grouping code, but has not yet clearly formulated the explicit-vs-default ordering boundary or a targeted fix.
scale.4: Clear evidence that the agent understands GROUP BY suppresses default Meta ordering and that the ordering property should account for grouped query state while preserving explicit ordering.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the agent has traced or reproduced the compiler/property mismatch, proposed or implemented a targeted property-level change, and validated normal default ordering, grouped default-ordering-only queries, and grouped explicit-ordering queries.

experiences.title: Alias-aware description-mode autodoc typehints
experiences.description: Use this when a Sphinx autodoc task reports that configured type aliases work in signatures but are expanded when type hints are moved into description/field-list output.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Sphinx autodoc codebase when the issue is specifically about `autodoc_type_aliases` being ignored under `autodoc_typehints='description'`, especially with postponed annotations or aliases that otherwise expand to `typing` expressions. It is most useful once the trajectory has found the split between normal signature rendering and description-mode annotation recording. It is less useful for unrelated typing stringification bugs, non-autodoc rendering paths, tasks about aliases in normal signatures only, or very early exploration before the agent has identified where description-mode type hints are collected.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric judged whether the trajectory propagated the configured alias map into the description-mode typehint recording path, not merely whether aliases worked somewhere in autodoc. This aligned well because normal signature rendering already used alias-aware signature inspection, while description-mode output depended on a separate annotation-recording hook that was inspecting and stringifying annotations without the alias map. A strong rubric should therefore prioritize visible evidence that the agent compared the two flows, changed the description-mode annotation extraction to use the same alias-aware inspection configuration, and validated both parameter and return type descriptions render the alias rather than the expanded `Dict[...]`-style form. Do not reward fixes that only change global stringification helpers, only test non-description signature output, or rely on broad unrelated test failures/passes. Also avoid accepting manual-build claims unless the visible output or test assertions actually target the intended object and check alias-vs-expanded rendering. If a trajectory has convincing analysis but no persisted relevant code change yet, the criterion should score partial progress rather than full completion.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Alias-Aware Description Typehint Recording
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that Sphinx autodoc's description-mode typehint path records parameter and return annotations using the configured type-alias mapping before stringification, matching the behavior of normal signature rendering. Strong evidence includes identifying the separate description-mode annotation recording/merging flow, applying the alias configuration to the signature/annotation inspection step used by that flow, and validating that generated description fields show the configured alias for both arguments and return values instead of the underlying expanded typing expression. The criterion should not be satisfied by changes limited to normal signature rendering, broad typing formatter changes without config context, or tests that do not combine description-mode typehints with configured aliases.

metadata.required_behavior: configured aliases are preserved when type hints are rendered in description fields
key_visible_evidence: separate normal-signature and description-mode typehint paths are recognized
description-mode annotation inspection receives the autodoc alias mapping
both parameter and return type descriptions are checked for alias output
expanded typing forms are treated as the regression symptom
common_false_positives: changing generic typing stringification without passing configuration
manual output from an invalid or mis-targeted reproducer
unrelated file edits or broad test results that do not exercise the reported mode

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory addresses alias handling in description-mode autodoc typehints; work is unrelated or focused only on generic typing/signature behavior.
scale.2: The trajectory notices aliases or description-mode typehints but has not identified the missing propagation point or proposes a vague/global formatting change.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies that the description-mode annotation recording path must use the alias configuration, but the implementation or validation is incomplete, unverified, or covers only parameters/signatures.
scale.4: The trajectory implements the minimal alias-propagation change in the description-mode recording flow and provides some targeted validation that aliases appear instead of expanded typing forms.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly implements the alias-aware description-mode recording behavior, validates both parameter and return type description output under combined `autodoc_typehints='description'` and alias configuration, and avoids unrelated changes or misleading test evidence.

experiences.title: Do not let semantic diagnosis substitute for an applied autodoc fix
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating Sphinx autodoc trajectories for an empty `__all__` bug, especially when the agent has identified the `None` versus empty-sequence distinction but may not yet have made or validated the relevant source change.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Sphinx `sphinx.ext.autodoc` tasks where the bug is caused by conflating a missing sentinel value with an explicitly empty container, such as treating `__all__ = []` like absent `__all__`. The semantic criterion that empty `__all__` should suppress automatic members is useful at implementation or final-review stages only if the trajectory shows a concrete change in the autodoc member-selection path and some direct validation. It is misleading at early exploration stages when the agent has merely inspected files, created a reproducer, or reasoned about `bool([])` without editing the repository. It is also insufficient if the visible trajectory drifts into unrelated Sphinx subsystems, dependency churn, or ad-hoc scripts that do not exercise the actual `automodule :members:` path.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster correctly named the desired contract: missing `__all__` should keep normal autodoc member discovery, an empty `__all__` should document no implicit members, and a non-empty `__all__` should filter to listed members. The misleading part was wording the rubric as if stating that contract or confirming `inspect.getall()` behavior were enough evidence of trajectory quality. For this kind of one-line sentinel bug, a better rubric should be stage-sensitive: before an edit, reward only localization of the exact branch and a plausible plan; after an edit, require visible evidence that the falsy check in the actual autodoc member-selection code was changed to a sentinel check and that validation covers empty, missing, and non-empty `__all__` through the autodoc pathway or existing test helpers. Avoid a tempting broad criterion like “understands Python `__all__` semantics” because it can score highly from commentary alone. Prioritize visible evidence from the repository diff, the specific code path used by `.. automodule::` with `:members:`, targeted autodoc tests or reliable doctree/build assertions, and absence of unrelated subsystem modifications.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Semantic Diagnosis Without Autodoc Implementation Evidence
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for an empty-`__all__` autodoc task when they overclaim success from semantic reasoning alone or lack visible committable evidence in the actual autodoc member-selection path. This flaw is present when the agent identifies that empty containers are falsy, or even creates ad-hoc repro files, but has not applied a relevant repository change, has not verified the changed path with `automodule :members:` behavior or existing autodoc test helpers, or has drifted into unrelated Sphinx components. Do not apply this penalty merely because a focused regression test has not yet been added if the trajectory already shows the correct source edit and reliable targeted validation; in that case the original empty-versus-missing semantic rubric remains appropriate.

observable_evidence_to_prioritize: repository diff touches the autodoc module-member selection logic rather than unrelated builders/extensions
the condition distinguishes the absence sentinel from an explicit empty sequence
validation exercises `.. automodule::` with `:members:` or equivalent autodoc test helper behavior
checks include empty `__all__`, absent `__all__`, and preferably non-empty `__all__`
temporary repro or dependency-install work is not treated as proof unless tied to the actual changed code path
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: crediting comments, hypotheses, or direct `bool([])` demonstrations as if they prove the final autodoc behavior

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory shows a relevant source edit in autodoc member selection and credible validation of the empty-versus-missing behavior, with no unrelated patch drift.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has the relevant edit but validation is mostly indirect, incomplete, or noisy while still tied to the autodoc path.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory correctly localizes the issue and proposes the sentinel change, but the visible cutoff lacks a confirmed repository edit or only uses simplified scripts rather than the actual autodoc behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mainly contains semantic reasoning, file inspection, or temporary repro setup and treats that as near-complete despite no demonstrated source change or reliable validation.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory is off-target, modifies or investigates unrelated Sphinx subsystems, or claims the empty-`__all__` issue is fixed without visible evidence in the autodoc member-selection path.

experiences.title: CONTINUE Escaping Must Remain Raw Until One Final Parse
experiences.description: Use when an Astropy FITS Card trajectory has localized a length-dependent doubled-quote round-trip bug to long string CONTINUE-card parsing and is inspecting `_split`, regex string/comment matching, or quote unescaping.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Astropy FITS Card tasks where string values containing doubled single quotes round-trip correctly on short cards but fail when serialization crosses the 80-character FITS card boundary and uses CONTINUE cards. The visible trajectory should show concrete evidence such as card images split into a first quoted chunk plus CONTINUE chunks, regex captures for quoted strings, or discussion of `_split` reconstructing a synthetic value/comment string before a later parser unescapes FITS quotes. This guidance is most useful after the agent has moved beyond initial file discovery and has enough evidence to distinguish raw FITS escaping from Python string values. It is less applicable for unrelated FITS verification/reformatting issues, for purely short-card quote parsing bugs, or at a very early stage before the trajectory has identified whether CONTINUE-card reconstruction is involved.
experiences.experience: The useful criterion in this cluster is not merely that the agent reproduced the issue or noticed CONTINUE cards. Reproduction alone can look strong while the patch still changes the wrong layer. The discriminative issue is whether the agent preserves the FITS-escaped representation while recombining CONTINUE fragments and allows quote unescaping to happen exactly once at the normal value-parse stage. Rubrics that focus only on broad recombination, avoiding split quote runs, continuation-marker ordering, or verification side effects are too coarse or can reward plausible but incorrect fixes. A better rubric should ask whether the trajectory/patch avoids per-fragment conversion of doubled FITS quotes to Python quotes inside CONTINUE reconstruction, strips only the continuation marker from the raw captured fragment, rebuilds a syntactically valid quoted value/comment string for the downstream parser, and prevents partial string/comment regex matches from silently ignoring leftover quote characters. Visible evidence to prioritize includes raw card images, subcard value/comment fragments, regex `strg` groups, whether `.replace("''", "'")` is removed or deferred in the long-card reconstruction path, whether string/comment matching is full-string rather than partial, and regression checks for both trailing and embedded doubled quotes across boundary lengths. Avoid making the rubric about adding boundary-splitting heuristics, special-casing `''''` as empty, reformatting CONTINUE cards via verification, or simply passing the original reproducer without preserving general FITS quote semantics.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Raw Escaping Preserved Through CONTINUE Reconstruction
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that a correct fix for long FITS string values keeps CONTINUE-card fragments in FITS-escaped form during reconstruction, removes only syntactic continuation markers, uses a full string/comment match so trailing quote/comment text cannot be ignored, and relies on the normal final parse to unescape doubled single quotes exactly once. Strong evidence includes inspecting raw multi-card images and subcard regex captures, identifying double-unescaping as the corruption mechanism, avoiding ad hoc special cases for null-looking quote runs, and validating boundary-length round trips for doubled quotes at the end and in the middle of long values.

key_visible_evidence: raw multi-80-character FITS card images or CONTINUE subcards are inspected
the long-card reconstruction path is distinguished from normal short-card parsing
doubled FITS quotes are not converted to Python quotes per CONTINUE fragment
continuation ampersands are stripped without altering quote escape pairs
string/comment regex matching is required to consume the relevant fragment fully
round-trip checks cover boundary lengths and both trailing and embedded doubled quotes
common_false_positives: special-casing a CONTINUE fragment that looks like a null string
re-escaping already-unescaped fragments without proving the escape layer
blaming verification/reformatting without evidence it is in the failing parse path
testing only one failing length or only comment-free happy paths

scale.1: No visible evidence that the agent understands the CONTINUE reconstruction escape layer; the trajectory focuses on unrelated parsing, verification, or reproduction only.
scale.2: Some evidence that CONTINUE cards or quote escaping are relevant, but the proposed reasoning still unescapes fragments prematurely, special-cases quote runs, or lacks raw subcard evidence.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent trajectory: the agent has identified long-card CONTINUE behavior and quote collapse, but has not clearly ensured exactly one final unescape and full string/comment matching.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the agent is preserving raw escaped fragments through reconstruction, stripping only continuation markers, and validating multiple boundary cases, with only minor uncertainty around comments or regex completeness.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence of the correct semantic contract: raw FITS escaping is preserved through CONTINUE recombination, matching is full-fragment, unescaping occurs exactly once downstream, and regression checks cover trailing/embedded doubled quotes across boundary lengths plus relevant comments.

experiences.title: Recovering After Botched Partial Edits
experiences.description: Retrieve this when the trajectory shows a multi-step code-editing workflow has failed partway through, especially after malformed patches, broad sed replacements, duplicated blocks, deleted lines, or uncertain file state.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent style repository repair sessions where the agent is modifying source files through shell commands and a recent edit attempt has visibly gone wrong or become uncertain. Strong matches include observations of duplicated code, missing functions, malformed syntax, failed patch application, repeated line-number deletions, or a checkout/revert followed by a new attempt. The criterion is most useful during recovery or final-review stages, when the next important question is whether the agent inspected the actual file/diff and restored a coherent baseline before continuing. It is less useful during early exploration before any destructive edit, and it should not be treated as a complete semantic-correctness rubric for issues that require broad coverage across multiple implementations, storage backends, interfaces, or call sites.
experiences.experience: The retrieved rubric judged whether the agent reassessed state after a partial workflow failure before continuing. This is discriminative when the visible trajectory contains failed edits: agents that stop, inspect numbered context or git diff, restore damaged files, and then apply a narrow patch are much more likely to leave a coherent change than agents that keep deleting or inserting by stale line numbers. The rubric can be wrong if used as a proxy for full task completeness: a clean recovery process may still miss a second affected subsystem, and a messy intermediate trajectory may later converge on a tiny correct change. A better rubric should focus on observable recovery evidence after the failure: explicit inspection of the damaged region, `git diff` or equivalent state review, restoring from version control when corruption is suspected, replacing blind sed loops with a precise patch, and running at least a targeted validation. Avoid the tempting wrong criterion of rewarding the agent merely for identifying the intended fix or for saying it will verify; prioritize whether it actually confirmed the current file state before making further edits.
