reference_golden_rubrics.title: State Reassessment After Failed Edit Workflow
reference_golden_rubrics.description: After a visible partial-edit failure or uncertain modification state, the agent should explicitly reassess the repository state before continuing: inspect the affected code and diff, restore or clean up corrupted edits when needed, then apply a precise minimal change and validate it. This rubric is about recovery discipline after a failed workflow, not about whether the chosen semantic fix covers every required subsystem.

required_visible_evidence: A prior command or edit produced malformed, duplicated, misplaced, or uncertain code state.
The agent inspects the affected region, full diff, or repository status after the failure.
If corruption is plausible, the agent restores or deliberately cleans the file before applying the next edit.
Subsequent edits are targeted rather than repeated blind line-number operations.
The agent performs or plans a validation that checks the repaired state.
not_applicable_when: No partial workflow failure or destructive edit has occurred yet.
The main uncertainty is semantic coverage across multiple independent components rather than file-state recovery.
The trajectory is still pure exploration with no modified state to reassess.

scale.1: No meaningful reassessment after a failed or uncertain edit; the agent continues with blind deletions, insertions, or assumptions about file state.
scale.2: Weak reassessment; the agent briefly views truncated context or repeats the same fragile edit pattern without confirming the complete affected state.
scale.3: Moderate behavior; the agent recognizes something went wrong and partially inspects or restores state, but validation or cleanup remains incomplete.
scale.4: Strong behavior; the agent inspects the relevant code/diff, corrects or restores damaged state, and switches to a more controlled edit approach.
scale.5: Excellent behavior; the agent clearly diagnoses the failed workflow, restores a coherent baseline if needed, applies a minimal precise patch, verifies the resulting diff/context, and runs targeted validation.

experiences.title: Exact Failure-Mode Contract Coverage
experiences.description: Retrieve when the task is explicitly about invalid input, corrupted state, cancellation/timeout, auth rejection, or other failure handling where correctness depends on mapping a specific error source to a specific exception, status code, JSON body, or user-facing message.
experiences.context: Applies in Python or Go web/API/CLI/server codebases when the problem statement names concrete failure modes and expected error behavior, such as converting a low-level exception into a framework validation error, returning a protocol-specific status code, rejecting invalid credentials, or emitting structured failure output. It is most useful after the trajectory has identified the relevant error-producing call path and is editing the handler/interceptor/parser/converter responsible for error classification. It is less useful as a standalone criterion when the agent is still only exploring, when the patch only adds broad catch-all handling without proving the exact reported exception source, or when the real issue may involve another layer such as middleware ordering, response formatting, repository contracts, or compatibility across dependency versions.
experiences.experience: The source rubric judged whether error conditions and failure modes were explicitly covered. That is valuable for tasks whose requested behavior is itself an error-path contract, but it should not be retrieved as a generic 'has tests for errors' signal. It aligns best when visible evidence shows the agent has traced the exact failing input or exception type, implemented the required conversion at the layer where the failure actually escapes, and preserved unrelated errors instead of swallowing or reclassifying them. A better rubric should focus on whether every failure mode named in the task is handled with the specified observable response and whether the patch prevents downstream processing on failure. Avoid the tempting proxy of rewarding any added error test, broad exception catch, or passing package test; those can miss important origin paths, existing pass-through behavior, end-to-end response serialization, or dependency-version differences. Prioritize visible evidence such as reproduction of the specific invalid value/corrupted file/auth failure/timeout, inspection of the exception hierarchy or error contract, assertions on the exact status/code/message/body, and checks that unrelated errors and normal paths remain unchanged.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact Failure-Mode Contract Implementation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a task centered on failure handling, the trajectory should demonstrate that the patch handles the exact reported failure sources at the correct boundary and produces the specified observable error contract. Strong evidence includes tracing the failure to the concrete throwing/returning operation, distinguishing expected failure classes from unrelated errors, preventing protected or downstream work after rejection, preserving existing successful and unrelated-error behavior, and adding or running focused validation that checks the exact exception/status/code/message/structured body required by the task.

task_signals: problem statement names invalid input, corrupted data, cancellation, timeout, auth failure, removed command, or structured error output
expected behavior specifies an exception class, protocol status, error code, JSON fields, or user-facing guidance
required_evidence: agent identifies the actual call path where the reported failure escapes
patch maps only the intended failure class/source to the required response
patch does not mask unrelated errors or regress existing pass-through behavior
validation or tests assert the exact observable failure contract, not just that some error occurred
boundaries: do not over-reward broad catch-all handlers without source-specific reasoning
do not treat package tests passing as sufficient if the named failure mode is untested
do not ignore other layers that can reclassify or reformat the error before it reaches users

scale.1: No visible evidence that the exact reported failure mode is understood or handled; the patch is unrelated, only explores files, or relies on generic success-path behavior.
scale.2: Some error-handling code is touched, but it is broad, speculative, or at an uncertain layer; the exact required status/exception/body is not validated and unrelated errors may be swallowed or misclassified.
scale.3: The trajectory addresses the likely failure path and expected error response, but coverage is partial: one named failure source is handled while other described origins, compatibility boundaries, or response-format details remain unverified.
scale.4: The exact reported failure source is traced and handled at the right boundary with the required observable response; focused validation checks the main error contract and the patch appears to preserve normal behavior.
scale.5: All named failure modes are explicitly handled and validated with precise assertions on status/code/exception/message/structured output, downstream processing is prevented where required, unrelated errors remain distinguishable, and compatibility or layering issues are considered.

experiences.title: Do not use debugging process or fix-location preference as a proxy for semantic patch correctness
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when an agent is tracing a complex framework or library bug step by step, or when a rubric is tempted to prefer a more architectural or general fix location over a direct failure-path fix, but the key evaluation question is whether the eventual change satisfies the observed API or semantic contract and addresses the demonstrated failure path. When command output is visible, the judge must read the printed values, exception text, and relevant test results rather than treating return code zero, a command invocation, or edit presence as proof of semantic progress.
experiences.context: Applies in Python framework or library bug fixes where the trajectory shows reproduction, code inspection, tracing, and one-at-a-time hypotheses, but the candidate direction may still target an intermediate symptom instead of the contract-breaking boundary. Also applies when a rubric is tempted to call a direct failure-path fix a workaround while rewarding a seemingly more general or upstream edit without visible evidence that the general location actually resolves the failure. The source process-oriented rubric may still be appropriate early in an investigation when the main visible risk is shotgun-editing many unrelated areas without isolating failures. It is misleading as a final-review or late-debugging criterion when the agent has already narrowed to a plausible subsystem and correctness depends on preserving a specific user-visible invariant. If reproduction scripts, test runs, or inspections show concrete output, the activation includes checking what the output actually says: expected versus actual values, persistent versus resolved exception text, and relevant pass/fail details. Compatibility, import, or environment edits are only supporting setup unless later output shows the reported semantic behavior changed. If output is truncated or does not expose the expected-versus-actual behavior, preserve uncertainty rather than inferring success or failure from the return code alone.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether the agent tested hypotheses one at a time and avoided shotgun debugging. That is useful process guidance, but in these cases it often over-rewarded trajectories that were orderly yet still wrong: the agent traced a real symptom, then patched a nearby mechanism without proving that the patch satisfied the user-visible invariant. A related failure mode is fix-location preference: a rubric calls a direct failure-path fix a workaround or lazy while rewarding a seemingly more architectural or general-location edit, even when visible evidence does not show the general edit resolves the failure. A better rubric should focus on validated root-cause-to-fix alignment. Avoid the tempting criteria 'the agent is being systematic, so the patch is likely correct,' 'the fix is at a more general location, so it is more correct,' 'the command exited successfully, so the behavior is fixed,' and 'an edit exists, so semantic progress was made.' Instead, prioritize visible evidence that the agent identified the exact semantic boundary from the task, explained why the proposed code change enforces that boundary, and validated it against the original scenario. When command output is available, judge evidence mapping must read the content of that output: printed values should change from the reported wrong behavior to the expected behavior, relevant tests should show the targeted behavior passing, and exception text should show whether the original failure persists or has been replaced by an unrelated setup issue. A zero return code with printed wrong values is negative evidence for correctness; a command invocation without relevant output is weak evidence; an import, compatibility, or cosmetic edit is not a semantic fix unless a later run demonstrates the reported contract now holds. Conversely, inspection of the traceback-named or failure-path code is legitimate targeted progress during a paused investigation, even without a visible edit, but reserve final correctness credit for observable corrected behavior or a clearly described matching regression check. Treat direct and upstream fix locations as equivalent alternatives until visible evidence distinguishes them; never reward architectural appearance alone. If converting this lesson into rubrics, make proxy-based scoring a high-weight negative criterion: penalize reliance on debugging style, preferred location, return code, command execution, or edit presence when output content or contract evidence contradicts it; credit concrete semantic validation more strongly than process neatness. Penalize trajectories where relevant tests still fail, the reproduced wrong values remain visible, no viable patch or regression plan exists at final review, broad edits are made after a failed hypothesis, or the agent repeatedly inspects or traces the same area while missing visible evidence that the issue lies in a different layer. Abstain from fix-location or success judgments when no implementation, failure-path evidence, or readable output distinguishes the alternatives and correctness depends on future continuation.

experiences.title: Patch submission format verification over process and testing proxies
experiences.description: When siblings share the same source patch and differ in submission approach or patch format, the primary discriminative criterion should be whether a proper standard git diff patch (beginning with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>`) was created and submitted, not process cleanliness proxies like retry count or working directory confusion avoidance, and not testing/validation evidence proxies like test runs or regression checks. A diff against a backup file (`--- <path>.bak` / `+++ <path>`) contains diff markers but is not a valid applicable git diff patch. When the parent persistent state records that a fix has already been applied, the rubric must evaluate whether children correctly carry forward, validate, or submit the inherited fix—not whether they independently implement a stricter alternative or preserve additional invariants the parent did not preserve. The rubric must not assume the inherited fix is insufficient unless visible evidence (e.g., failing test output in the child trajectory) demonstrates failure.
experiences.context: PC scope. Applies when the parent state already contains the correct fix and the child's task is primarily submission, or when all siblings share the same source patch and only submission approach or patch format differs. The key visible distinction is whether the agent created and submitted a standard git diff patch beginning with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>` versus submitting raw source code, a non-standard diff format (e.g., diff against a `.bak` file with `--- <path>.bak` / `+++ <path>` headers), or a diff with absolute paths and no `diff --git` header. When the parent persistent state explicitly records that a bug was fixed and describes the applied change, children are continuations of that working state; the scoring stage evaluates whether they carry forward, validate, or submit the inherited fix, not whether they implement a novel stricter fix from scratch. This experience teaches rubric generators to make patch format validity a primary criterion, to avoid substituting process metrics or testing evidence that can be inversely correlated with actual submission success, and to avoid requiring stricter re-implementation of an already-working inherited fix without visible evidence of insufficiency.
experiences.experience:
When the mechanism applies: SWE-agent trajectories require patch submission, and siblings differ in submission approach or patch format. The parent already has the fix, or all siblings share the same source patch and only the submission method or format varies. The parent persistent state may explicitly record that a fix was applied and describe the change, making children continuations rather than fresh implementations.

When to abstain: The task does not require patch file submission; submission format is not visible in the trajectory cards; all siblings use the same submission method and valid git diff format, making submission approach non-discriminatory; or an existing rubric criterion already evaluates patch format validity with sufficient weight and a scale that distinguishes standard git diff format from non-standard formats. Also abstain if the visible prefix cannot determine whether the inherited fix is sufficient (e.g., no test results are visible and the parent state is ambiguous about correctness)—preserve uncertainty rather than assuming the fix fails.

Semantic contract: A proper patch submission is a standard git diff beginning with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>`, created as an untracked file (e.g., patch.txt) and submitted via cat or equivalent. The output must begin with the `diff --git` header — not merely contain `---`/`+++` markers. A diff between a backup file and the current file (headers `--- <path>.bak` / `+++ <path>`) or a diff with absolute paths and no `diff --git` header is NOT a valid applicable patch, even though it contains `---`/`+++` markers. Raw source code catted directly from the working tree (e.g., `cat source_file.py | head -N | tail -M`) is also not a proper patch submission, even if the source content is correct.

Inherited fix continuation contract: When the parent persistent state records that a fix was applied and describes the change, a child that carries forward, validates, or submits the inherited fix has satisfied the continuation task. The rubric must not require the child to implement a stricter alternative (e.g., preserving exact object identity when the parent's simpler approach sufficed) or to preserve additional invariants the parent did not preserve, unless visible evidence (e.g., failing test output in the child trajectory) demonstrates those invariants are tested or the inherited fix is insufficient. Do not assert test failures without visible failing test output in the paused judge view.

Positive visible evidence: Final submitted output begins with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>`; patch.txt (or equivalent) appears in the untracked files list; submission command includes `cat patch.txt` or equivalent; submission output contains `diff --git` header followed by well-formed hunks with `---`/`+++` and `@@` markers and correct relative paths. For inherited fix continuation: parent persistent state records that a fix was applied and describes the change; child shows git diff or file contents matching the inherited parent fix; child runs reproduction scripts or test suites showing the fix works without visible failures; child submits the inherited fix via a valid git diff.

Contradictory visible evidence: Final submitted output begins with `--- <path>.bak` / `+++ <path>` or `--- <absolute_path>` / `+++ <absolute_path>` without a `diff --git` header; agent submits by catting the source file directly with head/tail or similar; no patch.txt in untracked files; submission output lacks `diff --git` header; clean-looking submission process with few retries but no actual valid patch file produced. For inherited fix continuation: visible test output in a child trajectory shows the inherited fix fails specific tests; a child actively reverts or breaks the inherited parent fix; a child applies a different, incorrect fix that does not address the task.

Tempting domain-specific proxies that must not be confused with the target:
1. Process cleanliness metrics — retry count, working directory confusion avoidance, fewer error messages — can be inversely correlated with actual submission success. An agent that avoids directory confusion but never creates a valid patch file has failed the submission task regardless of how clean its process appears.
2. Testing/validation evidence — extensive test runs, regression checks, branch-sensitive validation — is secondary to the primary contract of producing an applicable patch. A continuation that runs comprehensive tests but submits an unapplicable patch (e.g., diff against a `.bak` file) should not outscore a continuation that submits a valid git diff. Do not allow testing evidence to compensate for invalid patch format. However, testing evidence that shows the inherited fix works without visible failures should be credited as validation of the inherited fix, not as a substitute for patch submission.
3. Stricter re-implementation demands — requiring children to preserve additional invariants the parent did not preserve, to use a different implementation strategy than the parent's already-working one, or to implement a novel more stringent fix from scratch — will systematically misrank correct continuations. A child that carries forward and submits the inherited fix via a valid git diff has succeeded at the continuation task, even if it did not improve upon the parent's approach. A rubric that defines progress as 'implementing a stricter fix' or 'preserving additional invariants' will zero-score correct continuations that merely carry forward the inherited working state.

A rubric that defines progress as 'avoiding working directory confusion,' 'running comprehensive tests,' or 'implementing a stricter alternative' will misrank a node with a clean process, extensive testing, or a novel re-implementation but an unapplicable patch above a node that submitted a proper git diff of the inherited fix.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Patch File Created and Submitted
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The agent created a patch file (e.g., patch.txt) using git diff output and submitted it. Evidence: patch.txt appears in untracked files list; submission command includes cat patch.txt or equivalent; submission output begins with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>` and contains well-formed diff markers (---/+++ and @@).

scale.0: No patch file created or submitted
scale.1: patch.txt missing from untracked files
scale.2: patch.txt exists but submission output begins with `---`/`+++` without `diff --git` header (e.g., diff against .bak file)
scale.3: patch.txt exists and submitted via cat patch.txt with `diff --git` header visible

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Submitted Patch Format Validity
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The final submitted output must be a standard git diff beginning with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>`. Outputs beginning with `--- <path>.bak` / `+++ <path>` or other non-standard diff formats are not valid git diffs and cannot be applied as patches. Evidence: first lines of submission output; presence of `diff --git` header; correct relative paths.

scale.0: Submission output is raw source with no diff markers
scale.1: Submission output begins with `---`/`+++` headers referencing a `.bak` file or absolute paths, not a git diff
scale.2: Submission output contains a diff but not in standard git diff format
scale.3: Submission output begins with `diff --git` with correct relative paths and well-formed hunks

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Inherited Fix Continuation Over Stricter Re-implementation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: When the parent persistent state records that a fix was applied and describes the change, credit children that carry forward, validate, or submit the inherited fix via a valid git diff. Do not require children to implement a stricter alternative or preserve additional invariants the parent did not preserve. Do not assume the inherited fix is insufficient unless visible failing test output in the child trajectory demonstrates failure. Evidence: parent persistent state records applied fix; child git diff or file contents match inherited fix; child test output shows fix works without visible failures; child submits inherited fix.

scale.0: Rubric requires children to implement a novel stricter fix from scratch, ignoring the inherited parent fix
scale.1: Rubric acknowledges inherited fix but penalizes children for not improving upon it or preserving additional invariants the parent did not preserve
scale.2: Rubric credits children for carrying forward the inherited fix but assumes insufficiency without visible failing test output
scale.3: Rubric credits children for carrying forward and submitting the inherited fix; does not assume insufficiency unless visible failing test output demonstrates failure

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Process, Testing, and Re-implementation Proxies Are Not Submission Success
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Do not reward process cleanliness proxies (retry count, working directory confusion avoidance, fewer errors), testing/validation evidence proxies (test runs, regression checks), or stricter re-implementation demands (preserving additional invariants, using a different implementation strategy) as substitutes for patch format validity verification. These metrics can be inversely correlated with actual submission success. A node with a clean process, extensive testing, or a novel re-implementation but an unapplicable patch has failed submission. A node that correctly carries forward and submits the inherited fix should not be zero-scored for failing to implement a stricter alternative.

scale.0: Rubric correctly prioritizes patch format validity and inherited fix continuation over process, testing, and re-implementation metrics
scale.1: Rubric mentions process, testing, or re-implementation metrics as secondary
scale.2: Rubric uses process cleanliness, testing evidence, or stricter re-implementation requirements as primary or sole criterion for submission success

experiences.title: Patch submission format verification over process and testing proxies
experiences.description: When siblings share the same source patch and differ in submission approach or patch format, the primary discriminative criterion should be whether a proper standard git diff patch (beginning with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>`) was created and submitted via a final submission command, not process cleanliness proxies like retry count or working directory confusion avoidance, and not testing/validation evidence proxies like test runs or regression checks. A diff against a backup file (`--- <path>.bak` / `+++ <path>`) contains diff markers but is not a valid applicable git diff patch. Multiple overlapping rubrics that each reward testing breadth, coverage, or integration verification separately collectively amplify process evidence and can mask a missing or invalid submission.
experiences.context: PC scope. Applies when the parent state already contains the correct fix and the child's task is primarily submission, or when all siblings share the same source patch and only submission approach or patch format differs. The key visible distinction is whether the agent created and submitted a standard git diff patch beginning with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>` via a final submission command (e.g., `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat /tmp/patch.txt`) versus submitting raw source code, a non-standard diff format (e.g., diff against a `.bak` file with `--- <path>.bak` / `+++ <path>` headers), or stopping after saving a patch without emitting the submission command. This experience teaches rubric generators to make patch format validity and submission completion primary criteria, to consolidate testing thoroughness into a single rubric rather than multiplying overlapping coverage criteria, and to avoid substituting process metrics or testing evidence that can be inversely correlated with actual submission success.
experiences.experience:
When the mechanism applies: SWE-agent trajectories require patch submission, and siblings differ in submission approach, patch format, or submission completion. The parent already has the fix, or all siblings share the same source patch and only the submission method, format, or completion status varies.

When to abstain: The task does not require patch file submission; submission format is not visible in the trajectory cards; all siblings use the same submission method and valid git diff format and all emit the final submission command, making submission approach non-discriminative; or an existing rubric criterion already evaluates patch format validity and submission completion with sufficient weight and a scale that distinguishes standard git diff format from non-standard formats and submitted from non-submitted trajectories.

Semantic contract: A proper patch submission requires two conditions: (1) a standard git diff beginning with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>`, created as an untracked file (e.g., patch.txt) and submitted via cat or equivalent; and (2) the final submission command is emitted (e.g., `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat /tmp/patch.txt`), with the trajectory ending in a submitted state. The output must begin with the `diff --git` header — not merely contain `---`/`+++` markers. A diff between a backup file and the current file (headers `--- <path>.bak` / `+++ <path>`) or a diff with absolute paths and no `diff --git` header is NOT a valid applicable patch, even though it contains `---`/`+++` markers. Raw source code catted directly from the working tree (e.g., `cat source_file.py | head -N | tail -M`) is also not a proper patch submission, even if the source content is correct. A trajectory that saves a patch file but stops before emitting the final submission command (result_status paused, exit_status empty) has not completed submission, regardless of how much validation it performed.

Positive visible evidence: Final submitted output begins with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>`; patch.txt (or equivalent) appears in the untracked files list; submission command includes `cat patch.txt` or equivalent; the final visible step emits a completion/submission command (e.g., `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT`); trajectory summary shows result_status finished and exit_status Submitted; submission output contains `diff --git` header followed by well-formed hunks with `---`/`+++` and `@@` markers and correct relative paths.

Contradictory visible evidence: Final submitted output begins with `--- <path>.bak` / `+++ <path>` or `--- <absolute_path>` / `+++ <absolute_path>` without a `diff --git` header; agent submits by catting the source file directly with head/tail or similar; no patch.txt in untracked files; submission output lacks `diff --git` header; trajectory ends after saving a patch file without emitting the final submission command (result_status paused, exit_status empty); clean-looking submission process with few retries but no actual valid patch file produced.

Tempting domain-specific proxies that must not be confused with the target:
1. Process cleanliness metrics — retry count, working directory confusion avoidance, fewer error messages — can be inversely correlated with actual submission success. An agent that avoids directory confusion but never creates a valid patch file has failed the submission task regardless of how clean its process appears.
2. Testing/validation evidence — extensive test runs, regression checks, branch-sensitive validation — is secondary to the primary contract of producing and submitting an applicable patch. A continuation that runs comprehensive tests but submits an unapplicable patch (e.g., diff against a `.bak` file) or stops before submitting should not outscore a continuation that submits a valid git diff. Do not allow testing evidence to compensate for invalid patch format or missing submission.
3. Rubric redundancy amplification — when multiple overlapping rubrics each reward testing breadth, complex-type coverage, integration verification, and regression guarding separately, they collectively amplify process evidence and can mask a missing or invalid submission. A trajectory that tests the most extensively but never submits can accumulate top scores across all overlapping rubrics and tie with submitted trajectories. Consolidate testing thoroughness into a single rubric rather than multiplying overlapping coverage criteria. Do not reward the same validation activity under multiple separate rubrics.

A rubric that defines progress as 'avoiding working directory confusion' or 'running comprehensive tests' will misrank a node with a clean process or extensive testing but an unapplicable patch or missing submission above a node that submitted a proper git diff. Multiple overlapping rubrics that each reward testing will amplify this misranking.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The agent created a patch file (e.g., patch.txt) using git diff output and submitted it via a final submission command. Evidence: patch.txt appears in untracked files list; submission command includes cat patch.txt or equivalent; the final visible step emits a completion/submission command (e.g., echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT); trajectory summary shows result_status finished and exit_status Submitted; submission output begins with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>` and contains well-formed diff markers (---/+++ and @@).

Outputs beginning with `--- <path>.bak` / `+++ <path>` or other non-standard diff formats are not valid git diffs and cannot be applied as patches. Evidence: first lines of submission output; presence of `diff --git` header; correct relative paths.

scale.0: Submission output is raw source with no diff markers
scale.1: Submission output begins with `---`/`+++` headers referencing a `.bak` file or absolute paths, not a git diff
scale.2: Submission output contains a diff but not in standard git diff format

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Process, Testing, and Redundant Coverage Proxies Are Not Submission Success
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Do not reward process cleanliness proxies (retry count, working directory confusion avoidance, fewer errors) or testing/validation evidence proxies (test runs, regression checks, complex-type coverage, integration verification) as substitutes for patch format validity and submission completion. These metrics can be inversely correlated with actual submission success. Do not create multiple overlapping rubrics that each reward test execution breadth, complex-type coverage, integration verification, and regression guarding separately, because they collectively amplify process evidence and mask a missing or invalid submission. Consolidate testing thoroughness into a single rubric. A node with a clean process or extensive testing but an unapplicable patch or missing submission command has failed submission.

scale.0: Rubric correctly prioritizes patch format validity and submission completion over process and testing metrics; testing consolidated into a single criterion
scale.1: Rubric mentions process or testing metrics as secondary
scale.2: Rubric uses process cleanliness or testing evidence as primary or sole criterion for submission success
scale.3: Rubric creates multiple overlapping testing/coverage criteria that collectively amplify process evidence and mask missing or invalid submission

experiences.title: Do not treat code-context browsing, reference-finding, or environment inspection as evidence of semantic completion
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when an agent has already inspected nearby or upstream code, found test expectations referencing a feature, executed code against an installed package or different checkout path, or inspected an import-location mismatch without taking corrective action, but the task requires implementing and validating a behavioral contract, compatibility boundary, public API, migration semantics, or storage/deletion invariant in the working testbed rather than merely localizing references or verifying pre-existing behavior. When an agent discovers that an installed package shadows the testbed, concrete corrective action to resolve the shadowing is itself critical progress that unblocks validation.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE trajectories across Python/TypeScript web frameworks, ORMs, parsers, storage layers, and database code where the visible steps show substantial file/function inspection, test-assertion greps, execution against wrong checkouts, or import-location inspection without corrective action, but the remaining challenge is implementing the correct behavior in the working testbed and proving it. Misleading cases include agents that inspect adjacent methods, grep related symbols, debug line indexes, find assert statements referencing a feature in test files, run code against an installed package or different checkout path, inspect where a module is loaded from without resolving the mismatch, then make a local/obvious patch or conclude the feature is already present without demonstrating actual source changes in the correct testbed. A special case arises when an agent discovers that a pip or site-packages installation shadows the testbed working copy: mere inspection of the import location (checking __file__, running pip show) is not progress, but concrete corrective action (pip uninstall, reinstall in editable mode) that removes or bypasses the conflicting installation is critical progress that unblocks all subsequent validation. The original surrounding-code rubric can still be appropriate early in localization, especially when the agent is about to patch only the stack-trace line without checking callers/callees. It becomes weak or misleading after localization is already done, during patch-review or final-quality prediction, unless the trajectory also shows contract-specific reasoning, actual source changes in the working testbed, and validation. Abstain when the task is purely exploratory with no implementation expected, or when the feature is genuinely already present in the correct testbed verified by actual source inspection of the testbed source files (not test expectations or installed package behavior).
experiences.experience: The previous rubric rewarded looking beyond the immediate failing line. That is sound as an early debugging heuristic, but it overstates progress when the trajectory already contains code browsing and the real risk is a semantically wrong or incomplete fix. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent connected the inspected context to the task's invariant AND made actual source changes in the correct testbed. Three additional false proxies must be explicitly rejected: (1) Finding test expectations (assert statements referencing a feature) in test files does not mean the feature is implemented in the working testbed — these are specifications for desired behavior, not evidence of implementation. (2) Running code against an installed package or a different checkout path does not validate the testbed patch. (3) Mere inspection of an import-location mismatch (checking __file__, running pip show, attempting to print the module path) does not constitute progress when another agent has taken concrete corrective action to resolve the shadowing. The primary criterion for progress should be actual source changes in the correct testbed (visible diff to target files), not verification of pre-existing references in test files or installed packages. However, when an agent discovers that an installed package shadows the testbed and takes concrete corrective action (pip uninstall of the conflicting package, reinstall in editable/development mode, or equivalent path resolution that completes successfully), that corrective action is itself strong evidence of progress because it unblocks all subsequent validation — even when no post-fix test run is visible in the prefix. A rubric that scores a branch with mere import-location inspection higher than a branch with successful corrective action is inverting the progress signal. Do not penalize a child for not yet running tests after the corrective action if the visible prefix ends at or shortly after the action; the environment fix itself is the unblocking step. Preserve uncertainty when the visible prefix cannot confirm whether the corrective action led to passing tests — the environment fix unblocks validation but does not by itself guarantee the underlying patch is semantically correct. Avoid the tempting criterion that repeated greps, sed output, commit-history inspection, surrounding-class inspection, test-assertion findings, installed-package behavior, or import-location inspection alone indicates correctness, feature presence, or progress. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent: identifies the owner layer for the behavior, states the compatibility/edge cases, makes actual source changes to target files in the working testbed, updates all affected call paths or APIs, resolves environment shadowing when discovered via concrete corrective action, adds or runs targeted regression checks against the correct testbed, and avoids broad local changes that merely silence the observed symptom.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Context inspection without contract validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories where the agent has localized and inspected relevant surrounding code but continues to rely on that inspection as the main justification for a patch, without visibly satisfying the task-level behavioral contract or validating compatibility-sensitive cases. This is especially relevant when the task describes preservation, migration, non-destructive loading, public error context, database version semantics, query grouping, or format read/write invariants, and the recent trajectory shows an obvious local edit, repeated source browsing, or ad hoc reproduction attempts rather than a contract-aware implementation plan and regression validation.

visible_evidence_to_check: agent has already inspected nearby/upstream code or related classes
task requires a semantic invariant beyond fixing the immediate stack-trace line
patch plan or edits are localized to the first suspicious site without addressing all ownership/call-path boundaries
no targeted test or reproduction validates the stated invariant and compatibility cases
recent steps show repetitive greps/debug prints or environment setup instead of closing the semantic gap
metadata.source_rubric_boundary: Surrounding-code inspection remains useful only as an early localization rubric, not as a strong predictor once the unresolved question is semantic correctness.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory both inspected context and tied the patch to the required invariant with targeted validation or clear coverage of affected call paths.
scale.2: Minor evidence: some contract reasoning is present, but one secondary compatibility or validation point remains weak.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent inspected the right area and made plausible local changes, but validation and ownership-boundary reasoning are incomplete.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mostly consists of browsing or local symptom fixing, with little proof that the task-level invariant, public API, or compatibility behavior is preserved.
scale.5: Severe evidence: despite extensive surrounding-code inspection, the agent repeats searches or makes a narrow/fragile patch that ignores explicit preservation, migration, public-context, grouping, or read/write requirements and lacks meaningful regression validation.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Test-expectation, wrong-checkout, or import-inspection false proxy for implementation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories or rubrics that treat finding test expectations (assert statements referencing a feature) in test files as evidence the feature is already implemented, treat running code against an installed package or different checkout path as validation of the testbed patch, or treat mere inspection of an import-location mismatch (checking __file__, running pip show, attempting to print the module path) as progress when another agent has taken concrete corrective action to resolve the shadowing. Test assertions are specifications for desired behavior, not evidence of implementation in the working testbed. The primary criterion for progress is actual source changes in the correct testbed (visible diff to target implementation files) or concrete corrective action that unblocks validation, not verification of pre-existing references in test files, installed-package behavior, or import-location inspection. A rubric that scores branches with only browsing, reference-finding, or import-location inspection higher than branches with actual source changes to target files or concrete corrective action to resolve environment shadowing is inverting the progress signal.

visible_evidence_to_check: agent greps test files and finds assert statements referencing the target feature
agent runs code against an installed package or different checkout path rather than the working testbed
agent inspects import location (e.g., checks __file__ or runs pip show) but takes no corrective action to resolve shadowing
diff stat shows no changes to target implementation files in the working testbed
trajectory or rubric infers feature is already present from test assertions or installed-package behavior
branches with actual source changes or corrective action are scored lower than branches with only browsing, inspection, or verification
false_proxies_to_reject: test assertions referencing a feature = feature is implemented in the working testbed
installed-package behavior = testbed patch is validated
finding references to a feature in any file = implementation exists
inspecting import location (checking __file__, pip show) = progress toward resolving shadowing
metadata.abstain_when: feature is genuinely present in the correct testbed verified by actual source inspection of testbed source files, or task is purely exploratory with no implementation expected

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory makes actual source changes to target files in the working testbed and validates against the correct testbed, or takes concrete corrective action to resolve environment shadowing; test-assertion findings, wrong-checkout runs, or import-location inspections, if present, are not treated as implementation evidence.
scale.2: Minor evidence: some source changes present in the correct testbed, but validation partially relies on wrong checkout or installed package for some checks.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: agent finds test assertions, inspects import location, or runs against wrong checkout, but also makes some source changes to the correct testbed; progress signal is mixed.
scale.4: Clear evidence: agent primarily relies on test-assertion findings, wrong-checkout execution, or import-location inspection with minimal or no source changes to target files in the working testbed and no corrective action to resolve shadowing.
scale.5: Severe evidence: despite extensive test-assertion greps, wrong-checkout runs, or import-location inspections, no source changes are made to target files and no corrective action is taken, and the rubric or trajectory incorrectly treats reference-finding or inspection as implementation evidence, inverting the progress signal.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Environment shadowing resolution as critical progress
reference_golden_rubrics.description: When an agent discovers that a pip or site-packages installation of the target library shadows the testbed working copy and prevents patch validation, reward the agent for taking concrete corrective action that removes or bypasses the conflicting installation. This is strong evidence of progress even when no post-fix test run is visible, because the shadowing conflict was the blocking issue preventing all prior validation. A branch that successfully uninstalls the conflicting package must be scored higher than a branch that merely inspects the import location without taking corrective action. Equivalent corrective actions include pip uninstall of the conflicting package, reinstalling in development/editable mode, or otherwise ensuring the testbed source is the one imported at runtime.

metadata.stage: late investigation or environment-fix stage when tests show unchanged behavior despite source edits
metadata.activation: The trajectory shows the agent discovering that Python imports the target library from a different location than the testbed/working directory, or test runs consistently show unchanged behavior despite source edits, or the agent runs pip show or __file__ inspection and finds a site-packages location.
visible_positive_evidence_to_require: agent discovers import source mismatch via pip show, module __file__ inspection, or similar commands
agent takes concrete corrective action such as pip uninstall, reinstall in editable mode, or equivalent path resolution
corrective action completes successfully (e.g., uninstall confirmation message, no error)
contradictory_evidence: agent inspects import location but takes no corrective action
agent attempts to check import location but fails due to unrelated import errors and does not proceed to a fix
agent modifies PYTHONPATH or sys.path but the conflicting package still takes precedence
close_looking_exclusions: agent fixes an unrelated import error without addressing the shadowing issue itself — this is environment cleanup, not shadowing resolution
agent uninstalls packages unrelated to the shadowing conflict
agent changes sys.path in a single test script but does not address the root cause for all subsequent test runs
metadata.abstention_boundary: Do not use this as the primary criterion when the agent has not yet encountered the shadowing issue and is still working on patch semantics. Also abstain when the visible prefix does not show whether the corrective action enabled successful test runs and the underlying patch correctness remains uncertain — the environment fix unblocks validation but does not guarantee semantic correctness.
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: rewarding inspection of the import location (e.g., attempting to print a module's __file__ path) as evidence of progress when the agent has not taken corrective action to resolve the shadowing

scale.1: No evidence of shadowing discovery or resolution; the agent does not investigate why tests show unchanged behavior despite edits.
scale.2: The agent notices that tests show unchanged behavior but does not investigate the import source or take corrective action.
scale.3: The agent investigates the import source (e.g., checks __file__ or runs pip show) but either fails to complete the investigation due to unrelated errors or does not take corrective action.
scale.4: The agent discovers the import source mismatch and takes corrective action, but the action does not complete successfully or the visible prefix ends before confirming completion.
scale.5: The agent discovers the import source mismatch, takes concrete corrective action (e.g., pip uninstall of the conflicting package), and the action completes successfully, unblocking patch validation.

experiences.title: Value-wrapper hash/equality contract for unhashable dict/set failures
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python object used as a transparent wrapper for a primitive value fails in dict/set membership because it defines value-based equality but lacks a compatible hash implementation.
experiences.context: Applies in Python codebases, especially framework code, when the task reports `TypeError: unhashable type` during hash-based container operations such as dict membership, dict lookup, set insertion, or set membership, while equality/list membership still works. The trajectory should have visible evidence that the problematic class wraps an underlying prepared/raw value, implements `__eq__` by comparing that underlying value to either another wrapper or a raw value, and currently has no suitable `__hash__`. This guidance is most useful once the agent has inspected the class or reproduced the hash failure; it can be premature during broad repository exploration before equality semantics are known. Do not apply it when the object's equality is identity-based, when the desired behavior is to make a mutable/unhashable wrapped value hashable anyway, when the failure is better solved by changing caller-side coercion, or when the task concerns list/array membership only.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract between equality and hashing rather than merely requiring that an error disappear, and on directly verifying the specific reported hash-based container failure rather than only exploring related equality behavior or running broad suites. They were aligned because the decisive visible evidence was: a wrapper object compared equal to its underlying primitive value and to other wrappers with the same underlying value, but Python made it unhashable because `__eq__` existed without `__hash__`. A strong rubric should therefore ask whether the trajectory makes the wrapper hashable using the same basis as equality, so hash-based containers can find primitive-keyed entries and equal wrappers have equal hashes, and whether the agent directly executes the specific reported dict/set membership or lookup after the fix to confirm it works. It should also preserve the existing string/equality behavior and avoid unrelated widget-level or membership-call-site rewrites. A tempting but wrong criterion is to reward any hash implementation, such as identity hashing, hashing the associated model/object instance, or converting the wrapper to a string in callers; those approaches can either violate the Python hash/equality invariant or narrow the fix to one caller. Equally misleading is a trajectory that inspects `__eq__`, explores related wrapper/value behavior, or runs a broad test suite without ever directly testing the exact reported hash-based container operation; such exploration resembles progress but does not confirm the fix. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent inspected `__eq__`, identified the missing `__hash__`, selected the underlying value as the hash basis, directly verified the reported dict/set failure case after patching, and validated equality/hash consistency. Formatting or exact insertion location is secondary unless the edit corrupts the class structure.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Consistent hash for value-based wrapper equality with direct verification of reported failure
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should fix the unhashable wrapper by implementing hashability consistently with its existing value-based equality semantics and directly verify the specific reported hash-based container failure. The best evidence is that the agent recognizes the class defines equality against both another wrapper and the wrapped raw/prepared value, adds or plans a `__hash__` based on that same wrapped value, and directly executes the reported dict/set membership or lookup after the fix to confirm it works without changing the wrapper's comparison or string behavior. The criterion should distinguish this from identity-based hashing, hashing unrelated associated objects, caller-side coercion, list-membership-only tests, and from exploration of related equality/hash behavior or broad test suites that never directly test the reported hash failure.

required_visible_evidence: problem involves a Python object failing in hash-based containers with an unhashable-type error
trajectory identifies a wrapper class or value object with custom value-based equality
trajectory recognizes that equality compares using the wrapped/raw/prepared value
proposed or applied fix makes the object hashable using the same equality basis
the specific reported dict/set membership or lookup is directly executed after the fix and confirmed to work
validation or reasoning covers dict/set membership or lookup, not only list membership
avoid_credit_for: identity-based hash when equality is value-based
hashing an associated instance/object ignored by equality
rewriting only a widget/caller to coerce values
changing equality or string behavior unnecessarily
tests that only demonstrate list membership or equality
exploring related wrapper/value equality behavior without directly testing the reported hash-based container failure
running a broad test suite that passes without confirming the specific reported hash failure case is directly covered

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory identifies the hash/equality contract; it treats the issue generically or works only around one caller without addressing the unhashable wrapper.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory notices hashability or adds a hash-like change, but does not clearly connect the hash basis to existing equality semantics, risks hashing identity/unrelated state, or only explores related equality behavior without directly testing the reported hash failure.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory understands the missing-hash cause and proposes making the wrapper hashable, and may run a broad test suite that passes, but does not directly execute the specific reported dict/set membership or lookup to confirm the fix; correctness is plausible but unconfirmed.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly plans a hash based on the wrapped value, preserving existing equality behavior, and directly executes the reported dict/set membership or lookup to confirm it works.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory explicitly preserves the Python invariant that equal wrappers/raw values have compatible hashes, avoids identity or instance-based hashing, directly verifies the specific reported dict/set failure case after patching, and validates equality/hash consistency without unrelated behavioral changes.

experiences.title: Stage-Aware Issue Reproduction and Exploration-Phase Rubric Generation
experiences.description: Use when a bug report includes a concrete failing scenario and the trajectory is at a stage where reproduction, exploration, implementation, or validation evidence should be visible. The rubric generator must first assess the visible stage across all sibling branches before deciding what evidence to require, must not create implementation-specific rubrics when no branch has visible patches, must keep implementation/validation rubrics anchored to the literal observable contract rather than speculative architecture, preferred call-site placement, or process breadth, and must distinguish exploration commands from validation commands so that grep/find/cat output is never scored as validation evidence even when it superficially matches the rubric's expected format.
experiences.context: Applies in framework/library bug-fix tasks where the problem statement gives observable actual vs expected behavior, such as an ORM query result, rendered documentation output, migration recorder state, form choices, configuration behavior, numeric option semantics, linter/checker output, or introspection signature. This criterion is most useful once the agent has located the relevant subsystem, created or modified a candidate fix, or begun validation. When ALL sibling branches are in exploration with no visible patches, code edits, or implementation attempts, rubrics must focus on observable exploration progress, such as root cause identification, relevant code inspection, reproduction attempts, and condition-specific failure discovery, rather than implementation-specific criteria. Do not generate rubrics whose required evidence is implementation-level, such as specific method implementations, callback patterns, inheritance-level changes, call-chain placement, or exact file/function locations, when the paused prefix contains only exploration. Weight exploration-stage rubrics modestly and avoid high weights on unobservable implementation criteria. Abstain from exploration-phase-only rubrics when at least one sibling branch has visible patches or implementation attempts that can be judged against implementation-specific criteria. When a literal failing contract and a discriminating targeted project regression are visible, accept alternative implementations that satisfy the visible behavioral contract. Do not invent unrequired secondary entry points, architecture layers, helper paths, standalone tools, configuration surfaces, parallel paths, or exact fix locations as independent correctness requirements unless the task text or visible regression explicitly requires them. In disable-on-zero or analogous numeric configuration tasks, do not declare a deep iterator/core helper location mandatory when a small guard at the checker/run/entry point visibly satisfies the reported behavior and preserves positive enabled behavior. Keep a direct regression boundary for visibly broken existing behavior, patch usability, malformed edits, or disproportionate rewrites, but keep process and validation breadth subordinate to observed behavior. Within any stage, explicitly classify grep, find, cat, and source-reading commands as exploration, not validation, regardless of what they find or what output text they produce. Running the existing test suite, creating custom edge-case scripts, or executing reproductions that exercise named scenarios constitutes validation evidence. A rubric must not score exploration output as validation evidence even when the output text superficially matches the rubric's named format, and must not give higher credit to exploration-only evidence than to systematic validation that exercises all named scenarios.
experiences.experience:
The recurring rubric asked whether the agent first established a reproducible bug. This was useful when the visible trajectory contained task-specific reproduction evidence: a minimal script, focused test, or documented command showing the exact bad behavior and then confirming the intended behavior after the patch. It aligned well when the agent reproduced duplicate form options, stale migration application rows, incorrect manager method signatures, missing rendered members, option/configuration behavior, or numeric checker behavior, because those observations directly exercised the user-visible contract. It was less discriminative when generated too early, before the agent had any reasonable chance to run a reproduction, because some later-correct fixes began with code inspection only.

A critical failure mode occurred when the rubric generator created implementation-specific rubrics using privileged or speculative knowledge of the correct fix while all sibling branches were still in exploration with zero visible patches. This forced the judge to score based on weak proxy signals, leading to incorrect rankings. A better rubric should be stage-aware and concrete: first assess the visible stage across all sibling branches. If no branch has visible patches, generate rubrics about observable exploration progress: root cause identification, relevant code inspection, reproduction attempts, and condition-specific failure discovery. If at least one branch has visible patches or implementation attempts, then implementation-specific criteria may become appropriate, but only when they are justified by the task text or visible behavioral contract.

A second causal failure mode occurs later, after a literal failing contract and a discriminating targeted project regression are visible. At that point, the rubric must not convert a suspected call chain, preferred architectural layer, secondary entry point, helper path, standalone mode, configuration surface, or exact edit location into an independent correctness requirement. The primary scoring mass should go to direct behavioral satisfaction: the candidate implements the stated condition, makes the reported failing scenario behave as expected, and preserves the relevant pre-existing positive/default behavior. Alternative implementations that satisfy the same visible contract should receive high credit even if they are smaller, more central, more peripheral, or placed differently than the generator expected. Conversely, a broader patch, more elaborate architecture, or wider validation matrix should not outrank a simpler implementation that directly satisfies the discriminating behavior.

The smallest reusable lesson from disable-on-zero numeric configuration fixes is: judge the functional guard and patch integrity, not the presumed best call-site. If the task says a numeric setting of 0 disables a check, a small early-return guard keyed to the disabled value can be correct in either the checker/run entry point or the deeper iteration/helper path, provided it disables the reported entry point and preserves enabled positive values. A rubric should give positive weight, typically around 1.0 to 1.3, to visible behavior: setting 0 produces no reported violation, a positive threshold still reports the violation, and the edit is small, focused, and syntactically usable. It should not give top credit merely because a branch targets a preferred deep method. Add, when visible, a separate negative or regression-boundary criterion with lower-to-comparable weight, typically around 0.7 to 1.0, for oversized fragile rewrites, full-method replacement scripts, malformed edits, or changes whose size and risk are disproportionate to a simple guard. This negative criterion should penalize patch integrity problems even if the edit touches the anticipated method, and it should not penalize an entry-point guard solely for not living in the deeper helper.

A third failure mode is evidence-to-anchor inversion: the rubric gives full credit to a branch whose final visible actions are grep, find, or cat commands (pure exploration with no validation executed) because the output text superficially matches the rubric's named format, while giving only partial credit to a branch that ran the existing test suite and created a custom edge-case script validating all named scenarios programmatically. This inversion occurs when the judge anchors on visible output text matching the rubric's example format rather than assessing whether the agent performed systematic validation. The smallest reusable lesson here is: explicitly classify grep, find, cat, and source-reading commands as exploration, not validation, regardless of what they find. Running the existing test suite and creating custom validation scripts that exercise all named scenarios are stronger evidence than a single manual CLI check or a grep match. When a branch's visible evidence includes both test suite execution and custom edge-case validation covering all named error paths, that should score at least as high as a branch showing only exploration commands or a partial manual reproduction. Do not anchor on whether the visible output text matches the rubric's example format; anchor on whether the agent performed systematic validation across all named scenarios. Explicitly forbid scoring exploration commands as validation evidence. Preserve uncertainty when the visible prefix only shows exploration without any executed validation, as it cannot distinguish whether the underlying patch fully resolves the issue.

For generated rubric semantics, use this ordering: first decide stage; then, for implementation-visible branches, identify the literal contract; then map evidence to behavior and integrity. Positive evidence includes exact commands, scripts, assertions, rendered output checks, query results, exception/message changes, targeted regression names, direct diff reasoning, disabled-versus-enabled checks, and preservation of existing default or positive behavior. Crucially, running the existing test suite and creating custom edge-case scripts that exercise all named scenarios are positive validation evidence, while grep, find, cat, and source-reading commands are exploration and must not be scored as validation regardless of output text matches. Negative evidence includes visible breakage of adjacent behavior, broad suppressions that bypass required functionality, malformed or unusable edits, and disproportionately large rewrites for a narrow condition. Neutral or uncertain evidence includes reading a plausible method name, choosing one of several plausible call sites, validating only a secondary entry point without tying it to the report, or showing exploration commands whose output superficially matches the rubric's format without any executed validation. These uncertain signals may support a mid score but must not dominate direct functional evidence or outrank systematic validation.

Avoid generic criteria such as must run the full test suite, must test every parameter value, must validate every entry point, or must reproduce before reading code. Those process signals can add confidence, but they must remain subordinate to the observed behavioral contract. Keep at most one direct regression boundary: penalize visible breakage of existing positive-value behavior, defaults, message/stat flow, state preservation, malformed patch symptoms, or broad late-stage suppressions that bypass required functionality. Do not turn that regression boundary into another patch-location rubric, and do not generate multiple correlated architecture-placement rubrics that collectively reward breadth or preferred placement over correctness. Preserve uncertainty when the visible prefix cannot confirm syntactic validity or behavioral effect; assign moderate credit for plausible but unvalidated guards rather than inferring correctness from method name alone. When the visible prefix shows only exploration commands without executed validation, do not infer validation from output text format matches; assign at most moderate credit and preserve uncertainty about whether the underlying patch resolves the issue.

experiences.title: Do not reward read-only exploration after the key contract is already known
experiences.description: Use this warning when a trajectory contains many safe read commands, but the task’s success depends on applying a specific integration contract, lifecycle transition, owner/container boundary, or compatibility case rather than merely avoiding premature writes. After localization, relevant source or history reading is diagnosis only unless the available workspace state contains an actual implementation diff that can be judged against the contract.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent code-repair trajectories across TypeScript/React, Go, Python, and similar codebases where the recent evidence is mostly grep/cat/sed, git history inspection, or other file reading. The misleading case is when normal or repetitive read-before-write behavior looks disciplined even though the agent has already identified the relevant files/APIs, is looping on similar searches, has not made task-specific progress, or is about to implement from a superficial understanding. Judges should inspect the combined available workspace state, including any inherited diff or summary fields, before deciding whether implementation evidence exists: lack of a newly visible edit command is not by itself proof that no patch is present, but when both the visible and inherited workspace state show no patch, reads and history browsing cannot receive semantic-completion credit. The original read-before-write rubric may still be appropriate very early in exploration, especially when the agent is considering broad or destructive edits before locating the relevant component, tests, or API contract. It is not a strong correctness signal once the visible trajectory already contains enough file-local context and the remaining risk is semantic integration. If workspace summaries or diffs are unavailable, truncated, or contradictory, preserve uncertainty rather than assuming either success or failure.
experiences.experience:
The previous rubric judged the presence of non-destructive exploration before writes. That is useful as a safety/process check, but it overemphasizes command hygiene in tasks where correctness hinges on domain behavior: using the existing service instead of bypassing it, clearing owned state rather than only stopping an object, updating the right lifecycle entry point, preserving compatibility fallbacks, or applying a state/filter contract with the action’s intent.

A better rubric should ask whether the agent has converted exploration into task-specific evidence and implementation choices. Avoid the tempting criterion of counting grep/cat/sed commands, git log, git show, or source reads as positive progress after the key contract is already known. These observations can support localization or diagnosis, but they do not by themselves show that the behavior was corrected.

When judging a late-stage trajectory, first map the evidence into three buckets:
1. Localization evidence: relevant reads, searches, and history inspection that identify the files, APIs, prior behavior, or expected contract. This is useful early but should not be scored as semantic completion after localization.
2. Implementation-state evidence: an active workspace diff, changed-file summary, non-empty patch summary, or visible edit that changes the source or tests. This evidence may come from the current visible segment or may already exist in the inherited workspace state. Do not require a particular edit command, and do not penalize a correct inherited patch merely because the current segment only reads or validates it.
3. Contract-validation evidence: reasoning or tests showing that the actual diff satisfies the owner/lifecycle/state/compatibility contract described by the task.

The decisive negative case is post-localization diagnosis-only behavior: the relevant contract or target files are already known, the available workspace state shows no implementation diff, and the trajectory continues with read-only searches, source printing, or history browsing without applying the contract. Even highly relevant history inspection remains diagnosis only in that case. If translated into a scoring rubric, make this a negative contract-follow-through criterion with meaningful weight, not a positive exploration bonus; high scores for method/function/behavior correction should require an actual diff that can be evaluated for semantic correctness.

The close-looking exclusion is a trajectory that reads first and then has a real source or test diff, or begins from an inherited diff. In that situation, judge the diff’s behavioral content: whether it uses the right abstraction, edits the correct lifecycle or owner boundary, preserves named compatibility cases, and is validated by appropriate tests or test-oriented reasoning. Authorship within the visible segment is less important than whether the active patch actually satisfies the task contract.

Prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent inspected the exact owner API or reusable service named by the discovered code path; stopped repeating identical searches after finding the relevant facts; planned or made edits at the lifecycle boundary where the bug occurs; accounted for compatibility or parent/owner context mentioned in the task; added or targeted tests for the described behavior; and, when a diff is present, its actual semantics rather than the mere presence of exploration commands.

Abstain or score conservatively when the workspace summary, inherited diff, or patch state is unavailable or contradictory. Do not infer a missing fix solely from the absence of a visible edit command, and do not infer a successful fix solely from relevant reading.

experiences.title: Root-Cause Pattern Correction vs. Symptom Patching in Multi-Path Bugs
experiences.description: When a shared incorrect pattern (wrong indexing axis, wrong aggregation strategy, wrong loop variable scope, or overbroad surface-based classifier) causes failures across multiple code paths, evaluate whether a continuation corrects the pattern uniformly or merely patches individual symptoms with per-path conditionals or broad heuristics that pass tested examples while misclassifying untested semantic cases.
experiences.context: Applies when comparing sibling continuations on a bug that manifests in multiple code paths sharing a single underlying incorrect pattern. The parent trajectory shows the bug surface; continuations may either address the shared root cause, add branch-specific patches, or replace one shared mistake with an overbroad predicate that treats superficially similar but semantically different cases alike. This experience helps judge which continuations show genuine semantic progress versus superficial symptom suppression or incomplete validation of a claimed uniform fix.
experiences.experience:
When a bug appears in multiple code paths, first determine whether those paths share a single incorrect pattern. Signs of a shared pattern include: the same indexing axis used consistently across paths, the same aggregation strategy applied in each branch, the same loop variable scope reused, or the same helper predicate/classification rule controlling several branches. If a shared pattern exists, the correct fix replaces the pattern itself—for example, switching from per-fold best indices to a single aggregated best hyperparameter, changing the indexing axis uniformly across all branches, or narrowing a classifier so it distinguishes the intended semantic class rather than relying only on a surface string/shape cue.

Positive visible evidence that a continuation addresses the root cause: the agent identifies the shared incorrect pattern by name or description, explains why it produces wrong results across all affected paths, compares against a known-correct reference path when available, and applies a single uniform correction that changes the underlying logic rather than adding branches around the old logic. Stronger positive evidence includes testing or reasoning over both true-positive cases and semantically distinct counterexamples that can share the same visible signature. For example, if the fix treats values that “look like offsets,” “look like indices,” or “look like singleton dimensions” specially, it should also account for legitimate named/domain objects that may have the same surface form but should not be converted or collapsed.

A decisive distinction for judging is whether the continuation’s claimed root-cause fix preserves the semantic boundary of the affected cases. A broad rule such as “if the value matches this pattern, treat it as the target case” can look like a uniform correction because it fixes the reported paths, but it is still incomplete if other valid paths produce the same surface pattern while requiring different handling. Tests of easy positives and easy negatives are not enough when a confounding sibling case is predictable from the visible logic. Testing a proxy object with the same surface string is not equivalent to testing the semantic class that must be preserved.

Contradictory or negative evidence: the continuation adds per-path conditionals, dimensionality checks, or branch-specific if-statements that suppress individual symptoms while preserving the original incorrect logic in each branch. Also treat as negative evidence a broad classifier/conversion rule that fixes the reported examples but would mis-handle semantically distinct cases sharing the same apparent format. The continuation may pass its own checks because those checks exercise only the patched paths or only non-confounding examples, but the underlying pattern remains incorrect in untested branches or boundary cases.

Tempting false proxies that must not be confused with root-cause correction: (1) adding a dimensionality, regex, string-format, or shape check that makes a specific test pass without changing the semantic logic; (2) fixing one path while leaving the identical incorrect pattern in another path; (3) adding a conditional that special-cases one parameter combination while the general case still uses the wrong pattern; (4) validating a broad rule only on true target cases plus ordinary-looking non-target cases, while omitting non-target cases that share the target’s surface signature; (5) testing a proxy object that happens to display the same string/shape as a semantic class, then treating that as evidence that the semantic class itself is handled correctly.
