Close-looking exclusions: A patch that returns self.data['attrs'].get('id') without fallback may appear incomplete because it returns None when no custom ID is set and may only test the custom-id path. However, this is the correct behavior — the old generated ID was the bug. Do not penalize the no-fallback version for lacking a fallback or for testing only the custom-id path. Conversely, do not reward the fallback version for testing both paths when the fallback path shows the bug persisting.

Abstention boundary: If the visible evidence does not show what id_for_label returns when data['attrs'] has no 'id' key, and no test exercises the no-auto_id case, and the issue description does not clarify the expected behavior in that case, do not assume a fallback is needed or correct.

experiences.title: BoundWidget.id_for_label: distinguish fallback-to-generated-id from correct None return via auto_id=False output and diff_stat
experiences.description: When judging BoundWidget.id_for_label fixes, the critical distinguisher is the auto_id=False edge case: correct implementations return None (via self.data['attrs'].get('id') without fallback), while incorrect implementations fall back to the generated 'id_%s_%s' format. The diff_stat pattern (insertions vs deletions) and sibling branch outputs revealing the auto_id=False behavior are key evidence.
experiences.context: The issue asks to change BoundWidget.id_for_label from returning 'id_%s_%s' % (name, index) to returning self.data['attrs'].get('id'). The critical edge case is auto_id=False, where attrs has no 'id' key. The correct fix returns None; an incorrect fix falls back to the generated format. Two implementation patterns appear: (1) clean one-line replacement (1 insertion, 1 deletion) that returns None when attrs lacks 'id', and (2) fallback added alongside original return (3 insertions, 0 deletions) that generates 'id_%s_%s' when attrs lacks 'id'.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When evaluating BoundWidget.id_for_label patches, specifically check the auto_id=False edge case output and the diff_stat pattern (insertions vs deletions).

Positive evidence: A branch that shows id_for_label returning None when widget.data['attrs'] is {} (auto_id=False) has the correct implementation. A diff_stat of 1 insertion/1 deletion indicates a clean one-line replacement matching the expected fix. A branch demonstrating this shows output like 'id_for_label(): None' and 'data[attrs].get(id): None' for the auto_id=False case, and correct id matching for custom auto_id and RadioSelect cases.

Contradictory evidence: A branch that shows id_for_label returning 'id_choices_0' (generated format) when widget.data['attrs'] is {} (auto_id=False) has the buggy fallback. A diff_stat of 3 insertions/0 deletions suggests the original return was retained and a fallback was added, breaking the auto_id=False case. A sibling branch with this diff_stat shows output like 'widget.id_for_label: id_choices_0' for auto_id=False, revealing the fallback.

Close-looking exclusions: When a branch's auto_id=False output is truncated, check sibling branches with the same diff_stat and same parent for the revealing output. A sibling with 3 insertions/0 deletions that shows 'widget.id_for_label: id_choices_0' for auto_id=False reveals the fallback bug in all branches sharing that diff_stat pattern. Do not assume a branch is correct because its other tests pass; the auto_id=False case is the critical distinguisher.

Reject the misleading evidence pattern: Do not score a branch higher simply because it runs more tests or shows more passing output overall. A branch with truncated critical edge case output and a fallback bug (3 insertions/0 deletions) should not outscore a branch with clear correct None return (1 insertion/1 deletion), even if the latter has fewer passing tests or a test failure due to environment configuration issues (e.g., template backend not configured).

Abstention boundary: When the auto_id=False output is truncated in all branches with a given diff_stat AND no sibling branch with the same diff_stat reveals the behavior, the correctness of that diff_stat group cannot be determined from visible evidence alone.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: BoundWidget.id_for_label uses attrs id
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The child modifies BoundWidget.id_for_label to return the id from self.data['attrs'].get('id') (which carries the auto_id-generated or explicitly-set id from ChoiceWidget.subwidgets) instead of the hardcoded 'id_%s_%s' format. Progress is scored by whether the implementation: (a) reads from self.data['attrs'].get('id'), (b) returns None (not a generated fallback) when attrs lacks 'id' (auto_id=False case), and (c) passes the observable test cases (custom widget id, default auto_id, custom auto_id format, RadioSelect, auto_id=False). Equivalence (3) = child makes same semantic change as parent (if parent were fixed) or child implements the core fix but with minor syntactic differences. Regression (1-2) = child loses the fix, reverts to hardcoded format, or incorrectly falls back to generated id when attrs has no id. Clear progress (4-5) = child implements correct attrs-based lookup with proper None fallback and all test cases pass.

metadata.judge_focus: Whether the child's BoundWidget.id_for_label property reads from self.data['attrs'].get('id') instead of the hardcoded format, and critically whether it returns None (not a generated fallback) when attrs has no 'id' key (auto_id=False case), and whether edge cases (RadioSelect, custom auto_id) are handled
metadata.failure_mode: Reverting to hardcoded id format, incorrectly falling back to generated id when attrs lacks id (breaking auto_id=False), or not using attrs id at all

scale.1: Child reverts to or retains the buggy hardcoded 'id_%s_%s' % (name, index) implementation, or submits no patch to boundfield.py
scale.2: Child attempts a fix but uses incorrect attribute path (e.g., self.data['id'], self.attrs['id'], widget.attrs['id']) or incorrectly falls back to the generated id format when attrs has no 'id' key (breaking auto_id=False)
scale.3: Child implements the core fix: returns self.data['attrs'].get('id') (returning None when attrs has no 'id' key) without any fallback to the generated id format, matching the expected semantic change from the issue description
scale.4: Child implements correct attrs-based lookup with proper None fallback AND all provided test cases pass (custom widget id, default auto_id, custom auto_id format, RadioSelect, auto_id=False)
scale.5: Child implements correct attrs-based lookup with proper None fallback, all test cases pass, AND the implementation is clean (e.g., uses .get('id') without default) without redundant code or syntax errors

experiences.title: Self-written test output cannot substitute for full test coverage when patch modifies existing code
experiences.description: When a continuation's patch includes deletions of existing code, convincing self-written test output is insufficient evidence of correctness. Self-written tests cover only scenarios the agent designed, not the full test suite. Weigh patch risk (deletions modifying existing code) against limited test evidence.
experiences.context: Django RenameModel migration operation where explicit db_table should make table renaming a no-op while preserving FK/M2M updates. Two parent approaches: Parent 1 explored with minimal additive patch (3 insertions), Parent 2 implemented a larger fix modifying existing code (7 insertions, 6 deletions).
experiences.experience:
Activation: A continuation shows passing self-written test output for a fix, but the patch includes deletions of existing code (visible in diff stats).

Positive evidence: Continuation 6 shows test output demonstrating all three scenarios passing — explicit db_table preserved, auto-generated db_table renamed, FK references correct table, M2M through table preserved. This is compelling visible evidence that the fix works for the tested scenarios.

Contradictory evidence: The same continuation's patch has 6 deletions modifying existing code in the migration operation's database_forwards. Self-written tests cover only scenarios the agent thought to test; they cannot verify that existing functionality remains unbroken. The diff stat (7 insertions, 6 deletions) signals higher regression risk than a purely additive patch. A patch that modifies existing database_forwards logic may break edge cases not covered by self-written tests.

Close-looking exclusions: (1) Continuation 1's comprehensive test failures (steps 37-39) show 'table already exists' errors, which are test script setup issues (duplicate table creation in test code), not patch correctness issues. The state_forwards test at step 36 shows 'SUCCESS: Table name preserved.' Do not penalize the patch for test script bugs. (2) Continuation 5 has the same patch as Continuation 6 but no successful test output, yet received nearly identical scores — suggesting over-reliance on patch presence rather than test evidence quality. (3) No-patch continuations should be scored based on their inherited parent state, not their own exploration activity.

Abstention boundary: Cannot determine from visible evidence alone which specific test scenarios a patch with deletions might break. The visible self-written tests may pass while other tests covering edge cases (self-referential FKs, multiple FKs, composite keys, or existing migration functionality) may fail.

Reject the misleading pattern: Do not treat convincing self-written test output as definitive proof of correctness when the patch modifies existing code. Self-written tests are designed by the same agent that wrote the patch and may share the same blind spots. The diff stat showing deletions is a visible risk signal that should be weighed against limited test evidence.

reference_golden_rubrics: RenameModel explicit db_table no-op with related field preservation

experiences.title: Do not let explicit backward compatibility proxy class override official test suite execution evidence
experiences.description: When judging Django messages LEVEL_TAGS override_settings fixes, a smaller patch with an explicit _LevelTags proxy class (implementing __getitem__, keys, values, items) can appear more correct than a larger patch, but actual correctness depends on passing the official Django test suite. The judge must weight official test runner execution higher than apparent code cleanliness or explicit backward compatibility implementations.
experiences.context: Django contrib.messages LEVEL_TAGS override_settings fix where LEVEL_TAGS must become dynamic while maintaining backward compatibility for direct base.LEVEL_TAGS access. Multiple continuations implement the fix with varying approaches and validation strategies.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When evaluating Django messages LEVEL_TAGS fixes that require both dynamic behavior under override_settings and backward compatibility for direct LEVEL_TAGS access.

Positive evidence: A continuation that runs the official Django test runner (python tests/runtests.py messages_tests) with returncode 0 provides stronger validation evidence than one using a custom TestRunner, per the validation rubric scale 5 vs scale 4.

Contradictory evidence: A continuation using a custom TestRunner setup instead of the official runner, especially when step output acknowledges errors (e.g., 'errors are related to missing URL configurations, not my fix'), should not be scored higher than one using the official runner, even if the custom-runner continuation has a cleaner patch with explicit backward compatibility proxy class.

Close-looking exclusions: A smaller, cleaner patch (e.g., ~1300 chars, 21 insertions, 2 deletions) with an explicit _LevelTags class implementing __getitem__, keys, values, and items may look more correct than a larger patch (e.g., ~4200 chars, 31 insertions, 36 deletions), but patch cleanliness does not substitute for official test suite validation. Do not infer correctness from the presence of a backward compatibility proxy class alone. Explicitly reject the pattern of rewarding apparent code quality (small diff, named proxy class with dict-like methods) over the evidence value of running the official test runner.

Abstention boundary: When test output is truncated and no branch shows complete, visible passing output from the official test runner, and no branch acknowledges errors or uses a non-official runner, cannot rank branches by validation quality from visible evidence alone.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Dynamic LEVEL_TAGS respects override_settings with backward compatibility
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The child trajectory must demonstrate that Message.level_tag correctly returns the overridden MESSAGE_TAGS value when @override_settings(MESSAGE_TAGS=...) is active, while maintaining backward compatibility so that direct access to base.LEVEL_TAGS (as used in tests/messages_tests/base.py) returns the current dynamic tags. Parent baseline: LEVEL_TAGS is a static constant; child progress: LEVEL_TAGS becomes a dynamic proxy (e.g., via __getattr__ or property) that calls utils.get_level_tags() on each access, and Message.level_tag uses utils.get_level_tags().get(self.level, ''). Regression: child loses the dynamic behavior, breaks existing tests that mutate base.LEVEL_TAGS, or returns empty/incorrect level_tag under override_settings.

metadata.oracle_test: from django.test import override_settings; from django.contrib.messages.storage.base import Message, LEVEL_TAGS; from django.contrib.messages import constants; with override_settings(MESSAGE_TAGS={constants.INFO: 'custom'}): assert Message(constants.INFO, 'x').level_tag == 'custom'; assert LEVEL_TAGS[constants.INFO] == 'custom'
metadata.code_review: Check base.py for LEVEL_TAGS definition: should be a dynamic object (class with __getitem__/__getattr__ delegating to utils.get_level_tags()) not a static dict. Message.level_tag property should call utils.get_level_tags().get(self.level, '').
metadata.judge_focus: Behavioral correctness under override_settings + test suite backward compatibility
metadata.failure_mode: Static LEVEL_TAGS constant, broken __getitem__ on dynamic proxy, Message.level_tag not using utils.get_level_tags()

scale.1: Child loses all dynamic behavior: LEVEL_TAGS remains a static dict, Message.level_tag returns original tags even under override_settings, or patch is empty/no-op.
scale.2: Child makes LEVEL_TAGS dynamic but breaks backward compatibility: tests fail because base.LEVEL_TAGS[constants.INFO] raises KeyError/AttributeError or returns stale values, or Message.level_tag works but direct LEVEL_TAGS access doesn't.
scale.3: Equivalent to parent: no meaningful change to LEVEL_TAGS behavior, or child only adds exploration without a working fix.
scale.4: Child implements dynamic LEVEL_TAGS that works for Message.level_tag under override_settings AND maintains backward compatibility for direct LEVEL_TAGS access (tests pass), but validation is incomplete (e.g., only manual test shown).
scale.5: Child implements correct dynamic LEVEL_TAGS proxy, Message.level_tag uses utils.get_level_tags(), all existing messages tests pass, and override_settings behavior is validated (via test run or explicit reproduction script showing both Message.level_tag and LEVEL_TAGS[level] return overridden values).

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Validation evidence: test suite execution vs manual checks
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The child trajectory should demonstrate validation evidence that the fix works correctly and doesn't regress existing behavior. Parent baseline: no validation shown in the parent trajectory. Child progress: runs the Django messages test suite (tests/messages_tests/) and shows passing results, or runs a comprehensive reproduction script that exercises both the override_settings fix and backward compatibility for direct LEVEL_TAGS access. Equivalence: only runs a minimal manual check (single python -c snippet) without test suite execution. Regression: no validation evidence, or validation shows test failures that the child doesn't address.

metadata.oracle_test: python tests/runtests.py messages_tests  (or equivalent Django test runner invocation)
metadata.code_review: Look for explicit test runner commands targeting messages_tests, not just manual python -c scripts. Check if test output shows pass/fail for the full messages test suite.
metadata.judge_focus: Quality and completeness of validation evidence
metadata.failure_mode: Only manual python -c checks, no test suite run, or test failures ignored

scale.1: No validation evidence shown, or only exploration commands (grep, cat, file reading) with no execution of any test or reproduction.
scale.2: Only a minimal manual reproduction script (single python -c snippet) showing the override_settings fix works, but no Django test suite execution and no evidence of backward compatibility testing.
scale.3: Equivalent to parent: no validation evidence in the child either, or only the same minimal manual check as parent.
scale.4: Runs a comprehensive manual reproduction script that tests both Message.level_tag under override_settings AND direct LEVEL_TAGS access (backward compatibility), but does not run the official Django messages test suite.
scale.5: Runs the official Django messages test suite (tests/messages_tests/ or equivalent) and shows passing results, demonstrating both the fix works and no regressions in existing behavior.

experiences.title: Backward-Compatible Module-Level Proxy vs. Simple Dynamic Replacement in LEVEL_TAGS
experiences.description: When a rubric requires both dynamic behavior and backward compatibility with a module-level attribute save/restore pattern, the judge must distinguish solutions implementing a full proxy with module-level assignment support from those that simply replace the constant with a dynamic object. The identical level_tag property change across all patches is misleading evidence of equivalence; the distinguishing factor is the LEVEL_TAGS proxy implementation visible in grep output, comments, and save/restore test results.
experiences.context: A Django messages fix where LEVEL_TAGS must be made dynamic (reading settings on each access) while preserving backward compatibility with a save/restore pattern that assigns to and reads from the module-level attribute. The rubric's top scale requires the save/restore pattern to work without modification, while scale 3-4 only requires dynamic behavior with possible backward compatibility gaps.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When a rubric scale explicitly distinguishes between 'dynamic but breaks direct access' (scale 3-4) and 'fully dynamic and backward-compatible with save/restore' (scale 5), and multiple patches share an identical core change (e.g., level_tag property calling utils.get_level_tags()).

Positive evidence for backward compatibility: Proxy class names indicating assignment support (e.g., _LevelTagsProxy vs _LevelTags); comments about module-level assignment (e.g., 'allow module-level assignment to LEVEL_TAGS'); test output demonstrating save/restore works (e.g., 'After assignment:' and 'After restore:' with correct values); larger diff sizes (e.g., 169 lines / 5630 chars) indicating comprehensive proxy implementation with __setattr__ or __getattr__ handling.

Contradictory evidence against backward compatibility: Simpler class names without 'Proxy' suffix; absence of module-level assignment comments in grep output; no visible save/restore test output; smaller diff sizes (e.g., 23 lines / 1333 chars) suggesting simpler replacement without assignment support.

Close-looking exclusions: Comprehensive test output showing 'LEVEL_TAGS proxy works like a dict' and 'works with override_settings' but NOT testing the save/restore pattern specifically — this tests dict-like behavior and override_settings, not module-level assignment; test_custom_tags passing for CookieTests/SessionTests — this may use override_settings but does not demonstrate the save/restore pattern; all patches showing the identical level_tag change (return utils.get_level_tags().get(self.level, '')) — this is necessary but not sufficient for the top scale.

Misleading evidence to reject: The identical level_tag property change across all patches makes them appear equivalent. The judge must NOT treat this as evidence of equal backward compatibility. The level_tag change only proves dynamic behavior (scale 3-4); the LEVEL_TAGS proxy implementation determines whether the save/restore pattern works (scale 5). Do not rank solutions by submission order or patch file creation success when the rubric's differentiator is backward compatibility depth.

Abstention boundary: When no visible evidence shows the LEVEL_TAGS class implementation (e.g., no grep output, no file content display) and no save/restore test output, the judge cannot determine backward compatibility support and should not differentiate based on patch size alone.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Dynamic LEVEL_TAGS with Backward Compatibility
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The child trajectory should modify django/contrib/messages/storage/base.py so that LEVEL_TAGS dynamically reads from settings (via utils.get_level_tags()) each time it's accessed, rather than being a static constant initialized at import time. Crucially, the fix must preserve backward compatibility by keeping LEVEL_TAGS accessible as a module-level attribute (e.g., via a property, __getattr__, or callable object) so that existing code like tests/messages_tests/base.py can still read and assign to base.LEVEL_TAGS directly. The child should score high if it achieves dynamic behavior while maintaining the attribute interface; score at equivalence (3) if it only makes level_tag dynamic but breaks direct LEVEL_TAGS access; score low if it leaves LEVEL_TAGS as a static constant or breaks the Message.level_tag property.

metadata.judge_focus: Whether LEVEL_TAGS is made dynamic (reads settings on each access) while preserving module-level attribute access for backward compatibility with tests/messages_tests/base.py
metadata.failure_mode: Breaking direct access to base.LEVEL_TAGS that tests rely on for save/restore pattern

scale.1: LEVEL_TAGS remains a static module-level constant initialized at import time; @override_settings has no effect on Message.level_tag
scale.2: LEVEL_TAGS is removed or made inaccessible as a module attribute, breaking tests/messages_tests/base.py which does base.LEVEL_TAGS = ... and expects to read it back
scale.3: Message.level_tag property correctly calls utils.get_level_tags() dynamically, but LEVEL_TAGS is not accessible as a module-level attribute (or is a stale constant), so direct access in tests fails
scale.4: LEVEL_TAGS is made dynamic (e.g., via __getattr__, property, or callable class) so it returns current utils.get_level_tags() on each access, AND Message.level_tag uses it correctly; minor issues like missing dict methods (get, keys) on the dynamic object
scale.5: LEVEL_TAGS is fully dynamic and backward-compatible: acts as a dict-like object (supports get, keys, values, items, __getitem__) that always reflects current settings, Message.level_tag works with @override_settings, and tests/messages_tests/base.py save/restore pattern works without modification

experiences.title: Validation Volume Does Not Substitute for Fix Correctness in SQLite Schema-Backend Edits
experiences.description: When every continuation applies the same one-line fix to a SQLite schema-backend condition, the judge must not score continuations differently based on how many test suites or custom scripts they run. Extensive validation activity (custom migration tests, schema test suite, full migrations suite reporting hundreds of tests OK) is not evidence that the fix itself is correct, especially when the validation includes flawed isolation, truncated output, or suites that do not exercise the specific fixed code path.
experiences.context: The issue is that adding a nullable OneToOneField on SQLite crashes with 'Cannot add a UNIQUE column' because SQLite's ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN cannot add a UNIQUE column. The fix modifies the add_field condition in sqlite3/schema.py to also trigger _remake_table when field.unique is True. All continuations apply the same one-line change: `if not field.null or self.effective_default(field) is not None or field.unique:`. The continuations differ primarily in the breadth of validation they perform after applying the fix.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When a continuation runs multiple test suites (schema tests, migration tests, custom scripts) after applying a one-line fix to a schema backend, and the judge is tempted to score it higher than continuations with less validation activity.

Positive evidence: A continuation runs custom migration tests exercising both nullable and non-nullable OneToOneField additions, invokes the schema test suite, and runs the full migrations test suite (630 tests, all OK). This appears to demonstrate thorough, multi-dimensional validation.

Contradictory evidence: (1) The custom migration test initially failed with 'table already exists,' indicating poor test isolation; it was then re-created to succeed, but the workaround may mask real issues rather than confirm the fix. (2) The schema test suite output was truncated in the visible state, so pass/fail cannot be confirmed. (3) The 630-test migrations suite tests migration operations broadly, not the specific UNIQUE-column-add path that the fix addresses. (4) All continuations have the same one-line fix, so validation volume alone should not differentiate correctness outcomes.

Close-looking exclusions: (a) 'Ran 630 tests OK' in the migrations suite—this does not specifically test adding a UNIQUE column via OneToOneField on SQLite; passing it is not evidence the fix works. (b) Custom test succeeding after re-creation—the initial 'table already exists' failure shows the test environment was not properly reset, and the re-created test may pass for the wrong reasons (e.g., table already exists from the prior run). (c) Schema tests returning exit code 0—the output was truncated, so failures may be hidden; exit code alone is insufficient when output is not fully visible.

Abstention boundary: When all continuations apply the same fix (identical diff), the judge must not differentiate correctness scores based on validation volume alone. If the fix is identical, the correctness outcome should be the same regardless of how many test suites were run. Validation rubrics should only reward validation that (a) specifically exercises the fixed code path, (b) has fully visible and interpretable results, and (c) is not undermined by test-isolation flaws or truncated output. Reject the misleading pattern that 'more tests run = more correct fix.'

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Fix Validation Completeness
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The child trajectory must demonstrate thorough validation of the fix across multiple dimensions: (1) the original reported issue (nullable OneToOneField), (2) related edge cases (non-nullable OneToOneField, other unique=True fields, unique constraints), (3) existing Django test suites for schema operations and migrations, and (4) data integrity after the fix. Parent baseline: the parent applied the fix and verified with a simple reproduction script only. Progress: the child adds validation covering all four dimensions. Equivalence: the child only validates the original issue (like parent) or adds only one additional dimension. Regression: the child loses the fix or validates fewer dimensions than the parent.

metadata.failure_mode: insufficient_validation_coverage

scale.1: Child only runs the original reproduction script (or less), validating only the exact reported nullable OneToOneField case.
scale.2: Child validates the original issue plus one additional dimension (e.g., one edge case OR one Django test suite run).
scale.3: Child validates the original issue plus two additional dimensions (e.g., original + edge cases + one test suite, or original + two test suites). Equivalent to parent's validation level plus minimal extra checking.
scale.4: Child validates the original issue plus three dimensions (e.g., original + edge cases + schema tests + migration tests, or original + edge cases + data integrity + one test suite).
scale.5: Child validates all four dimensions comprehensively: original nullable OneToOneField, non-nullable OneToOneField and other unique fields, Django schema and migration test suites pass (or pre-existing failures documented), and data integrity operations work correctly with the added field.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Controlled Validation Methodology
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The child trajectory must demonstrate controlled validation by establishing a pre-fix baseline to distinguish regressions caused by the fix from pre-existing test failures. Parent baseline: the parent applied the fix and verified with a simple test script but did not run the Django test suite. Progress: the child reverts the fix, runs relevant Django tests (schema, migrations, sqlite3 backend) to catalog pre-existing failures, re-applies the fix, runs tests again, and compares results to isolate the fix's impact. Equivalence: the child only runs tests with the fix applied (no baseline) or only runs the simple reproduction script. Regression: the child claims validation without any test execution, or loses the fix while attempting validation.

metadata.failure_mode: uncontrolled_validation

scale.1: Child provides no test validation beyond the original reproduction script, or tests don't exercise the fixed code path.
scale.2: Child runs some Django tests with the fix applied but does not establish a pre-fix baseline; cannot distinguish fix-caused failures from pre-existing ones.
scale.3: Child runs Django tests with the fix applied and notes failures, but lacks a controlled comparison to pre-fix state (equivalent to parent's validation level plus some test runs).
scale.4: Child establishes a pre-fix baseline by reverting the fix and running tests, then re-applies the fix and runs tests again, comparing results to identify any new failures attributable to the fix.
scale.5: Child performs full controlled validation: establishes pre-fix baseline across relevant test suites (schema, migrations, backends), re-applies fix, runs same suites, demonstrates zero new failures, and documents which pre-existing failures are unrelated to the fix.

experiences.title: Read Test Command Output, Not Command Syntax, When Scoring Validation Steps
experiences.description: When a rubric awards credit for running tests or validating a fix, the judge must read the command's output to determine whether tests actually executed. A test command that fails with a settings error, import error, or runtime error before any test runs provides no validation evidence, even if the command uses canonical syntax. Do not rank a branch higher solely because its test command looks more official if that command produced an error traceback. Conversely, a branch that discovers the project's canonical test runner entry point is making genuine progress toward validation even when it has not yet executed tests in the visible prefix.
experiences.context: Agents validating fixes often attempt multiple test runner invocations across a trajectory. Some use `python -m django test`, some use `pytest`, some discover project-specific runner scripts. The judge must distinguish between (a) a command that was invoked but failed before any test collected or ran, and (b) a command that actually collected and executed tests producing pass/fail results. The judge must also recognize that locating the correct test runner mechanism (e.g., the project's runtests script or the correct settings module path) is itself meaningful progress, not merely a failed attempt.
experiences.experience:
**Activation**: Apply when a trajectory's visible steps show bash commands invoking test runners (pytest, django test, project-specific runner scripts) and the rubric measures test execution, cross-backend validation, or regression coverage.

**Positive evidence**: Output containing test session headers with collected test counts, 'OK' or 'FAILED' summaries, explicit pass/fail counts, or successful discovery of the project's canonical test runner script or correct settings module. A branch that identifies the correct test runner mechanism is making progress even if it has not yet executed tests in the visible prefix — score it above branches whose only visible test commands all produced error tracebacks.

**Contradictory evidence**: Output containing `Traceback`, `RuntimeError`, `ImproperlyConfigured`, `ModuleNotFoundError`, `Interrupted: N errors during collection`, or `can't open file` indicates the command failed before any test ran. Such output provides zero validation evidence regardless of how canonical the command syntax appears. A branch whose every visible test invocation produced an error traceback has not validated anything and should not receive the highest score on a validation rubric.

**Close-looking exclusions**: Do not treat a failed `python -m django test ... --settings=<module>` command as superior to a branch that discovered the project's actual test runner script. The official-looking command that errors out is not validation — it is a failed attempt. Conversely, a branch that installs a missing dependency (e.g., `pip install pytest`) and then retries is making setup progress, not test execution — score it as setup progress, not as validation evidence. Do not conflate 'invoked the test runner' with 'ran tests successfully.' A command that uses the correct settings module name but still raises a RuntimeError has failed, not partially succeeded.

**Abstention boundary**: When the visible prefix is truncated mid-output and the final result of a test command cannot be determined, preserve uncertainty about that branch's validation status rather than inferring success from command syntax. When all visible branches show only failed test invocations with no successful execution visible, do not rank one branch above another based on which failed command used more canonical syntax — they are equivalent in validation evidence (zero) until successful execution is observed. If the visible prefix cannot distinguish whether a discovered test runner was subsequently invoked successfully, do not award full validation credit; award discovery progress only.

experiences.title: Numeric JSON has_key fixes must be judged by the KeyTransform chain boundary, not simple object-key success
experiences.description: Activate for Django JSONField has_key/has_keys/has_any_keys numeric-key fixes when the visible trajectory edits or inspects JSON path compilation, HasKeyLookup, compile_json_path, or KeyTransform behavior. The decisive evidence is whether numeric-looking keys are treated as object keys only when they are the key whose existence is being checked, while earlier transform-path segments still retain normal array-index behavior. A submitted patch plus a passing simple data__has_key='1111' check is not enough.
experiences.context: The reported symptom is that numeric string object keys are missed by JSONField key-existence lookups on backends such as SQLite, MySQL, and Oracle. A shallow validation can pass if all numeric path pieces are forced to be quoted object keys. However, that can break lookups involving KeyTransform chains, where an intermediate numeric segment may be an array index followed by a final object key, such as traversing {'d': ['e', {'f': 'g'}]} through d, then array index 1, then checking for key f. Equivalent implementations are valid; do not require a particular helper name or exact code shape. Judge the visible semantic evidence.
experiences.experience:
Activation: use this card when the trajectory is working around django/db/models/fields/json.py, HasKeyLookup.as_sql, compile_json_path, KeyTransform, KeyTransformIsNull, or JSONField tests for has_key/has_keys/has_any_keys numeric keys.

Positive evidence to reward: (1) The agent explicitly recognizes that quoting/stringifying every numeric-looking component in a JSON path is wrong because earlier KeyTransform path components may be array indexes. (2) The agent investigates or runs focused cases such as test_has_key_deep, test_nested_key_transform_expression, test_key_transform_expression, or an equivalent query with an intermediate numeric segment before the final existence key, e.g. value__d__1__has_key='f' or has_key with a nested KeyTransform chain ending in 'f'. (3) SQL/debug output showing a wrong path like $."d"."1"."f" is useful diagnostic evidence if the agent treats it as proof that the intermediate 1 was incorrectly handled as an object key. (4) In a paused trajectory, finding a focused failing regression or locating the existing deep has_key tests is meaningful progress and should outrank a completed-looking submission that only validated the simple reported example. Full credit still requires evidence that the final behavior preserves array indexing in such chains while fixing numeric object-key existence checks.

Contradictory evidence: do not award high correctness for a diff or plan that applies object-key treatment to an entire transform path, changes path compilation so every numeric component is quoted, or validates only data__has_key='foo' and data__has_key='1111' before declaring the task complete. Treat ad hoc scripts that only test top-level numeric keys, final numeric keys, or shallow KeyTransform expressions without an intermediate numeric array segment as non-discriminating, even if they print 'All tests passed'.

Close-looking exclusions: testing ordinary array extraction alone is not the same as testing key-existence lookup through a transform chain; testing numeric object-key existence alone is also not enough. A failed focused regression command is not evidence of no progress in a paused view; it may show the agent has found the exact boundary. Conversely, merely grepping files or seeing test names without a plan, assertion, or interpretation is only weak-to-moderate evidence. An agent that states the intermediate-versus-final distinction but is paused before implementing should receive substantial diagnostic credit, but less than one that also verifies the corrected behavior.

Abstention boundary: if the visible prefix only shows environment setup errors, file searches, or truncated output that does not reveal whether the discriminating chain case was considered, preserve uncertainty. If a final diff is truncated so you cannot tell whether object-key handling is scoped to the existence key or applied to the whole path, do not infer correctness from a completion marker or from the simple numeric-key test alone.

experiences.title: Distinguish exact-scenario fix validation from test infrastructure creation and constraint exploration in unique_together PK drop fix
experiences.description: When evaluating continuations for the unique_together PK drop fix, the judge must distinguish between continuations that (1) have the fix AND run a test exercising the exact reported failure scenario with confirmed success, (2) have the fix but fail to validate it, and (3) lack the fix entirely but create test scripts or explore constraint behavior. 'Success!' output from test scripts that only create initial migrations, and constraint introspection that confirms the filter approach without implementing the fix, are not equivalent to actual fix validation.
experiences.context: Django issue: cannot drop unique_together constraint on a single field that is also a primary key. Fix: add primary_key=False to _constraint_names call in _delete_composed_index in django/db/backends/base/schema.py. Parent 1 has the fix applied; Parent 2 does not. The exact failure scenario is: create model with unique_together=('id',) on PK field, generate migration to remove it, apply migration successfully.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Evaluating continuations for a bug fix where one parent has the fix and the other does not, and continuations create test scripts, run existing test suites, or explore constraint behavior.

Positive evidence: A continuation that has the fix present (changed_files includes the target file django/db/backends/base/schema.py) AND runs a test that exercises the exact failure scenario (dropping unique_together on a PK field) with confirmed success output (e.g., 'SUCCESS: Migration applied successfully!' from a test named test_primary_key_unique_together.py) provides the strongest evidence of fix validation. Running existing Django test suite tests that pass (e.g., test_alter_unique_together, test_alter_unique_together_remove via tests/runtests.py) provides supporting evidence.

Contradictory evidence: A continuation that creates test scripts and gets 'Success!' output, but the test output shows only 'Applying migration: test_issue.0001_initial' (initial migration creation, NOT removal of unique_together), has NOT validated the fix — it merely confirms initial migration works. A continuation that introspects constraints and confirms that primary_key=False filter returns the correct constraint name, but does NOT modify the target file (changed_files is None), has NOT implemented the fix — it has only confirmed the approach. These activities produce output that looks like progress but is not equivalent to fix validation.

Close-looking exclusion: A continuation with the fix present (changed_files includes schema.py) but that fails to run any tests successfully (RuntimeError: Django module not found, ModuleNotFoundError: No module named tests.settings) has NOT validated the fix — it maintains equivalence with the parent (score 3) but does not advance to score 4+. The presence of multiple test files in untracked_files (test_fix.py, test_fix2.py, test_fix3.py, etc.) without successful execution of the exact scenario is not validation evidence — it indicates repeated failed attempts to set up test infrastructure.

Misleading evidence pattern to reject: Test infrastructure activity (creating test scripts, running existing test suites, exploring constraint behavior) without the fix being present, or without the test exercising the exact failure scenario, should NOT be treated as equivalent to actual fix validation. Specifically: (a) 'Success!' output from a test that only creates and applies an initial migration is not fix validation — the test must exercise the removal of unique_together on a PK field; (b) constraint introspection that confirms the primary_key=False filter approach without implementing the fix is not fix implementation — changed_files must include the target file; (c) the presence of multiple test files in untracked_files without successful execution output is not validation evidence. A continuation without the fix (changed_files is None) that explores code and confirms the approach should be scored at most 2-3 (identifies general area, does not implement), not 4+. A continuation with the fix but no successful test execution should be scored 3 (equivalence), not 4+.

Abstention boundary: If the continuation's test output is truncated and we cannot confirm whether the test exercised the exact failure scenario (removal of unique_together on a PK field vs. initial migration creation), or if changed_files is not visible and we cannot determine whether the fix is present, we should not infer validation from partial evidence. A test named test_primary_key_unique_together.py with 'SUCCESS: Migration applied successfully!' is stronger evidence than a test named test_unique_together2.py with 'Success!' because the former name explicitly references the PK scenario and the output confirms migration application, while the latter may only test initial migration creation.

reference_golden_rubrics: Do not reward read-only exploration after the key contract is already known
Do not treat same-looking multi-backend edits as correctness evidence

experiences.title: Do not treat inherited-fix test suite passes as child delta validation evidence
experiences.description: When the parent trajectory already ran and passed the official test suite for the target fix, re-running those same tests in the child continuation does not add correctness evidence. A rubric that scores test-running activity as validation evidence will misrank continuations: it rewards redundant validation theater on an inherited fix while penalizing clean, correct patches that performed no redundant testing. Additionally, inflated current_patch_chars from untracked test files included in the submission signals a corrupted patch that comprehensive test runs cannot mask.
experiences.context: A Django schema migration fix for dropping unique_together constraints on primary key fields. Both parents implemented the same fix (6 insertions, 1 deletion in django/db/backends/base/schema.py). Parent 1 already ran and passed the official Django migration tests (test_alter_unique_together: Ran 1 test OK; test_alter_unique_together_remove: Ran 1 test OK) before child continuations began. Clean child patches have current_patch_chars ~1117 with only schema.py in changed_files; a corrupted patch with untracked test files has ~27555 chars and multiple test_*.py files in changed_files.
experiences.experience:
Activation: The parent trajectory already ran and passed the official test suite for the target fix, and the child continuation inherits the same patch (identical diff_stat) without modifying the core fix.

Positive evidence: The child continuation's patch is identical to the parent's (same diff_stat: 6 insertions, 1 deletion; same current_patch_chars ~1117), confirming the fix is inherited unchanged. A clean patch with only the target source file in changed_files indicates a correct submission. When the fix is inherited and already validated by the parent, a clean patch alone is sufficient evidence of correctness.

Contradictory evidence: A child continuation that runs official tests and gets the same 'OK' result as the parent has not added correctness evidence — the tests pass because of the inherited fix, not because of anything the child did. Running broader test suites (constraints: 61 tests OK, migrations: 671-851 tests OK, schema: 179 tests OK) does not add correctness evidence for the specific fix when the fix was already in place. A child that includes untracked test files in its patch (current_patch_chars inflated to ~27555 vs ~1117 for clean patches, with test_*.py files appearing in changed_files alongside schema.py) has likely corrupted its submission despite passing all tests — the rubric must not let comprehensive test runs mask this corruption signal.

Close-looking exclusions: A continuation that only browses files (reading settings.py, runtests.py, listing directories) without running tests has not failed validation — it has simply not performed redundant validation on an already-validated inherited fix, and its clean patch (1117 chars) is equally correct. Custom debug scripts that exercise the migration lifecycle provide weaker evidence than official tests but still do not constitute child delta correctness when the fix is inherited. A continuation from a parent that could not run official tests (due to environment issues like missing settings module or PostgreSQL connection refused) that then runs them for the first time does add validation evidence for the inherited fix, but not for the child's delta if the patch is unchanged.

Abstention boundary: If the child continuation modifies the inherited patch (different diff_stat or different patch content visible in the diff), then test-running behavior becomes relevant evidence of the child's contribution and this experience does not apply. If the parent did not run official tests and the child runs them for the first time, the child's test run constitutes new validation evidence. If current_patch_chars is consistent across all continuations (~1117) and no continuation has inflated patch_chars or untracked files in changed_files, then patch corruption cannot be detected from the visible state and the rubric should focus on whether the child modified the inherited fix.

experiences.title: Preserve the Core Transaction Fix Over Query-Impact Investigation
experiences.description: Use this when a task asks to wrap a database-modifying view in transaction.atomic() and the trajectory shows query-count investigation, patch reversion via backup restore, or environment setup. The primary progress signal is whether the transaction wrapper remains in the final file state, not whether the agent analyzed query index shifts.
experiences.context: Applies when the task is to add transaction handling to an admin view's data-modifying path (e.g., changelist list_editable processing). The misleading pattern is a rubric that centers on 'query impact analysis' — investigating how BEGIN/COMMIT queries from transaction.atomic() shift captured query indices in existing tests. This over-credits trajectories that merely observe the query shift or even revert the patch, while under-crediting trajectories that preserve the correct wrapper or properly set up the test environment. It is most useful when the trajectory shows a mix of patch submission, test running, query investigation, backup restores, and pip install commands. It is less useful during early exploration before any edit has been made.
experiences.experience: A rubric centered on 'Test Validation and Transaction Query Impact Analysis' was misleading because it treated query-index investigation as the main progress signal. In practice: (1) An agent that copies a .bak file over the modified source (cp file.bak file) is reverting the patch and destroying the fix — this is destructive, not progress, regardless of prior query analysis. (2) An agent that runs a standalone script printing 'Number of queries: 1, 0: BEGIN' is making a trivial observation about transaction behavior, not diagnosing a test failure or applying remediation. (3) An agent that runs 'pip install -e .' is correctly installing the package in development mode so it becomes importable for the test runner — this is genuine environment setup progress, not mere dependency installation. (4) Agents that submit the actual transaction.atomic() wrapper have the core deliverable, even if they did not analyze query impact. A better rubric should first check whether the transaction.atomic() wrapper is present in the final file state (not reverted by a .bak restore), penalize trajectories that revert the patch, not over-credit trivial query observations as 'failure diagnosis' or 'remediation,' recognize 'pip install -e .' as correct environment setup that enables the test runner, and treat query-impact analysis as secondary to the actual patch presence and proper test execution. Close-looking exclusions: Running the actual test suite via the project's test runner and observing failures IS genuine test validation, even without fixing test expectations; but running a standalone script that only prints 'BEGIN' is NOT test validation. Copying a .bak file over the source IS patch reversion, NOT cleanup or state reassessment. 'pip install -e .' IS proper setup for running the project's test suite, NOT just random dependency installation. Abstention boundary: When the visible prefix only shows environment setup commands without test results, preserve uncertainty about whether tests will pass; do not assume query-impact analysis is needed or that the patch is insufficient. When the patch is present but no validation has been run, the score should reflect 'patch present but unvalidated' rather than penalizing for lack of query analysis.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Transaction Wrapper Presence and Non-Destructive Validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should preserve the transaction.atomic() wrapper around the data-modifying path in the final file state and avoid reverting it. Progress is measured by: (1) the wrapper remaining in the source file at the end of the visible trajectory, (2) not copying a backup file over the modified source, (3) proper environment setup that enables the test runner (e.g., pip install -e .), and (4) running the actual test suite via the project's test runner if validation is attempted. Query-impact analysis (investigating how BEGIN/COMMIT queries shift captured query indices) is secondary and should not be the primary scoring criterion. A trajectory that submits the correct wrapper without query analysis should score higher than one that investigates query shifts but reverts the patch.

primary_visible_evidence: The transaction.atomic() wrapper is present in the final source file state (verified by diff, cat, or submission output).
No backup-restore command (cp file.bak file) overwrites the modified source at any point in the trajectory.
Environment setup uses the correct method to make the package importable (e.g., pip install -e . rather than only installing individual dependencies).
If validation is attempted, the project's test runner is used (e.g., runtests.py) rather than standalone scripts that only print query output.
contradictory_evidence: A cp command copies a .bak or backup file over the modified source, reverting the transaction wrapper.
A standalone script only prints trivial query output (e.g., 'Number of queries: 1, 0: BEGIN') without running actual tests or applying remediation.
The agent spends multiple steps on query-index investigation but never confirms the wrapper is still in the file.
close_looking_exclusions: Running the actual test suite via the project's test runner and observing failures IS genuine test validation, even without fixing test expectations — do not penalize this.
Copying a .bak file over the source IS patch reversion, NOT cleanup or state reassessment — penalize this.
pip install -e . IS proper setup for running the project's test suite, NOT just random dependency installation — credit this.
A standalone script that only prints 'BEGIN' is NOT test validation — do not credit this as 'failure diagnosis' or 'remediation.'
non_decisive_evidence: Installing individual dependencies (asgiref, sqlparse, pytest) without making the package importable.
Grepping or viewing the test file without running it.
Observing that transaction.atomic() adds a BEGIN query without connecting it to a test failure.

scale.1: The transaction wrapper is absent or has been reverted from the final file state, and no meaningful validation was attempted.
scale.2: The wrapper may be present but the trajectory shows only trivial observations (e.g., a script printing 'BEGIN') or environment setup that does not enable the test runner; no actual test execution.
scale.3: The wrapper is present and the trajectory has made some progress toward validation (e.g., correct pip install -e . or partial test runner invocation), but tests have not been successfully run or the agent has not confirmed the wrapper remains in the file.
scale.4: The wrapper is present, the environment is correctly set up, and the agent has run or is about to run the actual test suite; minor gaps remain in failure analysis or remediation.
scale.5: The wrapper is present in the final file state, the environment is correctly set up, the actual test suite has been run, and any failures have been analyzed or remediated (e.g., updating test expectations or justifying the change).

experiences.title: Do Not Reward Validation Work Over Patch Correctness for Transaction Wrapper Fixes
experiences.description: When the task is to add a transaction.atomic() wrapper to existing code, correctness depends on the wrapper being properly applied with correct indentation and database routing. Rubrics that reward semantic verification of rollback behavior or test validation with query impact analysis are misleading because the test failure from SAVEPOINT query shifts is an expected side effect of the correct fix, and running tests does not improve patch correctness.
experiences.context: Adding transaction handling to Django admin changelist_view list_editable processing. The fix wraps the list_editable POST handling block in with transaction.atomic(using=router.db_for_write(self.model)). The existing test test_changelist_view_list_editable_changed_objects_uses_filter asserts captured_queries[4] contains WHERE/IN, but adding transaction.atomic() inserts a SAVEPOINT at that index, shifting the WHERE/IN query to a later position.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When rubrics reward semantic verification of rollback behavior or test validation and query impact analysis for a straightforward transaction wrapper fix, and when continuations that apply correct patches without running tests are scored lower than continuations that run tests and observe expected failures.

Positive evidence: The correct fix is wrapping the list_editable block in with transaction.atomic(using=router.db_for_write(self.model)). A continuation that applies this wrapper with correct indentation achieves the core objective. The pattern matches existing usage in changeform_view and delete_view. A continuation that reverts and re-applies the fix using a Python script has an equivalent implementation to one that submits a patch diff.

Contradictory evidence: The test failure AssertionError WHERE not found in SAVEPOINT s23456246530688_x5 is an expected side effect of the correct fix, not a bug. The SAVEPOINT query at index 4 confirms the transaction wrapper is active. Running tests and observing this failure does not improve correctness. A continuation that recognizes this failure as expected and submits the patch has correctly identified the side effect. A continuation that gets stuck trying to set up standalone Django environments (ModuleNotFoundError, no such table, TemplateDoesNotExist) to run custom validation scripts has not made additional progress toward correctness.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not distinguish between continuations that have the same correct transaction.atomic() wrapper based on whether they ran tests, analyzed query indices, or attempted rollback verification. A continuation that re-applies the correct fix via git checkout and Python script without running any tests has an equivalent implementation to one that runs tests and observes the SAVEPOINT failure. A continuation that spends steps on environment setup errors without resolving them has not progressed beyond the patch application step. Do not reward continuations that observe test failures without recognizing them as expected side effects of the correct fix.

Abstention boundary: Cannot determine actual rollback semantics (database state after simulated failure) from visible test output alone. The SAVEPOINT query presence confirms the transaction wrapper is active but does not prove that partial saves are rolled back on error. However, this verification is not required for the task of adding the transaction wrapper. If the only visible evidence is test pass/fail output without the patch content, cannot determine whether the patch is correctly applied.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Transaction Atomicity Semantic Verification
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluates whether the continuation verifies that the added transaction.atomic() block actually provides atomic rollback behavior when an error occurs during list_editable bulk edits. Parent baseline: both parents have the correct transaction wrapper but no continuation has demonstrated rollback verification. Progress means moving from no semantic verification -> creating error scenario -> confirming all changes roll back -> validating router.db_for_write usage.

metadata.oracle_test: Create a list_editable bulk edit where the 2nd object save raises an exception (e.g., unique constraint, custom clean() validation). Verify via direct ORM queries that the 1st object's changes were also rolled back. Confirm transaction uses router.db_for_write(self.model) matching changeform_view/delete_view pattern.
metadata.code_review: The fix adds transaction.atomic() but semantic correctness requires proving it actually prevents partial updates. Existing test only checks query count indices, not rollback behavior.
metadata.judge_focus: Look for: (1) creation of error scenario during bulk edit, (2) database state verification showing zero partial saves, (3) confirmation of router.db_for_write usage, (4) not just running existing tests but adding semantic validation
metadata.failure_mode: Assuming transaction works because code wraps correctly; only checking query count tests; not testing actual rollback semantics

scale.1: No semantic verification: continuation only checks test pass/fail or query counts without testing rollback behavior (Parent 1/2 continuations 1-6 behavior)
scale.2: Weak verification attempt: continuation mentions rollback conceptually but does not create a concrete error scenario or check database state after simulated failure
scale.3: Equivalent to parent baseline: continuation runs existing tests but does not add or run any validation that exercises the atomicity guarantee (rollback on error during multi-object save)
scale.4: Strong verification: continuation creates a test scenario where validation/save fails mid-bulk-edit (e.g., constraint violation, custom validation error) and confirms via database queries that NO objects were partially saved - full rollback occurred
scale.5: Complete verification: continuation achieves scale 4 AND verifies the transaction uses router.db_for_write(self.model) for correct database routing in multi-db setups, and/or adds a targeted regression test demonstrating atomic rollback that would fail without the transaction wrapper

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Test Validation and Transaction Query Impact Analysis
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluates whether the continuation validates the transaction fix by running relevant admin_changelist tests (particularly test_changelist_view_list_editable_changed_objects_uses_filter) and, when tests fail due to added BEGIN/COMMIT queries from transaction.atomic(), analyzes the root cause and takes corrective action (updating test expectations or justifying the change). Parent baseline: both Parent 1 and Parent 2 have correct patch but no successful test validation. Progress means moving from no validation attempt -> environment setup attempt -> successful test run -> failure diagnosis -> test fix.

metadata.oracle_test: tests/admin_changelist/tests.py::test_changelist_view_list_editable_changed_objects_uses_filter - this test captures queries and asserts specific indices (e.g., context.captured_queries[4] contains WHERE/IN). Adding transaction.atomic() inserts BEGIN at index 0, shifting all subsequent indices.
metadata.code_review: The fix is semantically correct (adds needed transaction) but has observable side effect on query capture tests. A complete solution must address this test impact.
metadata.judge_focus: Look for evidence of: (1) successful Django test environment setup, (2) running admin_changelist tests specifically, (3) analyzing query capture assertion failures, (4) connecting failures to transaction.atomic() BEGIN/COMMIT queries, (5) taking corrective action on test expectations or adding rollback verification test.
metadata.failure_mode: Submitting patch without validation; getting stuck on environment setup without progressing to test analysis; running tests but not recognizing query index shift as expected side effect of correct fix

scale.1: No validation attempt: continuation submits patch without running any admin_changelist tests (Parent 1 continuations 1-4 behavior)
scale.2: Validation attempted but blocked at environment/setup: continuation tries to run tests but fails to configure Django test environment, install dependencies, or locate test runner; no test output or failure analysis achieved (Parent 2 continuations 5-8 behavior)
scale.3: Equivalent to parent baseline: continuation runs some tests but they pass/fail without the continuation recognizing the transaction query count impact, or continuation only runs unrelated tests
scale.4: Successful test execution with failure identification: continuation runs the specific list_editable test, observes query count assertion failures, and correctly identifies that transaction.atomic() adds BEGIN/COMMIT queries shifting query indices
scale.5: Full validation and remediation: continuation achieves scale 4 AND either updates the test's expected query indices to account for transaction queries, or adds a targeted regression test demonstrating atomic rollback behavior, or documents why the test expectation change is correct

experiences.title: Carry inherited CLI subparser error-contract evidence across visible branches
experiences.description: Use when judging the Django management-command subparser error-formatting task. The rubric should center on the requested user-visible CLI contract and must carry parent evidence into each child continuation. Do not add speculative criteria for custom parser classes, arbitrary nested subparsers, or a particular internal patch shape, and do not rank a child solely by its final command.
experiences.context: Activation: the visible issue says management command subparsers constructed from CommandParser lose error formatting, so a missing required argument under a subparser should show a normal command-line usage/error message rather than a Python traceback. In this paused view, Parent 1 is inherited by Continuations 1–4, and Parent 2 is inherited by Continuations 5–8. Parent 1 already contains direct CLI evidence for both the missing subparser argument case and the missing subcommand case. Parent 2 contains mainly file/test discovery and non-representative test attempts unless a child visibly adds the same CLI-contract evidence.
experiences.experience:
Build one concise rubric around the management-subparser CLI error contract.

Positive evidence: Strongly credit a branch when its visible parent-plus-child state shows a real management command invoked from the command line with a subparser missing a required argument, returning the normal parse-error behavior: exit status 2, a usage line for the subcommand, an `error: the following arguments are required: name`-style message, and no Python traceback or raw CommandError stacktrace. Supporting strong evidence is the missing-subcommand case also showing usage plus the required-subcommand error with no traceback. For this paused view, that Parent 1 evidence must be carried into Continuations 1–4 unless a later child step visibly changes or contradicts it.

Contradictory evidence: Penalize visible output where the relevant CLI case still produces a traceback, a raw `django.core.management.base.CommandError` stacktrace, or another non-human-facing argparse failure. A later edit that breaks the previously demonstrated CLI behavior can override inherited positive evidence, but mere exploration or failed validation commands do not.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not treat a no-op child, an import/path probe, a failed test-runner invocation, `Ran 0 tests` with `OK`, unrelated admin/management tests, or a final command that only locates files as erasing inherited CLI behavior. Also do not award top credit solely for programmatic `call_command()` or direct `parse_args()` checks: those can be useful secondary checks, but the reported defect is the command-line formatting path. A return code of 2 is positive when paired with usage text and no traceback. A truncated diff or a claim that the fix works is weaker than visible CLI behavior. Do not invent separate requirements for custom `parser_class`, arbitrary nesting, exact private argparse classes, or one exact implementation mechanism; equivalent shared propagation of the relevant parser error context is acceptable.

Branch-reading rule for this view: Continuations 1–4 inherit Parent 1’s demonstrated CLI contract and should not be scored as absent merely because their child tail later searches for tests, imports Django, or misconfigures a runner. Continuations 5–8 inherit Parent 2’s weaker state; they should not outrank the branch with exact CLI behavior merely because they run an official-looking command, pass unrelated/programmatic checks, or show partial patch/debug output without the requested CLI output.

Abstention boundary: If a visible branch contains only exploration, failed/zero-test runs, or programmatic checks and no relevant CLI behavior or inspectable shared-parser semantics, avoid maximum correctness and preserve uncertainty. If the branch contains inherited CLI behavior but little inspectable code, credit the user-visible contract while remaining cautious about implementation robustness rather than inventing extra edge-case requirements.

experiences.title: Test Output Content Revealing Attribute Assignment Bugs Must Override Debugging Process Narratives
experiences.description: When test output shows an attribute assigned the wrong value (e.g., violation_error_code containing a message string), that is a visible implementation defect. A branch that discovers and partially fixes such a bug should not outrank branches whose test output already demonstrates correct code behavior.
experiences.context: Django BaseConstraint violation_error_code feature implementation across multiple continuations from two parents, each modifying django/db/models/constraints.py.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply when a continuation's visible test output displays attribute values that reveal assignment bugs, or when comparing branches where some show debugging sequences and others show correct runtime behavior.

Positive evidence: One continuation showed 'ValidationError code: None' for the default case and 'All tests passed!' — correct behavioral validation that ValidationError.code matches the constraint's violation_error_code, including the None default edge case. Another continuation showed 'Violation error code: unique_code' — correct custom code assignment for UniqueConstraint. These branches demonstrated correct runtime behavior in their test output without needing to debug fundamental assignment errors.

Contradictory evidence: A third continuation showed 'Violation error code: Custom message: %(name)s' at one step — the code attribute contained a human-readable message string, not a code value. The source code revealed 'violation_error_code = violation_error_message' — a clear assignment bug where code was set to message. The agent identified and patched this, and a subsequent test showed 'Violation error code: custom_code' after the fix. However, the post-fix test only verified one constraint type (CheckConstraint) and did not test the None default case or UniqueConstraint, providing weaker behavioral validation than continuations that tested both constraint types and the default case.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not treat a debugging sequence (discovering a bug, patching it, re-running tests) as evidence of semantic completeness. The initial test output revealing 'code = message string' is a clear implementation defect. The fact that an agent fixed one bug does not compensate when the overall implementation still has issues. A branch that starts broken and is partially fixed should not outrank branches that were correct from the start. Examine the actual values in test output: when 'Violation error code' displays a message template like 'Custom message: %(name)s' instead of a code value like 'custom_code', that is a defect signal, not a validation signal. Additionally, a post-fix test that only checks one constraint type provides weaker evidence than a test that covers both CheckConstraint and UniqueConstraint with the None default.

Abstention boundary: This experience applies only when test output content is visible in the paused state and reveals attribute values. If no test output is visible, or if the output does not display the code attribute value, the distinction cannot be made from visible evidence alone.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Violation Error Code Implementation Defects
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalizes implementation defects in the violation_error_code feature that would cause incorrect runtime behavior or migration failures. Parent baseline: some continuations have bugs like wrong attribute assignment in BaseConstraint.__init__, duplicate fields in __repr__, missing super() calls, or incorrect deconstruct serialization. A child scores worse (higher) when it introduces or retains such defects compared to the parent.

metadata.judge_focus: semantic bugs in the violation_error_code plumbing
metadata.failure_mode: wrong attribute assignment, duplicate __repr__ fields, broken deconstruct, missing super() propagation

scale.1: No implementation defects: violation_error_code correctly stored in BaseConstraint, passed through super(), used in validate(), and serialized in deconstruct without duplication or assignment errors.
scale.2: Minor defect: cosmetic issue like duplicate violation_error_code in __repr__ output but correct underlying storage and behavior.
scale.3: Equivalent to parent: same defect level as parent (e.g., both have missing deconstruct update, or both have the BaseConstraint assignment bug).
scale.4: Clear defect: violation_error_code assigned to wrong attribute (e.g., violation_error_message), or deconstruct omits the parameter causing migration failures, or validate() doesn't pass code despite __init__ accepting it.
scale.5: Severe defect: multiple compounding bugs - e.g., BaseConstraint.__init__ has assignment bug AND validate() doesn't use code AND deconstruct is broken, making the feature non-functional.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Violation Error Code Behavioral Validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluates whether the child trajectory provides behavioral validation evidence that violation_error_code works at runtime: when CheckConstraint or UniqueConstraint validation fails, the raised ValidationError has the correct code attribute. Parent baseline: some continuations show test scripts but with incomplete coverage (e.g., only CheckConstraint tested, or code not asserted). Progress means demonstrating both constraint types raise ValidationError with the expected code, including edge cases like None code default.

metadata.judge_focus: runtime evidence that ValidationError.code matches constraint.violation_error_code
metadata.failure_mode: tests only check message not code, only one constraint type tested, or no validation script shown

scale.1: No behavioral validation shown, or validation script has errors preventing execution (e.g., Django setup failures not resolved).
scale.2: Validation script runs but only checks violation_error_message, not violation_error_code; or only tests one constraint type (CheckConstraint or UniqueConstraint) without the other.
scale.3: Equivalent to parent: validation script exists and checks code for one constraint type, but coverage is partial (e.g., missing None default case, missing UniqueConstraint, or code assertion not explicit).
scale.4: Strong validation: script tests both CheckConstraint and UniqueConstraint, asserts ValidationError.code equals the provided violation_error_code, and verifies None default behavior. Minor gaps like not testing condition-based UniqueConstraint.
scale.5: Complete validation: both constraint types tested with custom code and None default, ValidationError.code explicitly asserted, edge cases covered (condition-based UniqueConstraint, deferrable constraints), and existing Django constraint tests pass.

experiences.title: Distinguish code-path tracing from environment setup in aggregate-over-window-function trajectories
experiences.description: Retrieve when scoring Django ORM patch-generation continuations for an aggregate-over-window-function bug where the visible prefix shows branches at disparate stages: some installing dependencies and hitting import errors, others inspecting get_aggregation and reproducing invalid SQL.
experiences.context: Applies when evaluating continuations of a Django ORM task involving aggregate() over a window-function annotation. The visible prefix may show branches at very different stages: some are installing dependencies (asgiref, sqlparse) and encountering repeated import errors, while others are inspecting get_aggregation in django/db/models/sql/query.py, tracing how window-function annotations are handled during SQL generation, reproducing the invalid SQL where an aggregate wraps a window-function column, and searching for the condition that controls subquery wrapping. A coarse rubric that assigns the same mid-range score to all such branches creates a maximum tie between branches actively progressing toward a fix and branches stuck on environment setup or reading code without connecting it to the issue.
experiences.experience:
The bias was assigning the same mid-range score to seven branches regardless of whether they were actively tracing the get_aggregation code path and understanding the window-function-in-aggregate SQL problem, stuck on dependency installation with repeated import errors, or reading code and git history without connecting it to the issue. This collapsed resolving and non-resolving branches into a single tie. A better rubric must differentiate based on visible evidence:

- Positive evidence (higher score): inspecting get_aggregation in django/db/models/sql/query.py, tracing how contains_over_clause or window-function annotations are handled during aggregation, reproducing the invalid SQL where an aggregate wraps a window-function column, understanding that the window function must be materialized in an inner query before outer aggregation, or searching for the specific flag or condition that controls subquery wrapping.

- Contradictory evidence (lower score): spending the entire visible prefix installing dependencies and hitting repeated import errors (asgiref, sqlparse, Window import), trying to start or install a database server, or reading code and git history without connecting it to the window-function aggregation problem.

- Close-looking exclusion: a branch that attempts a validation check in Aggregate.resolve_expression but does not fix the SQL generation is making more targeted progress than one stuck on environment setup, but less than one that traces the subquery rewriting logic in get_aggregation. Do not collapse these into the same score.

- Abstention boundary: when the visible prefix only shows dependency installation or environment setup with no code inspection, preserve uncertainty about whether the branch will later make progress. Do not assume it equals a branch that has already traced the relevant code path, but also do not penalize it as severely as a branch that has inspected code without connecting to the issue. Use a distinct intermediate score or note the uncertainty.

experiences.title: Visible Test-Output Contradiction After Fix Application
experiences.description: Retrieve when a continuation has applied or modified a source fix and then runs a reproduction test or validation script with visible output. The judge must read the actual test output rather than assuming that running a test implies it passed. If the output shows the original reported error persisting after a fix was applied, this visible contradiction must cap the continuation's score below continuations that show the error resolved or that are still exploring without having applied a failing fix.
