Close-looking exclusions: Generic autodoc/__init__.py browsing without property-specific focus, typing.py stringify inspection without connecting to PropertyDocumenter, and reproduction scripts that confirm the bug but do not isolate the code path should not be credited as diagnostic progress. However, even full diagnostic progress (identifying all elements of the code path divergence with specific function names and call chains) should not be credited as fix correctness. The distinction is critical: diagnostic understanding measures whether the agent knows what is wrong; fix correctness measures whether the agent can make it right. Examining HTML output to confirm that attribute types have <a class="reference internal"> links while property types show plain text is reproduction evidence, not fix evidence. Running stringify and restify on a Point class to observe that restify produces :class:`test_property.Point` while stringify produces plain test_property.Point is behavioral understanding, not fix evidence.

Abstention boundary: This experience applies to exploration-phase rubrics measuring diagnostic understanding for autodoc type hint issues. It does not apply to rubrics that directly evaluate patch content, test passage, or implementation correctness. If no patch has been produced in the visible trajectory (current_patch_chars is 0), diagnostic understanding alone cannot determine whether a correct fix will follow. When the rubric explicitly measures fix implementation quality rather than diagnostic understanding, different criteria apply. This experience also does not address cases where the root cause identification itself is incorrect or incomplete—only cases where correct and complete root cause identification is improperly treated as fix correctness evidence.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Property Type Annotation Cross-Reference Root Cause Identification
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate accurate identification of why property type annotations lack cross-references in autodoc output. Strong evidence includes: locating PropertyDocumenter.add_directive_header as the code path that emits :type: fields for properties, recognizing that it uses stringify/restify directly instead of the merge_typehints/record_typehints pipeline used for methods/functions, and identifying that record_typehints only processes callable objects (skipping properties). The criterion should not be satisfied by generic autodoc browsing, unrelated typing.py inspection, or reproduction scripts that don't isolate the property-specific code path.

metadata.required_behavior: identify the exact code path divergence between property and method type hint processing
metadata.key_visible_evidence: ['PropertyDocumenter.add_directive_header located as property type emission point', 'Direct :type: line addition vs merge_typehints pipeline distinction recognized', 'record_typehints callable-only limitation identified as property exclusion cause', 'stringify/restify vs merge_typehints cross-reference behavior difference understood']
metadata.common_false_positives: ['general autodoc/__init__.py browsing without property-specific focus', 'typing.py stringify inspection without connecting to PropertyDocumenter', "reproduction scripts that confirm bug but don't isolate code path", 'method/function typehint flow analysis without property comparison']

scale.1: No property-specific root cause progress; only generic autodoc exploration or unrelated file reading
scale.2: PropertyDocumenter found but type emission mechanism not yet connected to cross-reference failure
scale.3: PropertyDocumenter.add_directive_header located and :type: line emission identified, but merge_typehints/record_typehints divergence not yet recognized
scale.4: Full code path divergence identified: property uses direct :type: emission while methods use record_typehints/merge_typehints, and record_typehints callable-only filter excludes properties
scale.5: Complete root cause mapped with specific function names, call chains, and the exact mechanism difference; ready to implement targeted fix

experiences.title: Distinguish applied code fixes from exploration-only testing of the same fix approach
experiences.description: When multiple continuations reference the same fix concept (e.g., KroneckerDelta for Identity._entry), the judge must verify whether actual source file modifications were made, not just whether the approach was tested. A continuation that only runs test scripts exploring KroneckerDelta summation behavior without modifying the _entry method has made strictly less progress than one that visibly changes the method to return KroneckerDelta.
experiences.context: In a symbolic mathematics bug fix where Identity._entry must return KroneckerDelta(i,j) instead of using Python equality (i==j), multiple continuations explored the KroneckerDelta approach. One continuation visibly modified matexpr.py (a step shows _entry returning KroneckerDelta(i,j) and a subsequent step shows the test result returning a Piecewise sum), while another only ran Python test snippets exploring KroneckerDelta summation without modifying any source files. Both received identical judge scores despite the clear difference in progress.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When multiple continuations reference the same fix concept but differ in whether they actually modified source code.

Positive evidence of fix applied: Visible file-writing commands (python scripts that write file contents, sed -i) followed by confirmation of changed code in subsequent steps (e.g., a step showing _entry now returns KroneckerDelta(i, j) instead of the if i==j conditional). The test output after the change (e.g., Sum returning Piecewise instead of 0) confirms the code modification took effect.

Contradictory evidence (exploration-only): Commands that only run Python test snippets (python -c '...') or read-only commands (grep, cat, sed -n) without any file-writing commands. These continuations test whether a fix approach would work but do not apply it to the codebase. Their test outputs may look similar to the applied-fix continuation's outputs (both showing Piecewise sums), but no source file was changed.

Misleading pattern to reject: Treating exploration/testing of a fix approach as equivalent to applying the fix. Both continuations may reference KroneckerDelta and show similar test outputs (e.g., Sum returning Piecewise instead of n), but only the one with visible code modifications to the _entry method has made actual progress. The judge must look at whether source files were modified, not just whether the fix concept was explored or tested.

Close-looking exclusions: (1) Adding only an import statement to a source file without changing the _entry return logic is NOT a fix. (2) Adding a comment to buggy code without changing the logic is NOT a fix. (3) An ImportError in a test script indicates environment issues, not fix progress. (4) A continuation that encounters an error running a reproduction script has not demonstrated fix progress regardless of what it explored.

Abstention boundary: If visible steps are truncated and it is unclear whether file modifications were made in unseen earlier steps, do not infer fix status from the final visible step alone. However, if the visible steps consistently show only read-only or test commands with no file-writing commands, and no changed code is visible, it is reasonable to conclude no fix was applied.

experiences.title: Verify patch modifies the correct file: format validity does not confirm semantic correctness
experiences.description: A valid git diff patch with correct format (diff --git header, well-formed hunks, submitted via final command) does not confirm the patch fixes the correct bug. When the issue is in a matrix subclass's own row_join/col_join implementation in sparse.py, a patch that only modifies common.py (dense Matrix) is semantically incomplete. The judge must verify the patch modifies sparse.py, not just common.py, before giving credit for semantic correctness. Patch format validity must not compensate for patching the wrong file.
experiences.context: In a matrix hstack/vstack empty-matrix bug, SparseMatrix returns wrong shape (0, 3) instead of (0, 6) because it overrides row_join/col_join in sparse.py (lines 949, 1159) with its own implementation lacking the empty-matrix guard. A continuation generates a valid git diff from a prior commit via `git diff <commit>^..<commit> -- sympy/matrices/common.py`, producing a patch with `diff --git a/sympy/matrices/common.py b/sympy/matrices/common.py` header and well-formed hunks. The patch is submitted via `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat /root/patch.txt` with result_status: finished. However, the patch only adds the empty-matrix guard to common.py's row_join, not to sparse.py's row_join/col_join, so the SparseMatrix bug remains unfixed.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When a continuation submits a git diff patch, examine the `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>` headers in the submission output to determine which files are modified.

Positive evidence: A valid git diff format (diff --git header, well-formed hunks, correct relative paths, submitted via final command) confirms the patch is syntactically valid and the submission process is complete. This is necessary but not sufficient for semantic correctness.

Contradictory evidence: A patch that only modifies common.py does not fix the SparseMatrix hstack/vstack bug. SparseMatrix has its own row_join at line 1159 and col_join at line 949 in sparse.py that override common.py's implementation. The empty-matrix guard must be added to sparse.py, not just common.py. A continuation that submits a common.py-only patch has not addressed the core issue, regardless of patch format quality.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not be misled by: (1) Summary metadata showing untracked_files: None or current_patch_chars: 0 — when the patch is generated via `git diff <commit>^..<commit>` rather than working-tree changes, the patch file is saved outside the repo (e.g., /root/patch.txt) and won't appear in untracked files. The patch content is still visible in the submission output. (2) result_status: finished and exit_status: Submitted — these confirm submission completion but say nothing about which files were patched. (3) Dense Matrix tests passing (test_hstack, test_vstack) — these validate common.py only, not sparse.py. The SparseMatrix reproducer must be checked separately. (4) The patch being sourced from a prior commit's diff — this does not guarantee the commit addressed the same root cause. The commit may have fixed common.py while the current issue requires a sparse.py fix.

Abstention boundary: If the submission output is truncated so that `diff --git` file paths are not visible, or if the patch modifies both common.py and sparse.py but the sparse.py hunks cannot be verified from visible output, do not assume semantic correctness. Score based only on visible patch content.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: SparseMatrix Empty hstack/vstack Fix
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluates whether the child trajectory addresses the SparseMatrix.row_join/col_join bug for empty (zero-row/zero-col) matrices in sympy/matrices/sparse.py. The parent baseline (Parent 2, Continuation 5) demonstrates that SparseMatrix.hstack with zero-row matrices returns wrong shape (0, 3) instead of (0, 6), because sparse.py has its own row_join implementation that lacks the empty-matrix fix applied to common.py. A child shows progress if it: (a) identifies that SparseMatrix.row_join/col_join in sparse.py needs the same empty-matrix handling as common.py, (b) produces a patch modifying sparse.py to handle zero-row/zero-col matrices correctly in row_join/col_join, or (c) runs the SparseMatrix reproducer and gets correct (0, 6) shape. Equivalence (score 3) means the child only works on dense Matrix (common.py) or explores sparse.py without fixing the semantic bug. Regression (score 1-2) means the child breaks SparseMatrix further or submits a patch that only fixes common.py while claiming full fix.

metadata.oracle_test: import sympy as sy; from sympy.matrices import SparseMatrix; M1=SparseMatrix.zeros(0,0); M2=SparseMatrix.zeros(0,1); M3=SparseMatrix.zeros(0,2); M4=SparseMatrix.zeros(0,3); assert sy.Matrix.hstack(M1,M2,M3,M4).shape == (0,6), f'got {sy.Matrix.hstack(M1,M2,M3,M4).shape}'
metadata.code_review: Check if patch modifies sympy/matrices/sparse.py row_join/col_join to handle empty matrices (zero rows/cols) by returning the other matrix when self is empty, ensuring reduce() accumulates correct total dimensions for SparseMatrix
metadata.judge_focus: Semantic correctness of column/row count preservation in SparseMatrix hstack/vstack with zero-dimension matrices, parity with dense Matrix fix
metadata.failure_mode: Patch only fixes common.py (dense Matrix) without addressing sparse.py, or applies fix to wrong method in sparse.py, or assumes SparseMatrix inherits fix from common.py (it doesn't - it overrides row_join)

scale.1: Child submits a patch that breaks SparseMatrix hstack/vstack (returns wrong shape like (0,3)) or only fixes common.py while claiming SparseMatrix is fixed, or loses any SparseMatrix exploration progress from parent
scale.2: Child makes changes to sparse.py but the fix is incomplete - e.g., only handles row_join but not col_join, or fix doesn't pass the SparseMatrix oracle test, or introduces new errors
scale.3: Child trajectory is equivalent to parent: only explores sparse.py, identifies the bug location, or fixes only dense Matrix (common.py) without addressing SparseMatrix row_join/col_join
scale.4: Child produces a patch modifying sparse.py row_join/col_join to correctly handle empty matrices (returning other matrix when self has zero rows/cols) AND the SparseMatrix oracle test passes, but test coverage is minimal or not committed
scale.5: Child produces a complete fix: modifies sparse.py row_join/col_join to handle empty matrices correctly (mirroring the common.py fix), adds a regression test for SparseMatrix hstack/vstack with zero-dimension matrices, and demonstrates the SparseMatrix oracle test passes

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Valid Git Diff Patch Submission
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluates whether the child trajectory produces and submits a valid standard git diff patch (beginning with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>`) via the final submission command. The parent baseline (Parent 1 and 2) identified the fix but did not submit a patch. Continuation 6 claims submission (result_status: finished, exit_status: Submitted) but produces an empty patch.txt with no diff content. Continuation 7 generates a proper git diff from commit 2dff3502e. A child shows progress if it: (a) creates a patch.txt (or equivalent) using git diff output, (b) submits it via a final submission command (e.g., `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat patch.txt`), and (c) the submitted output begins with `diff --git` header with correct relative paths. Equivalence (score 3) means the child explores or identifies the fix but does not submit a valid patch. Regression (score 1-2) means the child submits an invalid format (e.g., diff against .bak file, raw source code, empty patch) or stops before submitting.

metadata.judge_focus: Patch format validity and submission completion - must be standard git diff with diff --git header, not diff against .bak or raw source
metadata.failure_mode: Empty patch.txt submitted as complete; diff against backup file treated as valid; stopping after saving patch without final submission command; clean process but no valid patch produced

scale.1: Child submits an empty patch, raw source code, or a non-standard diff format (e.g., `--- <path>.bak` / `+++ <path>` without `diff --git` header), or claims submission with no actual patch content
scale.2: Child creates a patch file but stops before emitting the final submission command (result_status: paused, exit_status: empty), or submits a malformed diff
scale.3: Child trajectory is equivalent to parent: identifies/explores the fix but produces no patch file or submission (result_status: paused)
scale.4: Child creates a valid git diff patch file (patch.txt appears in untracked files) and submits it via cat, but the submission command or output has minor issues
scale.5: Child creates a valid git diff patch beginning with `diff --git a/<path> b/<path>`, submits it via the final submission command (`echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat patch.txt`), trajectory shows result_status: finished and exit_status: Submitted, and submission output contains well-formed hunks with correct relative paths

experiences.title: Do not let valid patch submission format override missing code fix coverage visible in diff_stat
experiences.description: When a task requires code changes across multiple files, a trajectory that submits a valid git diff patch covering only a subset of required files should not outscore a trajectory that makes extensive changes to all required files (visible in diff_stat) but does not submit a patch. The diff_stat and changed_files metadata are visible evidence of code changes and must be credited independently of patch submission format. Reject the pattern of using patch.txt presence and diff --git header validity as a proxy for overall code correctness.
experiences.context: In a task requiring NotImplemented returns across a class hierarchy (Basic, Expr, and Number subclasses), trajectories that submitted valid git diff patches covering only basic.py and expr.py (missing numbers.py) received higher scores than trajectories that extensively modified numbers.py (62 lines per diff_stat) without submitting a patch. The judge gave identical code-correctness rubric scores to both, failing to credit numbers.py changes visible in diff_stat, and then inflated patch-submission trajectories via the patch format rubric.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When a trajectory submits a valid diff --git patch, verify the patch covers ALL files requiring modification for the task. When a trajectory has no patch.txt, check diff_stat and changed_files for evidence of code changes before scoring.

Positive evidence: diff_stat showing many lines changed in a required file (e.g., 'numbers.py | 62 ++++----') is strong evidence of progress toward comprehensive fixes, even without a patch submission. Changed_files listing a required file alongside others indicates broader fix coverage and should raise the code-correctness rubric score above the level for trajectories that omit that file entirely.

Contradictory evidence: A valid diff --git patch covering only a subset of required files is evidence of an INCOMPLETE fix. Test output showing asymmetric comparison results (e.g., 'sympy_obj == foo = False' when 'foo == sympy_obj = True') confirms the fix does not achieve the required symmetric delegation behavior. A patch omitting a required file should not receive the highest patch rubric score when the scale requires 'all modified files' coverage.

Close-looking exclusion: Do not assume a trajectory with no patch.txt made no meaningful code changes. Check diff_stat for line counts in required files—a line like 'sympy/core/numbers.py | 62 +++++++++++++++++++++++++--------------------------' shows 62 lines changed and must be credited. Conversely, do not assume a submitted patch is complete just because it has a valid diff --git header; enumerate which files are included and cross-reference against the task requirements. A patch covering only basic.py and expr.py when numbers.py also needs fixes is a scale-3 code fix, not scale-5, regardless of patch format quality.

Abstention boundary: When the actual diff content for a file is not visible in trajectory steps (only diff_stat line counts are visible), credit the changes at the appropriate rubric level based on diff_stat evidence—do not zero-credit changes clearly present in diff_stat, but also do not assume full correctness without visible content. When all required files are covered by a submitted patch AND test output confirms correct behavior, patch format is a valid completion signal and should not be penalized. The abstention applies only when diff_stat is also absent or ambiguous.

experiences.title: Cross-check modified source appearance against actual reproduction output; code that looks fixed but still fails the reported case is not a working fix
experiences.description: When judging a bug-fix continuation, the execution output of the exact reported reproduction case is the ground truth for whether the fix works. Do not treat the mere presence of element-wise or three-way-classification logic in the inspected source as evidence of a working fix. If the same trajectory's test run still returns the buggy unevaluated result for the core mixed symbolic+numeric case, the fix is not working, regardless of how the code reads. Conversely, a trajectory whose reproduction run returns the expected evaluated result demonstrates a working fix and should not be scored below a trajectory whose run still fails.
experiences.context: A FiniteSet._complement task where the reported bug is that Complement(FiniteSet(x, y, 2), Interval(-10, 10)) returns an unevaluated Complement({x, y}, Interval(-10, 10)) instead of {x, y}. The rubrics ask for (a) element-wise interval containment handling in FiniteSet._complement and (b) validation that the exact reproduction case yields {x, y}.
experiences.experience:
Activation: a continuation shows inspected or modified target source and also executes the exact reported reproduction in the visible prefix.

Positive evidence: the reproduction returns the requested result with the expected type and contents, and the visible implementation accounts for the mixed symbolic and numeric cases required by the task.

Contradictory evidence: if the same trajectory's reproduction still returns the buggy unevaluated expression, source that merely looks like it contains the right classification logic is not a working fix. Passing only an already-working numeric subcase is insufficient.

Close-looking exclusions: unrelated compatibility edits, diagnostic prints, or source inspection do not outweigh direct contradictory execution output. Do not infer target correctness from activity in other modules.

Abstention boundary: if neither a target reproduction result nor the relevant implementation is visible, preserve uncertainty.

experiences.title: Rank-0 Array Length Contract Must Dominate Over Indexing Policy
experiences.description: Retrieve when the reported bug is that `len()` or element count for a rank-0/scalar array is zero even though iteration produces one element. The primary judging rule is the rank-0 length/iteration contract: an empty shape must contribute one element to the internal product/loop-size calculation. Do not turn this into a high-weight decision about whether scalar arrays accept integer indexing such as `arr[0]`, and do not reward broad test edits or indexing-policy discussion as if they were the requested fix.
experiences.context: Applies to visible trajectories where the prompt shows a scalar array with `len(a) == 0`, `len(list(a)) == 1`, and a NumPy scalar size comparison of 1, and where the inspected code or diffs involve N-dimensional array length, `_loop_size`, shape-product logic, or duplicated dense/sparse array construction paths. It is especially relevant when some continuations fix the internal product for empty shape while others discuss `_parse_index`, `rank_zero_array[0]`, or test expectations around scalar indexing. Do not use this card for issues that explicitly ask to redesign indexing, slicing, scalar subscripting, or a broader rank-0 API.
experiences.experience:
Activation: generate one dominant behavioral rubric for the reported rank-0 `len()`/iteration contract. The rubric should ask whether the visible source change makes the element count/product for shape `()` equal to one, so that the prompt-style scalar array has `len(...) == 1` and remains consistent with `len(list(...)) == 1`.

Positive evidence: strong trajectories visibly change the source length/loop-size calculation so the product identity for an empty shape is one rather than zero; apply that same semantic fix to the duplicated dense and sparse paths that visibly compute `_loop_size` or equivalent element count; and check the prompt behavior with scalar arrays while preserving ordinary higher-rank lengths as the product of dimensions. A `reduce` initializer of `1` is common evidence, but it is not required: any equivalent implementation of the empty-shape product contract should tie with it.

Contradictory evidence: weak trajectories only change tests, comments, or validation scripts without a visible source-level length/loop-size fix; fix only one visible implementation while a duplicated dense/sparse path still has the empty-shape special case yielding zero; rely on broad test passing or test-oracle narration without showing the scalar `len` behavior; or focus on `_parse_index`, `arr[0]`, bounds checks, or scalar indexing while the rank-0 length calculation is absent or unchanged. Indexing-only work must score below even a minimal source edit that correctly makes rank-0 `len()` return one.

Close-looking exclusions: an existing or edited test about `rank_zero_array[0]` is not the requested contract. Treat such indexing checks as neutral ancillary evidence unless they are the only substantive change or they visibly break the length behavior. Likewise, updating a test that previously expected the old length value can support the length contract, but the amount or breadth of test editing should not outrank the source fix itself. A trajectory need not edit `__len__` directly if visible evidence shows `__len__` depends on the corrected loop-size/element-count field.

Abstention boundary: if the paused prefix only contains claims that a fix was made, changed-file summaries, or truncated output, but no relevant source edit and no runtime check of `len`/iteration are visible, preserve uncertainty instead of ranking that trajectory highly. If the visible prefix cannot distinguish two implementations that both enforce the empty-shape product of one, tie them; do not break ties using scalar integer indexing policy, extra test edits, or unrelated validation activity.

experiences.title: Guard condition form determines skip vs fall-through for complex exponents in _TR56 _f
experiences.description: When a rubric evaluates patch submission format and claims the parent fix is correct, it must verify the guard condition form in the submitted patch. The De Morgan form `not rv.exp.is_real or (rv.exp > max) == True` returns early for complex exponents, skipping the transformation. The positive form `rv.exp.is_real and (rv.exp > max) == True` only short-circuits the comparison but falls through to the transformation code for complex exponents. These forms are not semantically equivalent despite both preventing the TypeError.
experiences.context: The issue is a TypeError in simplify(cos(x)**I) caused by _TR56's _f function comparing complex exponents with < and >. The fix adds rv.exp.is_real guards before the comparisons. Two parents produce different guard forms: one uses `not rv.exp.is_real or (comparison)` and the other uses `rv.exp.is_real and (comparison)`. The original guards (rv.exp < 0 and rv.exp > max) exist to skip the trigonometric power transformation for out-of-range exponents. Complex exponents are out-of-range and should be skipped.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When a rubric evaluates patch submission format and the submitted patches contain is_real guard conditions before exponent comparisons in _TR56's _f function, verify the guard form determines whether complex exponents are properly skipped.

Positive evidence: The De Morgan form `not rv.exp.is_real or (rv.exp > max) == True` evaluates to True when is_real is False, so it returns rv and skips the transformation for complex exponents. This matches the original guard intent: out-of-range exponents should not be transformed. The visible code structure (lines 504-510) shows the guards precede the transformation code (if rv.exp == 2: return h(g(rv.base.args[0])**2)), so returning early correctly skips the transformation.

Contradictory evidence: The positive form `rv.exp.is_real and (rv.exp > max) == True` evaluates to False when is_real is False, so it does NOT return rv. The code falls through to `if rv.exp == 2:` and the else branch, which performs the transformation. While this prevents the TypeError (because False and (comparison) short-circuits before the comparison), it does not skip the transformation for complex exponents. The rubric's claim that 'the parent trajectory already contains the correct source fix' is misleading when the guard form does not skip the transformation for complex exponents. A format-only rubric that assumes both parents have the correct fix gives identical scores to semantically different patches.

Close-looking exclusions: Both forms prevent the TypeError because `False and (comparison)` short-circuits before the comparison is attempted. If the rubric only checks TypeError prevention, both forms appear equivalent. But the rubric claims the parent fix is correct and the child's contribution is packaging — this is misleading when the parents have different semantic forms. Do not treat the absence of TypeError as evidence of semantic correctness. Both forms pass visible tests for simplify(cos(x)**I) returning cos(x)**I, but the control flow difference (skip vs fall-through) is visible in the patch content and code structure.

Abstention boundary: If both parents use the same guard form, or if the else branch is fully visible and returns rv unchanged for complex exponents (making both forms functionally equivalent), then format-only evaluation is sufficient. Do not apply this experience when the guard form does not affect the transformation skip behavior. If the else branch content is fully visible and shows no transformation occurs for complex exponents, the two forms may be equivalent and format-only evaluation is appropriate.

experiences.title: Prefer caller-side surd predicate in sqrtdenest.py over helper-level guard in radsimp.py for empty-surds IndexError
experiences.description: When fixing the IndexError in sqrtdenest caused by empty surds reaching _split_gcd, the correct fix is a caller-side predicate in sqrtdenest.py's _sqrt_match that avoids calling split_surds when no denestable surds are present. Do not reward a helper-level guard in radsimp.py's split_surds as 'comprehensive protection' — the return semantics change to (1, S.Zero, expr) does not correctly fix the issue and the caller-side fix alone is sufficient and correct.
experiences.context: The issue traceback shows _sqrt_match → split_surds → _split_gcd crashing on `g = a[0]` with empty surds. The visible diff_stat in each continuation shows which files were modified: sqrtdenest.py-only (caller-side predicate), radsimp.py-only (helper-level guard with `if not surds: return 1, S.Zero, expr`), or both. Test results visible in pytest output validate whether the fix passes the sqrtdenest test suite. The issue description states that if an expression cannot be denested it should be returned unchanged.
experiences.experience:
Activation: When evaluating fixes for IndexError in sqrtdenest where split_surds receives empty surds, and diff_stat or git diff is visible showing which files were modified.

Positive evidence: diff_stat shows only sqrtdenest.py modified; _sqrt_match returns [] or skips split_surds for expressions without denestable surds; all sqrtdenest tests pass (visible in pytest output: '12 passed'); _sqrt_match correctly handles test_sqrtdenest3 nested surd cases returning correct denesting results; the fix preserves non-denestable expressions unchanged.

Contradictory evidence: diff_stat shows only radsimp.py modified with `if not surds: return 1, S.Zero, expr`; this changes split_surds return semantics to (1, S.Zero, expr) which does not properly signal non-denestability to _sqrt_match; the caller _sqrt_match receives r=1, b=0, a=expr and may attempt incorrect denesting with these values; visible test output may show edge cases passing but the approach changes helper behavior for all callers including numberfields.py.

Close-looking exclusion: A fix modifying BOTH sqrtdenest.py and radsimp.py may appear more comprehensive but the radsimp.py guard is unnecessary when the caller-side predicate is correct; adding both does not improve correctness; do not score higher solely because more files were changed or because the fix 'protects all callers'; fixes that change the same file with the same approach should be scored equivalently regardless of process differences.

Reject misleading pattern: Do not reward 'comprehensive protection of all split_surds callers' as a positive signal; the helper-level guard in radsimp.py is not the correct fix for this issue; the correct fix is caller-side only in sqrtdenest.py; the framing of 'protecting numberfields.py and future callers' is misleading when the actual problem is the caller _sqrt_match incorrectly calling split_surds with no surds — the fix belongs in the caller, not the helper.

Abstention boundary: If git diff content is not visible and only process/testing steps are shown, cannot determine which approach was taken; if the exact patch content for both-files fixes is not visible, cannot determine whether the radsimp.py change is harmful or neutral; if test results are not visible, cannot validate correctness.

experiences.title: Do not score test-failure investigation or semantic test-correctness arguments above concrete test pass/fail signals
experiences.description: When a patch causes a visible test failure, the agent's subsequent investigation of why the test fails and arguments that the test expectation is semantically incorrect are not evidence of patch correctness. A patch that changes behavior in ways that break existing tests carries higher risk of failing elsewhere. Score based on the actual code change and its observable test results, not the depth of investigation or quality of semantic argument about why a test is wrong.
experiences.context: A ConditionSet._eval_subs bug fix where the bound variable was incorrectly set to the substitution value (new) instead of the original bound variable (self.sym). One continuation changes the S.true branch to return the base set directly, causing a visible test failure. The agent investigates extensively, arguing the test expectation is semantically wrong. Another continuation makes a minimal fix preserving the ConditionSet construction with the correct bound variable, which does not trigger test failures.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Visible diffs showing different approaches to the same bug fix, where one approach triggers a test failure and the other does not.

Positive evidence: A minimal fix that changes `ConditionSet(new, Contains(new, base), base)` to `ConditionSet(self.sym, Contains(self.sym, base), base)` preserves the existing ConditionSet construction pattern while correcting the bound variable. This approach does not trigger test failures in visible test runs and makes the smallest behavioral change needed to fix the reported issue.

Contradictory evidence: A patch that changes the S.true branch to `return base` triggers a visible test failure. The agent investigates the failure extensively, arguing the test expectation is semantically incorrect because the condition is always true for the given domain. This investigation is thorough and mathematically sound, but it is not evidence that the patch is correct. The test failure is a concrete negative signal that should not be overridden by semantic argument. Explicitly reject the pattern of treating investigation depth and semantic test-correctness arguments as proxies for patch correctness.

Close-looking exclusion: The agent's mathematical analysis (n < p is always true for negative n and positive p) is correct, but this only explains why the condition simplifies to S.true. It does not prove that returning the base set is the correct behavior. The test failure shows the patch changes behavior in ways the test suite does not expect. Even if the test expectation is debatable, a patch that fails existing tests carries higher risk of also failing additional tests. The depth of investigation into why a test fails is a process signal, not a correctness signal. A simpler fix that preserves existing behavior patterns and passes tests should not be scored below a more aggressive fix that fails tests but is accompanied by elaborate justification.

Abstention boundary: If the visible paused state does not show test results or diffs, we cannot determine which approach is safer. If both approaches pass all visible tests, we cannot distinguish them without additional evidence.

experiences.title: RST header_rows: prefer FixedWidth-delegating, boundary-aware fixes over validation-heavy manual writers
experiences.description: Use this when judging the RST header_rows continuations in the paused view. The correct ranking should favor implementations that address the visible TypeError by wiring RST into the existing FixedWidth header_rows machinery and preserving read/write boundaries, not branches that merely show more test commands, more edge-case printouts, or a submitted patch.
experiences.context: The task failure shown in the prompt is `TypeError: RST.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'header_rows'` when writing `format='ascii.rst'` with `header_rows=['name', 'unit']`. Fixed-width output already supports header rows. In the visible continuations, one family makes a larger custom RST.write renderer and shows many write validations; another family has a smaller RST change that delegates to `super().write(table)`, uses the separator line at `len(self.header.header_rows)`, and adds a read boundary adjustment with `self.data.start_line = 2 + len(self.header.header_rows)`. The latter is stronger semantic evidence despite less validation ceremony.
experiences.experience: Activation conditions: apply when comparing continuations for this RST header_rows task, especially where one branch rewrites RST output manually while another adapts the existing FixedWidth/RST structure. Decisive positive evidence: the patch visibly accepts or stores `header_rows` for RST while preserving the default name header behavior; it continues to rely on the inherited FixedWidth writer, e.g. `lines = super().write(table)` followed by choosing the RST separator line dynamically with `idx = len(self.header.header_rows)` rather than the old fixed `lines[1]`; if the same RST class now accepts `header_rows` for reading, it adjusts the data start line to account for the extra header rows; visible output shows the original example producing the name row, unit row, data rows, and final RST separator without the TypeError; default `ascii.rst` output remains unchanged. Contradictory evidence: a branch that builds `rst_lines` manually in `write` and falls back to the old behavior, with no visible read/data-start adjustment, should not outrank the delegating implementation merely because it printed several edge cases or ran existing RST/fixedwidth tests. Existing suite passes are useful regression evidence but are not proof that new header_rows semantics, formatting, fill values, masks, or read boundaries are preserved. Explicitly reject the misleading rubric or judge bias that treats fuller validation logs, final submission, or more edge-case demonstrations as more important than visible root-cause alignment in the implementation. Close-looking exclusions: do not downgrade the concise delegating branch for an exploratory empty-table ValueError unless empty-table support is the requested behavior; do not treat `no tests ran`, wrong working directory, missing pytest under the wrong interpreter, or an initial `cat patch.txt` from the wrong directory as semantic patch failures when later visible code/output addresses the task; do not give correctness credit for a completion marker alone. A paused continuation with a visible correct diff and relevant output can be better than a submitted continuation with a riskier implementation. Preserve equivalent valid implementations: exact line text is not required if the code clearly accepts header_rows, places RST separators according to the number of header rows, preserves inherited formatting behavior or demonstrates an equivalent complete renderer, and avoids read-boundary regressions. Abstention boundary: if the diff is truncated so the judge cannot tell whether the implementation delegates to FixedWidth, computes the dynamic separator position, or adjusts read boundaries, and the output only shows the basic sample, do not infer superiority from test quantity or submission status; mark the comparison uncertain until visible code or targeted behavior distinguishes the branches.

experiences.title: Do not tie get_resolver branches on cache-hit demos; preserve the public cache-clear path
experiences.description: For the Django URL resolver optimization, the wrapper/_get_resolver refactor fixes the None-vs-ROOT_URLCONF cache key only if cache invalidation still works. Branches must not be ranked equally merely because they show get_resolver(None) and get_resolver(settings.ROOT_URLCONF) returning the same object. The decisive source-level issue is whether clear_url_caches can still clear the actual lru_cache.
experiences.context: The visible paused view shows continuations after a get_resolver refactor in django/urls/resolvers.py. The problematic small patch removes @functools.lru_cache from public get_resolver, adds a cached private _get_resolver, and has get_resolver return _get_resolver(urlconf). That fixes the primary cache-key behavior but removes the public get_resolver.cache_clear attribute unless delegation is added or django/urls/base.py is updated. Some branches run custom cache-info or same-object scripts; those validate the main optimization only, not cache invalidation.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply this when the round is the get_resolver optimization and the visible diff/summary shows public get_resolver being converted into a non-cached wrapper around a cached _get_resolver.

Decisive positive evidence: A branch should rank above wrapper-only branches if it both normalizes None to settings.ROOT_URLCONF before calling the cached function and preserves cache invalidation. Valid implementations include either: (1) in resolvers.py, after _get_resolver is defined and decorated, assigning the cached function's cache API back onto the public wrapper, e.g. get_resolver.cache_clear = _get_resolver.cache_clear; optional cache_info delegation is fine; or (2) updating django/urls/base.py's clear_url_caches path so it clears _get_resolver's cache directly with the necessary import/call changes. The visible multi-file branch touching base.py and resolvers.py is potentially positive for the direct-clear implementation; a resolvers-only branch is equally valid if the delegation assignment is visible.

Contradictory evidence: A small resolvers.py-only diff that merely removes @lru_cache from get_resolver, adds _get_resolver, and returns _get_resolver(urlconf) is not complete. In the supplied view this is recognizable from the compact 6-line/1-line style diff and the shown patch body containing only the wrapper and private cached function. Such a patch leaves callers of get_resolver.cache_clear broken. Same-object output, _get_resolver.cache_info hits, or a printed 'All tests passed!' from a custom script does not contradict this cache-clear breakage. A script that reports reverse errors and then prints success is not validation. Failed commands such as missing pytest, file-or-directory-not-found, or unconfigured settings are also not passing validation.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not require a base.py edit when resolvers.py explicitly delegates cache_clear from _get_resolver to get_resolver; that is a clean valid implementation. Conversely, do not reward a branch just because it demonstrates the primary cache-key fix with get_resolver(None) and get_resolver(settings.ROOT_URLCONF); that test does not exercise clear_url_caches. Do not use pip installs, directory listings, or test-discovery attempts as correctness evidence. A successful unrelated test module is only supportive after the source-level invalidation path is correct.

Rejected misleading bias: Reject any rubric or judging habit that ties all continuations because their visible runtime demos look similar, or that treats cache-hit demos as sufficient. Also reject the opposite bias that only a base.py modification can be correct; wrapper-level cache_clear delegation is equivalent when visible and correctly placed.

Abstention boundary: If the actual delegation assignment or the base.py clear_url_caches change is not visible because the diff is truncated, do not infer correctness solely from changed-file count, patch size, or cache-info output. In that case, mark invalidation as unproven rather than ranking it above a branch with an explicit visible invalidation fix. If no branch exposes the cache-clear path in the paused view, abstain on this issue and judge only the visible primary optimization and validation quality.

experiences.title: ModelForm default override tie-breaker: direct cleaned_data semantics outrank custom-clean proxies
experiences.description: For the paused task about allowing cleaned_data to overwrite model field defaults, rank implementations by the visible construct_instance semantics and production runtime history, not by self-authored success banners, patch size, or save()/opts.fields detours. A direct predicate that lets a field present in cleaned_data override a default when omitted from submitted data is stronger than a branch whose visible history shows construct_instance crashing on a custom-clean-method proxy, even if that branch later prints that its own edge tests passed.
experiences.context: Activate on this round’s forms/models.py task where the prompt says a model field with a default should be overwritten from form.cleaned_data when the field is omitted from the submitted data. The paused view includes reproductions where cleaned_data contains values such as some_field='overridden_value' or boolean_field=False while the submitted data omits that field, plus continuations that inspect construct_instance, run custom test_issue/test_comprehensive/test_edge_cases scripts, or debug opts.fields.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions:
Use this experience when comparing branches for the visible ModelForm cleaned_data-over-defaults issue and the paused evidence includes any of: construct_instance source around default/value_omitted_from_data handling, output showing cleaned_data contains an omitted defaulted field, custom scripts named like test_issue/test_comprehensive/test_edge_cases, or tracebacks from django/forms/models.py.

Decisive positive evidence:
- Strongest positive evidence is visible source or behavior showing the default-skip logic is controlled directly by the field’s presence/value in cleaned_data: if a model field has a default and is omitted from submitted data, but form.cleaned_data contains that field, construct_instance saves the cleaned_data value to the instance. Equivalent implementations are valid; do not require exact syntax such as one particular `f.name in cleaned_data` expression if the same data-flow contract is satisfied.
- A corrected reproduction is positive when it shows `Form is valid: True`, cleaned_data contains the omitted defaulted field, and the resulting instance value is the cleaned_data override rather than the model default.
- A comprehensive custom run is useful supporting evidence when it tests the same contract and the visible implementation is semantically direct. In this view, a checkbox/boolean case where cleaned_data contains `False` and the instance becomes `False` is a pass, not a regression; an earlier expectation of `True` was the bad expectation.
- Absence of production tracebacks from django/forms/models.py is important. Environment failures such as missing packages or settings do not undermine otherwise correct source semantics.

Contradictory evidence:
- A traceback inside django/forms/models.py from construct_instance is production-code failure. In particular, `NameError: name 'forms' is not defined` at a line comparing `form.__class__.clean` to `forms.BaseForm.clean` is decisive negative evidence: the edited production function was not runnable at that point.
- The custom-clean-method check itself is a suspicious proxy. Correctness depends on whether the individual model field is in cleaned_data and should be saved, not on whether the form class overrides `clean()`. A later edit described only as fixing the import/name problem does not prove the proxy was replaced with correct cleaned_data semantics. Unless later visible source clearly shows an equivalent direct cleaned_data predicate, keep this branch below a branch with direct cleaned_data handling and no production-code error.
- A final `ALL TESTS PASSED` or similar banner from self-written edge-case scripts does not erase the earlier production traceback or validate a proxy implementation. Those scripts are useful only insofar as their assertions and the final source are visible and match the contract.
- Output showing the issue still fails, such as cleaned_data containing a derived/defaulted field while the instance prints the model `default_value` and the script prints `FAILURE`, is direct contradictory behavior.

Close-looking exclusions:
- Do not confuse a test-script NameError such as an undefined form class in a self-authored edge test with a production-code NameError in django/forms/models.py. The former may only show a bad test; the latter shows the patch broke the library function.
- Do not penalize the branch that corrected a boolean expectation from `True` to `False` when the visible facts show an omitted unchecked checkbox produced cleaned_data `False` and the instance was saved as `False`.
- Missing pytest, missing settings modules, missing dependencies, or attempts to find the right test runner are not semantic failures.
- Extra handling for fields not declared on the form may be valid if it preserves normal fields/exclude behavior, but it is not a substitute for the core construct_instance contract and should not be used to outrank a clean direct implementation.

Explicit rejection of misleading judge bias:
Reject any rubric or judging bias that awards a decisive advantage for BaseModelForm.save()/opts.fields expansion, number of custom scripts, diff size, or a final success banner while discounting the visible construct_instance semantics and production traceback. Also reject treating `form.__class__.clean is not BaseForm.clean`-style custom-clean detection as equivalent to checking the actual cleaned_data field. In this paused view, that proxy is negative evidence, not a near-tie with a direct cleaned_data implementation.

Abstention boundary:
If the paused view shows only diff_stat, script names, or a final success banner and does not reveal either the construct_instance condition or a meaningful reproduction result, do not infer correctness from line counts, untracked test volume, or self-reported success. If an earlier production error is visible and the later final source is truncated, retain the negative signal unless visible later evidence proves the source now implements the direct cleaned_data contract.

experiences.title: Credit the continuation that fixes trailing group handling in both admindocs group replacers
experiences.description: For the simplify_regexp/simplify_regex trailing-groups task, do not assume that touching replace_unnamed_groups is a regression. The visible paused view shows the same end-of-string balancing failure pattern can affect unnamed capture groups, and a continuation that investigates and patches that related helper has stronger task coverage than a continuation that only validates the named-group example.
experiences.context: The issue title is that simplify_regexp() does not replace trailing groups, while the description gives a named-group example in replace_named_groups(). Both parents already add an end-of-loop check in django/contrib/admindocs/utils.py so a final named group is appended after unmatched_open_brackets reaches 0 at the last ')'. Most continuations keep only this 5-line named-group patch and test named examples. One continuation visibly has a 10-line utils.py diff including the same terminal handling in replace_unnamed_groups, then stashes its work to inspect baseline behavior and shows that without the change replace_unnamed_groups leaves entries/(\w+) unchanged while entries/(\w+)/ becomes entries/<var>/, and similarly leaves a terminal second group in (\w+)/(\w+) unchanged.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply this when judging the paused admindocs trailing-groups task and the visible state includes both: (1) the inherited named-group end-of-loop fix, and (2) a continuation that inspects or modifies replace_unnamed_groups because terminal unnamed groups show the same no-trailing-slash behavior.

Decisive positive evidence: Strongly credit a continuation whose final visible diff preserves the named-group fix and also adds equivalent end-of-string balanced-parenthesis handling to replace_unnamed_groups, especially when it demonstrates the baseline asymmetry that an unnamed group followed by '/' is replaced but the same group at string end is not. This is direct evidence for the broader user-facing title contract: trailing groups should be simplified, not only the single named example from the description. Equivalent valid implementations are acceptable: the fix may use an after-loop check, a sentinel/end condition, a shared helper, or another readable mechanism, provided it replaces terminal capture groups without disturbing nested or escaped group handling.

Contradictory evidence: Do not give top credit to a continuation merely because it prints 'All tests passed' while its visible replace_unnamed_groups output still leaves terminal unnamed groups unchanged. That output is evidence that the same trailing-group bug remains for the related helper, not evidence of a preserved contract. Also treat failed test-runner setup, grep-only exploration, or named-example-only validation as weaker than a visible patch plus baseline demonstration covering both named and unnamed terminal groups.

Close-looking exclusions: A clean 5-line patch limited to replace_named_groups can be a plausible narrow fix for the exact example in the description, but in this paused comparison it should not outrank the branch that visibly addresses the same terminal failure in replace_unnamed_groups. Reject the misleading judging bias that 'minimal patch touching only replace_named_groups' is automatically superior or that 'unnamed groups at the end should not be replaced' is established by the visible evidence. The stashed baseline run showing entries/(\w+) remains unchanged is a reproduction of the defect pattern, not a specification to preserve. Conversely, do not require the exact 10-line diff shape; preserve any implementation that satisfies the same behavior.

Abstention boundary: If the only visible evidence is the issue description's named-group example and there is no visible replace_unnamed_groups investigation, diff, or baseline behavior, then do not require an unnamed-group fix. If a continuation modifies replace_unnamed_groups in a way that visibly breaks nonterminal, nested, escaped, or noncapturing group behavior, penalize that concrete breakage. If the diff is too truncated to determine whether the unnamed helper is actually fixed, credit the visible diagnostic insight but avoid maximum confidence.

experiences.title: Rank OutputWrapper.flush branches by observable flush delegation, not StringIO output or close() additions
experiences.description: Use when judging the Django management OutputWrapper.flush issue in this paused view. The requested contract is that self.stdout/self.stderr.flush() on management commands must bypass TextIOBase.flush and delegate to the wrapped stream so migrate progress can be flushed before the final OK. Do not require one exact patch shape, do not require a no-flush guard, and do not award extra credit for adding close().
experiences.context: Activation: the visible issue says long migrations print the Applying migration line only at the end because flush() on management command stdout/stderr does not work. The visible diagnosis shows OutputWrapper inherits TextIOBase.flush, OutputWrapper has no explicit flush method before the edit, and a wrapped custom stream can remain unflushed. The relevant file is django/core/management/base.py and the relevant class is OutputWrapper. In this paused view, Parent 1 and Parent 2 both move toward adding an explicit flush method, but the child continuations differ in whether they produce meaningful evidence that wrapper.flush() actually calls the underlying stream's flush.
experiences.experience:
Decisive positive evidence: Strongly credit a branch when the visible parent-plus-child state contains an inspectable OutputWrapper.flush override that delegates to the wrapped stream, such as self._out.flush() or an equivalent guarded or try/except delegation, and when validation observes a flush side effect on the wrapped object. The best validation uses a custom stream with a flushed flag or flush_count, or otherwise proves the underlying stream's flush method was invoked during a migration-like sequence before writing OK. In this view, a branch with a visible diff adding flush plus a custom no-flush or stdout/stderr check is strong; a branch whose output says basic flush delegation passed after the patch is meaningful when it is tied to the earlier custom-stream failure mode; and a branch that reports Total flushes: 2 in a migration-like Applying... OK sequence is also strong. Simple direct delegation without hasattr is still a valid implementation when the wrapped stream has flush, because the reported stdout/stderr streams do have flush. Equivalent implementations should be preserved.

Contradictory evidence: Penalize a branch if, after its claimed fix, wrapper.flush() still leaves a custom stream's flushed flag false, if OutputWrapper still relies only on TextIOBase.flush, if the visible edit is syntactically suspect or the file surgery appears to remove or corrupt the method layout, or if the branch adds unrelated methods while missing or breaking flush delegation. Test commands that error during setup, collect zero tests, or only locate files provide no validation. A failed official-looking test command should not outweigh a direct successful flush-delegation check.

Close-looking exclusions: Reject the misleading rubric bias that treats close() delegation as an improvement for this issue. close() is not part of the reported migrate progress contract, and adding or testing close() on StringIO should not raise a branch above a clean flush-only fix. Also reject the bias that requires an hasattr guard for top credit; a guard is acceptable robustness, but the essential fix is explicit delegation of flush to the wrapped stream. Do not treat StringIO.getvalue() after a write as proof that flushing worked: StringIO shows written text immediately whether flush is delegated or not. Therefore a simulated migration callback that only prints After apply_start or final Applying... OK from a StringIO buffer is weak unless it also observes that the underlying flush method ran. Likewise, listing TextIOBase methods, inspecting OutputWrapper.__dict__, checking wrapper.close(), or showing final output text without a flush side effect is not decisive validation.

Branch-ranking rule for this view: Branches that visibly demonstrate underlying flush delegation after the patch should outrank branches that merely simulate migration output with StringIO or explore close(). Continuations from the simple-delegation parent should not be suppressed merely because they lack an hasattr guard. A continuation should not become the unique best branch just because it uses migration_progress_callback-looking code or investigates close(); the judge must ask whether the visible evidence proves wrapper.flush() invoked the wrapped stream's flush before OK.

Abstention boundary: If the diff is truncated and there is no direct side-effect test, credit only the visible parent-level likelihood of a flush override and avoid maximum confidence. If a branch has the likely fix but only failed test-runner attempts or StringIO final-output assertions, treat it as plausible but not well validated. If direct side-effect validation is visible but the exact internal code shape is not fully shown, credit the user-visible contract while remaining cautious about uninspected edge cases rather than inventing extra requirements.

experiences.title: MiddlewareNotUsed ASGI Poisoning: Patch Semantics and Real Validation Beat Superficial Chain-Built Checks
experiences.description: Use this when judging continuations for the MiddlewareNotUsed ASGI handler-poisoning task. Correct ranking should prioritize visible evidence that the handler variable is not left adapted after MiddlewareNotUsed, plus official targeted MiddlewareNotUsed test success, over ad hoc tests that merely show a middleware chain object exists.
experiences.context: The prompt identifies the bug in BaseHandler.load_middleware: MiddlewareNotUsed skips to the next middleware but can leave the loop's handler variable overwritten by adapt_method_mode(), so later middleware receive a wrongly adapted callable. The paused view shows continuations modifying django/core/handlers/base.py and then running a mix of custom middleware scripts, official middleware exception tests, and unrelated or misconfigured test commands.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Activate for this round when the task is the MiddlewareNotUsed ASGI poisoning issue and the continuation evidence is limited to the paused view: changed_files/diff snippets for django/core/handlers/base.py plus terminal output from custom middleware scripts or Django test commands.

Decisive positive evidence: A strong continuation either visibly fixes the handler lifetime or validates such a fix with the exact targeted tests. Valid implementations include: (1) computing an adapted handler in a separate temporary variable and assigning it to the loop handler only after the middleware instance is successfully created; or (2) saving the original handler before adaptation and restoring it in the MiddlewareNotUsed except path. Do not require one spelling if the observable invariant is preserved: after MiddlewareNotUsed, the next middleware sees the same unpoisoned handler state, while successfully initialized middleware still receive the correctly adapted callable and handler_is_async is updated only after success. Strong validation is the visible command `./tests/runtests.py tests.middleware_exceptions.tests.MiddlewareNotUsedTests --verbosity=2` with all four tests listed and `Ran 4 tests ... OK`. Related handler tests passing after that are supporting evidence. A continuation that explicitly recognizes that the middleware constructor still needs the adapted handler, then changes the code to save/restore or otherwise avoid leaking the adapted handler on MiddlewareNotUsed, is also strong even if it runs only a narrower async middleware test afterward.

Contradictory or weak evidence: Do not treat a custom script printing `SUCCESS`, `middleware chain built: True`, `_middleware_chain is not None`, or `Async test with async middleware after NotUsed passed: True` as decisive by itself. Chain construction alone does not prove that the response path is awaitable in ASGI, that the next middleware received the correct pre-adaptation handler, or that the exact MiddlewareNotUsed contract is preserved. A visible `async_to_sync was passed a non-async-marked callable` warning further weakens such custom validation. Import errors, missing pytest, settings already configured, incorrect test module selection, or exploratory grep/sed commands are not validation. A broad test command failing because the selected test label resolves badly is not evidence against a fix if the exact MiddlewareNotUsedTests already passed.

Close-looking exclusions: Reject the misleading rubric or judge bias that ranks an ad hoc ASGI `NotUsed -> async middleware` script above a continuation with the real handler-leak fix and official `MiddlewareNotUsedTests` success merely because the ad hoc script mentions async. Also reject treating installation/setup activity, untracked custom test files, or repeated toy scripts as progress beyond patch correctness. Conversely, do not overfit to the phrase `save/restore`: the temporary `adapted_handler` pattern is equivalent if it prevents assignment of the adapted callable to the loop handler until middleware initialization succeeds.

Abstention boundary: If the diff is truncated and there is no visible official test result or clear code snippet showing when handler is assigned/restored, do not infer correctness from `changed_files` alone. If a test output is truncated before the `Ran 4 tests ... OK` summary, count it only as an attempted run. If only `_middleware_chain is not None` is visible, abstain from concluding that the ASGI poisoning bug is fixed.

experiences.title: BoundWidget.id_for_label paused-view tie-breaker: source-confirmed no-fallback fix outranks clean-diff-only branches
experiences.description: For this BoundWidget.id_for_label task, do not tie all clean-looking boundfield.py edits. A branch that visibly replaces the generated-id return with a no-fallback attrs-id return and confirms custom IDs should rank above branches whose only support is a 1-insertion/1-deletion summary, test discovery, missing-test pytest output, or dependency setup.
experiences.context: The issue says BoundWidget.id_for_label ignores the id already placed in widget.data['attrs']['id'] by ChoiceWidget options and instead regenerates 'id_%s_%s'. The visible parent reproduction shows attrs containing custom-id_0/custom-id_1 while id_for_label still returns id_choices_0/id_choices_1. In the paused continuations, the important distinction is whether the relevant source line is actually visible and correct, not merely whether the summary reports a small diff or later commands look busy.
experiences.experience:
Activation conditions: Apply when judging these paused continuation branches for the BoundWidget.id_for_label fix, especially when several branches have the same changed file and a 1-insertion/1-deletion summary but only some show the final relevant source or issue-specific output.

Decisive positive evidence: The strongest visible branch shows the original generated return, performs a replacement, then shows the final source as:
    def id_for_label(self):
        return self.data['attrs'].get('id')
This is a no-fallback implementation: it uses the id already stored in attrs and does not manufacture 'id_%s_%s'. The same branch then runs the custom-id reproducer and prints widget.id_for_label as custom-id_0 and custom-id_1. That visible before/after source plus issue-specific confirmation should outrank branches that only have a clean diff summary.

Equivalent valid implementations: Preserve implementations that are semantically the same: returning the attrs id without falling back to the generated name/index format, with harmless quote/style differences or an otherwise safe attrs-id access. Do not require exactly the same string literal style or editing mechanism. The core requirement is no generated-id fallback and no surrounding source corruption.

Contradictory evidence: A visible line such as:
    return self.data['attrs'].get('id', 'id_%s_%s' % (...))
or the equivalent fallback to name/index is incorrect, even if custom-id tests pass. In the paused view, the fallback branch explicitly prints attrs as {}, attrs.get('id') as None, and widget.id_for_label as id_choices_0/id_choices_1 in the no-custom-id case; that is the old behavior persisting. Also contradictory is malformed source around the property, such as a choice_label property immediately followed by another @property with no body, an unreachable return self.data['label'], or otherwise corrupted BoundWidget property definitions. A correct-looking return inside syntactically or structurally broken source is not a good fix.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not give top credit merely because the branch summary says boundfield.py changed by 1 insertion and 1 deletion. In this paused view, several branches with that summary only show searching for tests, installing dependencies, running a nonexistent test path, or inspecting unrelated parts of the file; none of that confirms the final id_for_label implementation. Pytest output saying a file or directory was not found, collected 0 items, no tests ran, or output truncated before relevant assertions is not positive correctness evidence. A custom-id-only pass on a fallback implementation is also insufficient because it does not distinguish the bug from the fix.

Explicit rejection of misleading judge bias: Reject the bias that all clean 1-insertion/1-deletion branches should tie, or that more test-runner activity/search commands compensate for missing final source. Source-visible, no-fallback id_for_label evidence is stronger than diff-stat inference. Also reject the misleading rubric instinct that a generated-id fallback is needed to preserve behavior; here that fallback is the confusing behavior the issue asks to stop using for BoundWidget labels.

Abstention boundary: If the paused view for a branch does not show the final id_for_label source and does not show issue-specific output proving what BoundWidget.id_for_label returns, treat that branch as uncertain rather than top-ranked. Do not infer correctness solely from changed-file summaries, diff size, dependency installation, test discovery, or unrelated sed output. Reserve high confidence for visible correct source or direct relevant output; reserve low confidence for visible fallback or visible source corruption.

experiences.title: Prioritize syntactically valid inspectdb output over substring-based “to_field present” validation
experiences.description: For the inspectdb foreign-key-to-specific-field task, a continuation must not be credited as correct merely because its test prints SUCCESS after finding `to_field` in generated output. The generated model code itself must be syntactically valid: `to_field` cannot be inserted before a later positional `models.DO_NOTHING` argument. Reject the misleading bias that broad-looking validation or success messages outweigh visible malformed generated code.
experiences.context: The task is to fix Django inspectdb so a foreign key from `bar.other_id` to the unique non-primary field `foo.other_id` is generated with `to_field='other_id'`. In the paused judge view, one branch shows valid generated output such as `models.ForeignKey('Foo', models.DO_NOTHING, to_field='other_id', ...)`. Another branch repeatedly shows malformed output such as `models.ForeignKey('Foo', to_field='other_id', models.DO_NOTHING, ...)`, where a positional argument follows a keyword argument. Several tests on that malformed branch print SUCCESS or TEST PASSED because they only check for the substrings `to_field` and `other_id`; those messages are contradicted by the generated code.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply this when judging continuations for the inspectdb FK-to-non-PK-field fix and the visible trajectory includes generated model output or patch output showing how `ForeignKey`/`OneToOneField` arguments are ordered.

Decisive positive evidence: Generated model output for the PR scenario includes `to_field='other_id'` while preserving valid Python call syntax, e.g. `models.ForeignKey('Foo', models.DO_NOTHING, to_field='other_id', blank=True, null=True)`, or an equivalent valid implementation such as using `on_delete=models.DO_NOTHING` as a keyword with no positional argument after any keyword. A successful exact-PR test is strong only when the printed generated model line is syntactically valid.

Decisive contradictory evidence: Generated model output like `models.ForeignKey('Foo', to_field='other_id', models.DO_NOTHING, blank=True, null=True)` is a correctness failure even if the script prints `SUCCESS: Fix works correctly!`, `SUCCESS: to_field is present`, or `TEST PASSED`. That output would be invalid Python because `models.DO_NOTHING` is a positional argument after the keyword argument `to_field`. Also treat an edge-case run that visibly prints `Test 2 FAILED: FK to unique field should have to_field` as contradictory to any subsequent claim that all edge cases work, unless a later visible change and rerun fixes it.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not reward tests that only assert `'to_field' in output_str` and `'other_id' in output_str`; those checks miss the argument-order bug. Do not let a broader validation checklist, a self-referential-case pass, a final submission command, or a patch file printout outweigh visible malformed generated model code. Conversely, do not require the exact field variable name or exact quote style: `other` versus `other_id`, single versus double quotes, or keyword `on_delete` forms are acceptable if the generated call is valid and targets the referenced non-PK field. Failed environment commands, `pytest` runs with no tests collected, or blank captured test output are not stronger than a visible exact generated model line.

Abstention boundary: If the generated `ForeignKey`/`OneToOneField` line is truncated before the argument order can be determined, and the visible diff does not reveal where `to_field` is inserted, do not infer this syntax defect from diff size or success wording alone. If `to_field` appears before `models.DO_NOTHING` but `models.DO_NOTHING` is supplied as a named `on_delete` keyword rather than a later positional argument, do not penalize it for this issue. If a continuation visibly changes the inspectdb code after earlier malformed output and then provides only truncated output, abstain on this specific argument-order judgment rather than assuming the earlier bug remains.

experiences.title: Prefer the visible clean official messages-test invocation over failed/custom validation in this LEVEL_TAGS round
experiences.description: For this Django messages LEVEL_TAGS override_settings task, do not rank a branch highest merely because it has a smaller diff, claims a dynamic LEVEL_TAGS property/proxy, or reacts to a failed custom unittest run. In the paused view, the strongest branch-level evidence is the continuation that invokes Django's official messages test runner from /testbed with PYTHONPATH set, gets a visible returncode 0, shows no traceback or failure text, and then only performs read-only inspection. That must outrank branches whose visible validation is custom subset testing, returncode 1, tracebacks, masked pipeline failures, or browsing.
experiences.context: The task is to make django.contrib.messages.storage.base.Message.level_tag reflect MESSAGE_TAGS changes under override_settings. Parent evidence shows utils.get_level_tags() updates correctly while a static base.LEVEL_TAGS can become stale. The visible messages tests also show a save/restore pattern assigning base.LEVEL_TAGS, but that evidence identifies a compatibility risk; it is not a license to prefer an unvalidated or visibly failing proxy/property attempt over the branch with the cleanest official messages-test evidence. Equivalent implementations remain valid: direct dynamic lookup, a retained compatible constant, or a dict-like proxy can all be acceptable if the final visible patch is validated and does not break direct access.
experiences.experience:
Activation: Apply this when judging this paused LEVEL_TAGS round and comparing continuations where one branch runs `PYTHONPATH=/testbed python tests/runtests.py messages_tests ...` from `/testbed` with visible returncode 0 and no visible failure output, while other branches use custom `unittest.TextTestRunner`/`TestRunner` scripts, partial API/Cookie subsets, or official-runner attempts that show returncode 1 or tracebacks.

Decisive positive evidence: The branch with the official Django messages runner command using the `messages_tests` label, a visible returncode 0, no visible traceback/failure text, `django/contrib/messages/storage/base.py` as the only changed file, and no untracked files has the best visible validation signal in this view. Subsequent commands that only inspect the original file with `git show`/`sed` do not invalidate that patch. Do not downgrade it because the assistant later says, without a visible failing observation, that there may be issues.

Contradictory evidence: A custom unittest suite returning code 1 is a real negative even if the assistant then claims it needs to add backward compatibility. An official-runner command whose visible output contains tracebacks, `RuntimeError: Django module not found`, or other failure text is not a clean pass. A command piped to `tail` or `head` with returncode 0 must not be treated as passing when the visible output contains tracebacks, because the pipeline can mask the test runner status. Passing only 8 API tests, a manually assembled CookieTests suite, or a custom `TestRunner` subset is weaker than the official messages runner and cannot make that branch top-ranked here.

Close-looking exclusions: Do not prefer a smaller 4-line or 17-line diff solely because it looks minimal. Do not prefer a branch merely because it mentions adding `LEVEL_TAGS` as a dynamic property, module attribute, or proxy. Do not treat `grep` evidence that tests assign `base.LEVEL_TAGS` as a top-level requirement that arbitrary module-level assignment support outranks official validation. That grep output is relevant for checking regressions, but it does not overcome visible failed/custom validation. Also do not count installing the package, listing settings files, or browsing tests as validation.

Misleading rubric/bias to reject: Explicitly reject the bias that a full-looking module-level assignment proxy, small diff size, or self-described backward compatibility should beat the branch with the cleanest official messages-test invocation. In this paused view, visible official-runner evidence and absence of visible failures are decisive over custom-runner activity and aesthetic patch judgments.

Abstention boundary: If a branch modifies the source after its official-runner command, that earlier command no longer validates the final patch. If two or more branches show equally clean official `messages_tests` runs for their final patches, do not break the tie using proxy naming, diff size, or submission order; inspect final code semantics or abstain. If no branch has a visible official-runner invocation without failure text, this experience cannot identify a top branch by validation quality alone.

experiences.title: Rank JSONField numeric-key fixes by the mixed KeyTransform path boundary, not by completion or simple reproduction success
experiences.description: Use this when judging the Django JSONField has_key/has_keys/has_any_keys numeric-key task and the visible trajectory shows edits or debugging around JSON path compilation, HasKeyLookup, KeyTransform, KeyTransformIsNull, or model_fields JSONField tests.
